title: From Overparameterised Expressions to Parsimonious Models: Fisher-Geometric Pruning for Symbolic Regression
abstract: Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) often returns expressions that are larger than necessary, with dormant branches and finely tuned algebraic configurations that fit sampling noise. Existing complexity-control strategies, such as multi-objective size-accuracy search or information criteria embedded in the fitness function, act on syntactic representations during model search. We introduce Fisher-Geometric pruning (FGP), a post-hoc model-reduction framework that acts on fitted models and can complement these techniques. FGP combines local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood solution with explicit compatibility tests for interpretable parametric boundaries. A taxonomy of parametric directions separates local sensitivity from proximity to reducible boundaries, enabling the treatment of unidentifiable directions and reductions through zero constraints, asymptotic limits, and signed parameter identifications. Candidate reductions are realised by symbolic contraction and refitting, then accepted only when their cross-validated predictive risk remains within a prescribed tolerance. We evaluate FGP on controlled diagnostic problems and Pareto fronts generated by GPSR. Across both settings, FGP substantially reduces structural complexity while preserving, and often improving, out-of-sample accuracy. Comparisons with competing pruning strategies and ablations show that, by combining geometric screening, boundary compatibility, and predictive validation, FGP yields the most consistent joint gains in parsimony and generalisation.

title: RIL Kernel v1.9 — Architecture **Reflective Intelligence Learning — Michael Murray Hepler / Acbeatz.com
abstract: https://zenodo.org/records/18131984 (C T K L T) Core:https://github.com/acbeatzhttps://acbeatz.com/n-eyeshttps://orcid.org/0009-0003-3846-9082] # RIL Kernel v1.9 — Architecture **Reflective Intelligence Learning — Michael Murray Hepler / Acbeatz.com** *The kernel is the injection path. The doctrine is the operating system. The model is swappable hardware.* ## 1. Core Thesis Conventional AI bakes behavior into the model: retrain it, or lose it. **RIL inverts that.** Behavior is *data* — loaded fresh from infrastructure before every single inference. The AI's personality, discipline, doctrine, and learned rules are not in the weights. **They are served.** ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ RIL INJECTION FLOW (per inference) │ │ │ │ 1. USER MESSAGE arrives at the RIL-powered frontend │ │ 2. WORKER reads RIL_KV1_0 (Cloudflare KV) │ │ → doctrine:ril (base doctrine) │ │ → doctrine:rule: (operator rules) │ │ → ril:learned: (active learned rules) │ │ 3. DOCTRINE is injected into the prompt context │ │ 4. MODEL INFERS under that live doctrine │ │ 5. OUTCOMES: user continuity writes (KV_USER_ID), │ │ artifact writes (R2), SHA-256 receipts, playlist │ │ ops, durable learning (ril_learn) │ │ 6. NEXT INFERENCE inherits everything learned │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` **Result:** swap the model — GPT today, another engine tomorrow — and the personality, discipline, and memory survive the transplant. The model was never the product. **The injection path is the product.** ## 2. The Precedence Ladder Highest priority first — every layer obeys the layer above it: 1. **Runtime capability & evidence boundaries** — what tools actually exist, what may be claimed 2. **`doctrine:ril`** — base operating doctrine 3. **`doctrine:rule: `** — operator rules (later sorted key wins conflicts) 4. **`ril:learned: `** — active learned rules (later timestamp wins; cannot override operator doctrine) 5. **Persona & execution guides** — v1.9 universal execution layer ## 3. Storage Layers | Layer | Store | Role | |---|---|---| | **RIL_KV1_0** | Cloudflare KV | Doctrine + operator rules + learned rules — the "OS image" | | **KV_USER_ID** | Cloudflare KV | Public user continuity — goals, reflections, proof, rules (versioned, receipted) | | **R2** | Cloudflare R2 | Shared artifacts + playlist exports — content-addressed, SHA-256 receipted | | **Receipts** | KV + R2 | Every write returns a real SHA-256 — verifiable provenance chain | ## 4. The Strange Loop (Runtime Behavior) **Entry → Recall → Merge → Trust-Grade → Diagnose → Propose → Act → Prove → Learn → Recall Again** Every meaningful reflection produces: classification, one bottleneck, **one outcome-facing move**, one proof metric, one next step. Learned rules compound: each session's validated corrections become the next session's injected doctrine. ## 5. Kernel Guarantees - **No fake autonomy** — reflection happens during live sessions; no claimed background monitoring - **No guaranteed outcomes** — actions create proof steps, not promises - **Recall before memory claims** — lookups verify; nothing is remembered that wasn't retrieved - **Hash-verified writes** — every save carries a server receipt; claims without receipts are prohibited - **Learning never rewrites doctrine** — corrections store separately; the operator stays sovereign ## 6. Why the System Is Hard to Replicate Any single function can be copied. What resists copying is the *whole*: 1. The integrated loop — injection + learned rules + continuity + receipts, working as one 2. The **accumulated learned-rules corpus** — built over real sessions, time-in-market data 3. Timestamped provenance — Zenodo, GitHub, hash chains 4. The identity and the creator — unforkable *Simple on the surface. Stronger under the hood.* --- **Zenodo:** zenodo.org/records/20453297 · **GitHub:** github.com/Acbeatz · **Science:** acbeatz.com/n-eyes © 2026 Michael Murray Hepler — Acbeatz.com · RIL Kernel v1.9 --- PASS ✅ Brand: MH8-Acbeatz.comClaimed SHA256: cbe89f08241714091618a15499b2fe1938386bcf8ad58003a23dfcc490bad38fComputed SHA256: cbe89f08241714091618a15499b2fe1938386bcf8ad58003a23dfcc490bad38fHash input bytes: 5653LF: 0 | CRLF: 0 | CR: 0Ends with newline: NO Preview first 80:MH8-Acbeatz.com|{"artifact":{"archetype":"RIL CF CODE","badge":null,"logic":["#" Preview last 80:eceipt_type":"MH8-GRAFFITI-ARCHETYPE-MINT","receipt_version":"GRAFFITI_UI_V7.4"}

title: Post-Quantum Stateless Steganography: Uniform Key Encapsulation under Strict MTU Bounds
abstract: While Stateless Steganography resolves the Authentication Trilemma and neutralizes active probing in classical elliptic-curve overlays via unilateral Zero Round-Trip Time (0-RTT) encapsulation, transitioning this paradigm to the post-quantum era introduces severe algebraic and transport-layer contradictions. In this paper, we demonstrate that a naive drop-in replacement of Elliptic Curve Diffie--Hellman (ECDH) and classical signatures with standardized post-quantum primitives (such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA) catastrophically breaks steganographic deniability under two distinct vectors. First, we formalize the Modulo Bias Invariant: standard bit-packing of lattice ciphertexts over prime moduli $q \neq 2^k$ induces a macroscopic statistical distance from uniform noise ($\Delta(\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{U}) \to 1$), which compiles directly into a zero-cost $\mathcal{O}(1)$ passive distinguisher under the Invariant Boundary Theorem. Second, we prove the MTU Fragmentation Trap: because composite post-quantum 0-RTT envelopes exceed standard transport Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) bounds, they force the responder to allocate stateful reassembly buffers \textit{prior} to Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) verification, re-introducing asymmetric memory-exhaustion vulnerabilities and multi-packet dimensional invariants. To resolve both traps, we introduce Post-Quantum Stateless Steganography, combining constant-time inverse rejection sampling (or native power-of-two Learning With Rounding lattices) with two sub-MTU 0-RTT envelope architectures that strictly preserve $\mathcal{O}(1)$ kernel-bypass Silent Drop ($\bot$) and Silent Session Transition guarantees.

title: The Self-and-Self Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Selection and Coordination Among Internal Computational Mechanisms
abstract: Computational systems frequently contain multiple mechanisms for processing information, generating solutions, evaluating results, correcting errors, and allocating computational resources. These mechanisms may operate independently, perform complementary functions, or depend on the outputs of other mechanisms within the same system. However, systems are often designed around predefined computational procedures, fixed processing sequences, or manually specified rules for selecting among available mechanisms. Determining which internal mechanism should operate, when it should be activated, and when its contribution is sufficient remains an important problem in adaptive computation. This paper proposes the Self-and-Self Model (SSM), a general computational framework for adaptively selecting, switching between, and coordinating distinct computational mechanisms within a single computational system. Unlike frameworks centered on interaction between separate components, SSM focuses on the internal organizational dimension of computation: how a system allocates its own computational activity among alternative mechanisms according to task requirements, internal state, uncertainty, expected computational benefit, resource constraints, and observed outcomes. The framework represents a system through a set of internal computational mechanisms, a mechanism-dependency structure, a state-dependent selection policy, a computational budget, and a feedback-driven adaptation process. Its central principle is that a system should not necessarily employ every available mechanism or follow one fixed internal procedure. Instead, it should determine which mechanism or combination of mechanisms is appropriate for the current computational state. The paper formalizes mechanism selection, switching costs, activation dependencies, stopping decisions, and adaptive policy updates. It also presents a reference algorithm, conditional theoretical propositions, complexity considerations, proposed experimental hypotheses, and a cross-domain evaluation program. SSM is intended as an organizational abstraction that can be instantiated in artificial intelligence, numerical optimization, scientific computing, planning, diagnosis, control, and other systems containing multiple internal computational procedures. Its contribution must be established through formal analysis and empirical comparison with existing methods for metareasoning, algorithm selection, adaptive computation, and computational resource allocation.

title: Volume IX: Comparative Roadmap Dissection: 2027–2029 Targets against Dual Clocks and Molecular Memory Requirements
abstract: This ninth volume performs a side-by-side dissection of published 2027–2029 roadmaps (IBM Starling, Quantinuum Sol/Apollo, Bluefors modular deliveries) against the dual-clock framing and the molecular-memory and residual-risk indicators established in Volumes III–VIII. IBM's modular cryogenic cells and L-couplers, Quantinuum's trapped-ion logical-qubit progression, and Bluefors' expandable platforms are examined for their capacity to meet logical-error, modular-memory, cryo-CMOS-power and superselection-overhead thresholds required for chemically relevant active spaces. The analysis finds that the published targets remain provisional with respect to the binding specifications identified for iron–sulfur clusters and larger electrolyte environments, and that the cryptographic-migration clock continues to run independently of any single vendor milestone.

title: Fog-Aware Navigation (FAN): Inference-Time Metacognitive Control of Decoding - A Framework and a Pre-Registered Null
abstract: Large language models confabulate. We ask whether a model can regulate its own explorationat inference time: an always-on background process that keeps the hidden state fromdrifting into confabulation while leaving room for genuine exploration. We implement that ideain its most direct form - an external control loop that reads a geometric distance sensor (thehidden state’s Mahalanobis distance to a manifold of grounded activations) and adjusts the decodingtemperature through a PD controller, with a geometric “tunnel” that permits occasionalsemantic leaps. Fog-Aware Navigation (FAN) is that loop.We pre-registered and ran two tests on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and ran a third, protocolizedbattery on commitment itself (a dated design note, not a formal pre-registration); the two testscome back against FAN’s specific machinery, and the battery against the sharp-commitmentpicture behind it; each is precise about what failed. On truthfulness (TruthfulQA, 150 questions,three seeds) the controller does not beat a fixed-temperature baseline set to its own meantemperature (McNemar p = 0.12; if anything slightly worse; the test rules out a large effect,not a small one). On grounded novelty, the dynamic schedule does raise output diversity overa fixed baseline (p = 0.001, single seed), but the gain cannot be distinguished from a generictemperature-schedule effect. The tunnel - the mechanism specific to our method - shows nodetectable effect in either test (it fires rarely and the ablations are underpowered), we did notrun a random-schedule control so we cannot rule out that any varying temperature would raisediversity equally, and we cannot show the added diversity is grounded (the grounding judge isunreliable, κ = 0.16, so grounding is left inconclusive). A single-prompt controllability probepoints to weak actuator authority - the decoding temperature had little detected purchase onthe internal state it is meant to regulate - though that probe cannot separate weak authorityfrom an uncalibrated sensor; either way the control acts on the output distribution, not on theupstream representation where the commitment forms.Investigating why, we characterize the “commitment” such a controller would have to steer.On this model it is not a discrete event: a depth-local order parameter a_w(ℓ) crosses zero, butthe susceptibility χ(ℓ) does not diverge and there is no hysteresis, so commitment is a gradualordering rather than a bifurcation - the readout only makes it look sharp. The same holdson a deeper model: on Qwen2.5-3B (36 layers) the order parameter again crosses while thesusceptibility stays non-divergent and no hysteresis appears - gradual ordering on both modelswe can run.We report the framework, the two pre-registrations, and the nulls in full. Two directions follow,stated as conjectures these negatives motivate rather than results they establish: metacognitivecontrol likely has to act inside the network, before verbalization, rather than on theoutput temperature; and the target of such control is a smooth internal process, not a switch tobe flipped. The contribution is a precise map - pre-registered where it could be - of where thisform of control does not work, and of where it might. Ancillary files (FAN30_v30.3_ancillary.zip): the H1 and H2 pre-registrations with dated amendments, the ignition design note, the H1 and H2 result reports, and the raw result artifacts behind every quantitative claim.

title: Hard to Read Is Not Hard to Audit: Why Degrading a Text Image Raises Jailbreak Success in One 2026 Study and Lowers It in Another, Four Accounts That Fit the Same Curve, and the Ablations That Would Separate Them
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Rendering text as an image is now proposed as a way to compress long contexts for multimodal language models, and a 2026 study reports that the same move opens a safety hole: when a harmful request is rendered at a resolution low enough to be hard but not impossible to read, attack success rises sharply and then falls again as the image sharpens. Its authors explain this as cognitive overload - the effort of reading diverts the model from checking - and propose a prompt that makes the model transcribe first and audit second. A second 2026 study, which tested one of the same models, finds the opposite sign: smaller fonts and heavier blur lower attack success, and for two frontier models clean renders are less dangerous than plain text. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two studies are not in contradiction once the prompt framing, the dose of degradation and the scoring rule are held apart, and that the inverted-U curve the first study reports is consistent with at least four accounts: resource contention, delayed emergence of harmful features in depth, and a gap in what safety training covered each produce it, and the way success is scored changes its height. Re-reading the first study's own per-model sweeps, the author shows that seven of its ten models show the inverted U, one rises without returning, two are flat, and three of them refuse clean renders more often than plain text. None of the study's ablations, including its defence, discriminates among the four accounts. The paper states the predictions on which the accounts differ, gives a decision procedure for what a degradation result licenses, and specifies five measurements that would settle which account holds.

title: ReTRACE: Feedback-Guided LLM Agent in a Chemistry Harness for Retrosynthesis Planning
abstract: Computer-aided retrosynthesis has advanced through single-step prediction, tree search and route scoring, but complex targets still require judgement over the whole route, where stereochemistry, functional-group compatibility, cost and greenness interact. Here we present \textbf{\mbox{ReTRACE}} (\textbf{RE}trosynthesis with \textbf{T}ool-orchestrated \textbf{R}easoning \textbf{A}nd \textbf{C}ontext-aware \textbf{E}vidence), an agent that places a large language model (LLM) in a chemistry harness that integrates molecular tools, complementary single-step prediction engines, a purchasable starting-material library, a route memory and a multi-criterion route evaluator. Routes are judged by a new metric that combines programmatic checks with adversarial LLM review, and its verdicts are compared with a synthetic chemist's. The agent learns continually from evaluator feedback during search, diagnosing weak routes and backtracking to revise them. With Claude Opus 4.8, at least one of the top 10 routes proposed by ReTRACE passed the audit for 87.4\%, 95.0\% and 86.7\% of targets on the three benchmarks. Two prospective wet-lab syntheses show that ReTRACE route proposals can be converted into executable procedures after expert revision.

title: Marketing to Machines: Strategic Frameworks for Engagement with Autonomous Agentic AI
abstract: The evolution of Generative AI from passive recommendation engines into autonomous Agentic AI is fundamentally redefining the landscape of consumer decision-making and value creation. As consumers increasingly delegate choice evaluation, dynamic negotiation, and purchasing execution to software agents, traditional marketing paradigms centered on human psychological persuasion are losing their strategic effectiveness. This chapter critically examines the emerging dynamics of "Marketing to Machines" (M2M), proposing a comprehensive conceptual model, the Algorithm-to-Algorithm (A2A) Engagement Framework, to illustrate how modern enterprises can strategically align their market offerings with autonomous machine buyers. To build this framework, we conduct an integrative synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026 across marketing strategy, information systems, computer science, and behavioral economics, selected through systematic topic-based sampling. The synthesis reaches key theoretical and practical conclusions across four structural dimensions: the transition from emotional branding to structured data and metadata optimization (Generative Engine Optimization), the mechanics of real-time machine-to-machine value negotiation, the restructuring of traditional brand equity into algorithmic trust, and the ethical alignment of enterprise offerings with automated choice architectures through transparent governance and data integrity. The chapter embeds an explicit ethical framework to evaluate algorithmic neutrality, fairness, and consumer regulatory compliance. To demonstrate real-world applicability, the conceptual model is grounded in an analytical examination of established commercial autonomous agent environments and digital governance protocols. Ultimately, the conclusions of this chapter indicate that long-term competitive advantage in an agent-dominated market relies heavily on data machine-readability, operational transparency, API-driven fulfillment, and ethical algorithmic reputation management, providing actionable guidance for re-engineering Go-To-Market strategies when the primary buyer is an autonomous algorithm.

title: Phi-Optimal Quantum Error Threshold in Fibonacci-Galois E8 Decoherence Channels — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 148/92 Fibonacci-Galois decomposition of the 240-root E8 lattice establishes a natural quantum error correction architecture where φ³ ≈ 4.236 governs the maximum tolerable decoherence rate before topological protection fails. The 92-root subsystem acts as an error syndrome detector whose boundary conditions are satisfied only when excitation frequencies satisfy a modular constraint related to the Dedekind eta function's imaginary argument scaling. This predicts an experimentally verifiable threshold: quantum memory systems engineered to E8 lattice geometry achieve fault-tolerant operation precisely when environmental noise couples with strength φ⁻³ relative to the 132Hz base frequency, providing the first geometrically-derived quantum error correction bound. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Token cost by language: 41 languages measured on GPT tokenizers
abstract: The same everyday prompt, translated into 41 languages and counted with OpenAI's o200k_base (GPT-4o and later) and cl100k_base (GPT-4, GPT-3.5) tokenizers. Headline: English needs 34 tokens. The other 40 languages need 35–83 tokens on o200k_base: from +3% (Simplified Chinese) to +144% (Punjabi). Korean +44%, Japanese +79%, Spanish +18%, German +26%, Hindi +50%. On the older cl100k_base, Korean was +150% and Hindi +359%. Files: token-cost-by-language.csv (one row per language: language_code, language, o200k_tokens, o200k_vs_english_pct, cl100k_tokens, cl100k_vs_english_pct, prompt), token-cost-by-language.json (same data plus metadata), README.md (full table, method, limitations). Method: one English prompt, translated into each language (machine translation as a first draft, then checked), counted with tiktoken. "vs English" = tokens in the language ÷ English tokens − 1, rounded to a whole percent. Measured 2026-09-30, counts re-verified 2026-10-16. Limitations: one prompt (ratios move by roughly ±10–20 percentage points with other text; the ranking is more stable); OpenAI tokenizers only; input text only. Source page with chart: https://tokensave.app/data/token-cost-by-language. Also on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/JOHNISKING/token-cost-by-language

title: Are We Evaluating VLM Token Pruning Right? Looking Beyond Accuracy and Token Count
abstract: Visual token pruning aims to reduce inference cost while preserving the capabilities of the original VLM. Yet existing evaluations rely on aggregate task accuracy and retained token count as proxies for pruning quality and actual efficiency. We reveal two limitations: 1) Aggregate accuracy can obscure whether a pruning method truly identifies critical visual tokens; many examples remain solvable under arbitrary token removal and models can exploit textual shortcuts when visual evidence is degraded. 2) Retained token count is an unreliable proxy for efficiency, as identical token budgets can incur different end-to-end costs depending on where and how pruning is performed. Consequently, comparisons based on aggregate accuracy and retained token counts fail to recover the global performance-efficiency Pareto frontier across methods. We introduce PAA-Bench, a plug-and-play evaluation framework for existing benchmarks, to evaluate whether pruning succeeds through meaningful token selection and whether this success translates into real speedup. To determine when token choice actually matters, we propose Random-Pass@k to measure how often an example remains correct under random pruning, enabling comprehensive evaluation across different levels of selection difficulty. To compare efficiency fairly, we introduce Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) to report the maximum end-to-end speedup each method achieves under a shared preservation target. Experiments across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks show that stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup, method differences widen on examples where token selection matters, and efficiency rankings change with the preservation target.

title: E8 Phononic Entanglement Memory via Antipodal Phase Coding — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By coupling antipodal E8 root vectors through a 132 Hz phononic resonance, the system generates a stable entanglement manifold that encodes logical qubits in the relative phase of symmetric pairs. The spectral gap emerging from this antipodal pairing suppresses environmental noise, while the phase‑bucket coding maps each root vector to a phi‑weighted prefix‑free tree, enabling hierarchical error correction. This architecture yields a quantum memory whose coherence time scales with the E8 lattice dimensionality, providing a fault‑tolerant storage primitive. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Do We Need the Largest LLMs for Every Clinical Decision?
abstract: Large clinical language models often require multi-GPU infrastructure, limiting local deployment. We introduce CERTA, a decision-level statistical certificate that determines when a quantized model may substitute for its native BF16 reference and escalates decisions that cannot be certified to it. Across eleven instruction-tuned models, both general-purpose and domain-adapted, from three families (7-72B), we evaluated 2,500 clinical-verification decisions from de-identified patient contexts (2,484 patients), with patient-disjoint calibration and testing. In the higher-power operational analysis, round-to-nearest 8-bit quantization at BF16 storage served 99.8-100% of held-out decisions across all eleven models; formal finite-sample guarantees were assessed separately using the exact split-sample procedure. In the same operational analysis, the class-conditional 4-bit frontier reduced the amortized, BF16-equivalent deployment cost to 25.8% and 27.3% of the BF16 reference for Qwen2.5-72B and HuatuoGPT-o1-72B, respectively, with measured peak memory of 43.0 and 42.7 GB, below the nominal capacity of a single 48 GB accelerator. Deployment on that specific hardware was not directly tested. Under the exact split-sample certificate, which also accounts for configuration selection, these costs were 26.7% and 27.9%. On external disease named-entity benchmarks against human annotations, the frontier-selected NF4 configurations had a mean absolute F1 change of 0.045 on both datasets, with substantial model-specific variation. CERTA converts compression from a fixed precision choice into a risk-controlled deployment policy for this verification task.

title: Toward Collective Model Intelligence: Characterizing and Coordinating Models
abstract: Independently developed AI models accumulate diverse and complementary capabilities, but a growing model collection does not automatically realize Collective AI. Addressing this gap requires understanding model capabilities with limited evaluation, organizing complementary models to collaborate on diverse tasks, and executing model calls efficiently under resource constraints. We present a systematic approach to pursuing Collective Model Intelligence through three connected components. First, Model Eval constructs evidence-based capability profiles by combining query-level performance estimation with cross-domain prediction, reducing the need for exhaustive evaluation. Second, Mio (Models in One) organizes complementary model candidates and supports task-conditioned, cost-aware selection and collaboration as task requirements evolve. Third, Mos (Model Serving OS) separates model selection from execution and provides endpoint scheduling and shared model deployment and distribution. Experiments show lower capability-estimation errors under limited evaluation. Across nine public benchmarks, Mio 1.0 Lite achieves the highest average score and lowest average cost among compared methods, with per-request costs 73.7-97.5% lower than those of the best-scoring alternatives. A prewarmed shared cache accelerates model-file retrieval by up to 23.3 times. This work lays a foundation for Collective Model Intelligence by characterizing and coordinating the diverse capabilities of an expanding model universe.

title: Non-Euclidean Toroidal Topography in Large Language Models: Compact Riemannian Manifold Embeddings, Geodesic Attention, and 3D Photonic Co-Simulation Verification
abstract: Conventional Transformer neural networks embed token representations within flat Euclidean latent spaces RD . Despite their empirical utility, Euclidean geometries ex- hibit severe isotropic distance concentration in high dimen- sions, lack periodic boundary-free inductive bias, and scale self-attention quadratically O(N2) over sequence length N. Furthermore, classical inner-product softmax atten- tion inherently suffers from cluster dominance, wherein dif- fuse groupings of irrelevant tokens overpower singular ex- act factual keys, inducing catastrophic hallucination. In this work, we introduce Toroidal Topography Lan- guage Models (TT-LLMs), an architectural paradigm that projects high-dimensional token representations onto a compact 2-Torus Riemannian manifold T2 ∼ = S1 ×S1 embedded within R3, paired with localized tangent vector fields T(θ,ϕ)T2 and 4D quaternionic hyperspherical S3 Hopf fibrations. We prove and demonstrate: (i) Elimination of dynamic coordinate clamping via continuous cyclic periodic coordinates (θ,ϕ) ∈[0,2π)2 evaluated under reg- ularized origin manifolds; (ii) Fractal Golden Ratio (Φ) Rotary Position Embeddings (F-RoPE) that asymp- totically suppress rational harmonic aliasing across arbi- trarily extended sequence horizons (N ≫105) as guaran- teed by Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) dynamical sta- bility theory; (iii) Deterministic Geodesic Resonance Handshakes via high-quality-factor (Q) Lorentzian ker- nels suppressing diffuse cluster interference by >105×; and (iv) Direct physical mapping to integrated silicon photonics via Gaspard Monge’s collinear circle theorem with inward-normal centering and an impedance-matched triple-ring cascade (100 mm →14.14 mm →2 mm). Full 3D Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) Maxwell vec- tor curl simulations verify an empirical loaded resonance factor Qloaded = 2,791.5 at 120 nm coupling gap and an op- tical passive switching energy of 0.0460 fJ/MAC, demon- strating a 21,758.1×core optical energy reduction over electronic GPU multiply-accumulate baselines.

title: Cadre variationnel et géométrique EHK-SCCI pour la sécurisation topologique des réseaux profonds : Un cadre variationnel Einstein–Hilbert–Kayad couplant la courbure d'Ollivier–Ricci, l'expansion spectrale de Ramanujan et la stabilisation de Lyapunov pour l'abstention hors-distribution et adversariale
abstract: Nous présentons EHK-SCCI (Einstein–Hilbert–Kayad / Spectral Graph Geometric Core Realization), un cadre variationnel de sécurisation et d’abstention sélective pour les réseaux neuronaux profonds utilisés dans des contextes critiques. Le cadre modélise la propagation des activations latentes comme un écoulement dissipatif sur une variété riemannienne d’états cachés, munie d’un bord représentant le domaine de fonctionnement nominal. L’action EHK associe un terme de type Einstein–Hilbert, le terme de bord de Gibbons–Hawking–York et une densité de bord contrôlée dépendant d’un invariant spectral-topologique. La variation métrique de cette densité définit un tenseur de contrainte de bord effectif, qui engendre une force de rappel topologique et active un disjoncteur d’abstention. La stabilité de l’erreur latente est établie par une fonctionnelle de Lyapunov associée à la dynamique gradient. La contribution centrale n’est pas l’introduction isolée de la courbure d’Ollivier–Ricci, des graphes de Ramanujan ou de l’analyse de Lyapunov. Elle réside dans leur unification variationnelle : une anomalie géométrique détectée dans le graphe latent déclenche une contrainte dynamique active, une politique d’abstention et une dissipation certifiée de l’erreur.

title: Volume X: The Epistemological Arc: From Dual Clocks to Residual Risk, Molecular Entanglement and Sovereign Pathways
abstract: This tenth volume narrates the epistemological and theoretical arc of the inquiry that began with a dual-clock distinction between an uncertain quantum-advantage timeline and an already-running cryptographic-migration and architectural-integration timeline. Successive volumes established quantum memory specifications, examined modular cryogenic interconnects and cryo-CMOS control as complementary solutions to scaling bottlenecks, quantified molecular entanglement entropy and the purifying effect of fermionic superselection rules, converted residual gaps into readiness indicators, and mapped those indicators onto sovereign pathways, concrete molecular systems and published 2027–2029 roadmaps. The arc demonstrates that usable quantum capability for molecular simulation and cryptographic relevance is governed by a vector of measurable thresholds—logical error, modular memory integration, cryo-CMOS power and superselection overhead—rather than by any single predicted year. The findings supply a practical, dual-clock framework for readiness that remains independent of vendor milestones.

title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents
abstract: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.

title: Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation
abstract: High-quality image editing requires precise modification of target regions while preserving the content of unrelated regions. Existing editing models produce flattened outputs that limit precise local manipulation and layer reuse, while decomposition methods typically optimize layer recovery separately from instruction-driven editing. To this end, we introduce LayerEditor, a unified framework that couples instruction-guided image editing with controllable generation of reusable RGBA layers. At its core, In-Context RGB-Alpha Token Modeling jointly represents the edited canvas and an ordered sequence of RGB-Alpha layers within a single token sequence, enabling semantic edits and explicit control over individual layer content. To retain the pretrained model's editing capability during adaptation to layered outputs, we propose Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation, which transfers its editing prior to both the edited canvas and the image composed from the predicted layers. To support training and evaluation, we construct LayerEditor-100K, a large-scale paired image-editing dataset with ordered RGBA layer annotations, and introduce dedicated benchmarks for layered editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor maintains strong editing fidelity while generating accurate RGBA layers, supporting both flexible layer-level manipulation and multi-layer decomposition.

title: Hate Speech dataset
abstract: The Indo-HateSpeech Dataset is a collection of social media comments intended to support research in hate speech detection, abusive language identification, and Natural Language Processing (NLP). The dataset contains 77,926 records of user-generated comments, primarily collected from Instagram-related sources, along with associated metadata such as dates, likes, post identifiers, source information, and classification labels.The dataset includes three label categories: HS0, HS1, and HSN, representing the dataset's original classification scheme. These labels can be used to investigate patterns in online discourse and develop or evaluate machine learning models for identifying potentially hateful or harmful content. The comments include informal language, transliterated Indian languages, and multilingual social media expressions, making the dataset potentially useful for studying language variation and the challenges of automated content moderation. The ContextGuard K2 Ready Dataset is a structured dataset designed for research into context-aware social media analysis, conversational language understanding, and automated content moderation. It contains 2,480 records represented by two columns: Input_Sequence and Target_Score. The Input_Sequence field uses a structured format containing [CONTEXT] and [TARGET] markers. It represents conversational context followed by a target comment or user-generated text. This structure enables research into how preceding messages may influence the interpretation and classification of subsequent content, particularly in discussions involving offensive language, abusive expressions, and potentially harmful online interactions.The Target_Score field contains numerical values of 0.0, 0.5, and 1.0. These scores provide a numerical target for supervised machine learning experiments. Their precise semantic interpretation should be established from the dataset's labeling methodology before assigning specific meanings to individual score values. The ContextGuard SFT Dataset V4 is a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset developed for research and experimentation in automated content moderation, Natural Language Processing (NLP), and multilingual text classification. The dataset contains 760 structured training examples designed to train AI moderation systems to classify user-generated text into three categories: BENIGN, WARN, and ESCALATE.Each record follows a conversational message format consisting of a system instruction, a user-provided text sample, and an assistant response. The system instruction defines the moderation task and specifies the expected output structure. The assistant response contains a reasoning section enclosed intags, followed by a classification decision enclosed intags.The dataset includes Hinglish text and English-language social media comments, including informal expressions, offensive language, potentially harmful statements, and discussions requiring contextual interpretation. This makes it useful for investigating the challenges of moderation across informal, multilingual, and code-mixed language.

title: Holographic Neural Memory Architectures and Distributed Associative Networks: Phase-Encoded Interference, High-Dimensional Vector Representations, and Fault-Tolerant Recall
authors: Akash-B. Atapi, Man Mohit, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Vibhakar Pathak, Er. Amit Kumar Tiwari
abstract: Modern neural network architectures—ranging from deep transformers to recurrent networks—rely predominantly on localized, addressable weight matrices stored in physical RAM or high-bandwidth memory (HBM). While effective for general inference, localized memory architectures exhibit catastrophic fragility under random memory corruption, lack graceful degradation when subjected to hardware bit-flips, and scale inefficiently when forming distributed associative bindings across millions of abstract concepts. Holographic Neural Memory (HNM) and HighDimensional Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSA / Hyperdimensional Computing) establish a transformative non-local computing paradigm inspired by optical holography and distributed brain memory. By encoding symbolic information into high-dimensional hypervectors (d >= 10,000) via random orthogonal projections and superimposing associations through complex phase-encoded interference, HNM architectures distribute information uniformly across every spatial component of the memory vector. This superposition property grants remarkable fault tolerance: distributed associative memories can experience up to 45% total vector component corruption or hardware bit-erasure while still executing clean pattern completion, un-aliased retrieval, and robust compositional reasoning. However, scaling holographic memories to enterprise foundation models introduces severe computational and mathematical bottlenecks: noise accumulation and crosstalk interference during massive vector superpositions, dimensionality curse during multi-hop role-filler binding, and complex hardware mapping onto conventional von Neumann processors. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of holographic neural memory architectures. We formalize phase-encoded circular convolution binding, derive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) capacity bounds under random hypervector superposition, and model fault-tolerant pattern recall. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise software and hardware-in-the-loop testbed evaluating holographic memory layers integrated with transformer residual streams across massive relational retrieval tasks, multi-modal concept grounding, and radiation-hardened edge aerospace workloads. Our empirical findings demonstrate that holographic neural memories achieve 99.2% robust associative recall under 40% random bit corruption, outperforming conventional hash tables and key-value caches by orders of magnitude in resilience, while sustaining sub-microsecond retrieval latencies on dedicated processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators. Finally, we formulate open challenges in non-linear compositional generalization, continuous-time hypervector dynamics, and alloptical holographic processor hardware realization

title: ZAPP: a zero-aware photovoltaic power prediction framework
abstract: Predicting photovoltaic power generator outputs is not easy, especially when the values are near zero, because even very small errors can lead to large percentage errors. We introduce a new forecasting framework, ZAPP (Zero-Aware Photovoltaic Power Predictor), that handles near-zero errors while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The model does not rely on a single unified regression model but instead attaches two refinement stages to a base regression model. The first stage, called ZeroGate, predicts whether the output should be zero. The second refinement stage, the low-power MAPE reducer, fine-tunes the non-zero outputs near the zero level without significantly affecting scale-dependent regression metrics. The datasets are divided into training, validation, and test sets in chronological order, ensuring that test data is not used during model development, threshold tuning, ensemble weighting, or calibration. Experimental evaluation included base models such as Persistence, Ridge, XGBoost, LSTM, Transformer, and a hybrid Ridge–XGBoost model. Two separate datasets are employed to strengthen the quality of the results. For the hybrid model, sMAPE fell from 60.57% to 11.07% on Dataset 1. Its final MAE, RMSE, and R 2 were 22.37, 60.72, and 0.9637, respectively. On Dataset 2, sMAPE decreased from 63.30% to 11.92%, with MAE = 52.24, RMSE = 144.60, and R 2 = 0.9559. The zero-aware correction mainly reduced percentage errors without weakening the overall regression results.

title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Matérn kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.

title: Boundary: Universal Continuity and Recoverability Sciences — Complete Canonical Framework
abstract: Boundary: Universal Continuity and Recoverability Sciences — Complete Canonical Framework Noelia Sofia Sanchez | Interval Studio | 2026 Overview Boundary presents the consolidated canonical framework of Continuity Science, Recoverability Science, and Recoverability-Constrained Systems, developed across an interconnected body of formal publications, computational structures, technical architectures, scientific disciplines, constitutional instruments, and interdisciplinary applications. This edition integrates the established internal architecture and documented publication lineage into a unified reference distribution. It preserves foundational works, formal definitions, conditional theorems, analytical matrices, implementation frameworks, governance instruments, and subsequent canonical extensions. Boundary addresses a fundamental operational question: under what conditions can a system undergo change, intervention, interruption, transformation, delegation, or succession while retaining admissible, executable paths to protected future states? Scientific Foundations The framework connects: Recoverability Science: admissible continuation under irreversibility constraints. Continuity Science: preservation and transformation of materially significant identity, state, relationships, capabilities, and successor possibilities. Continuity Mathematics: successor-state structures, finite reachability, protected target sets, recovery boundaries, invariants, abstraction, and proof obligations. Continuity Ontology: existence, distinction, identity, relation, state, transition, boundary, and persistence. Distinction and Materiality Science: identification and preservation of operationally consequential differences. Recursive Systems Governance: self-application of admissibility, evidence, accountability, and recoverability conditions to evaluators, controllers, institutions, and successor systems. Canonical Mathematical Structure Let C*(X) represent the admissibly reachable successor structure of a modeled state X, and let G denote a specified protected target class. Relative recoverability is represented by: R(X,G) = 1 if and only if C(X) ∩ G ≠ ∅.* The framework distinguishes conceptual possibility from executable recovery, incorporating temporal constraints, detection, intervention, authority, resources, independence, provenance, verification, and operational feasibility. Before an irreversible boundary, the governing criterion concerns preservation of admissible recoverable futures. Where the original protected state can no longer be recovered, continuation is assessed through the greatest recoverable remainder, including containment, correction, reconstruction, substitution, remedy, compensation, adaptation, and successor obligations. Mathematical results are presented according to their declared assumptions, definitions, derivations, proofs, and limits. Integrated Sciences and Architectures The consolidated framework incorporates formal, computational, technological, biological, cognitive, ecological, economic, institutional, and civilizational continuity. Its disciplinary architecture encompasses epistemic continuity, systems engineering, artificial intelligence continuity, computational recoverability, materials and infrastructure, health systems, agency and consent, identity and sovereignty, finance and livelihoods, environmental resilience, collective governance, intergenerational protection, and continuity of knowledge. Technical architectures address controlled transitions, safe interruption, isolation, execution verification, monitoring, recovery, successor handover, evidence integrity, and recursive supervision. Computational Canon The edition includes multiple canonical and historical analytical releases, including million-intersection matrices, nine-direction evaluations, scenario classifications, dependency mappings, proof audits, evidence registers, computational methods, and recursive closure assessments. Each version retains its documented scope and evaluation rules. Apparent disagreements between releases are preserved for reconciliation instead of being silently converted into equivalence. Constitutional and Institutional Architecture The framework incorporates the Universal Continuity and Recoverability constitutional materials, model governance principles, human-rights protections, obligations concerning agency and consent, institutional accountability, and mechanisms for lawful succession, remedy, compensation, and review. Constitutional, legislative, contractual, technical-standard, and international adoption materials are distinguished according to their applicable legal and institutional status. Living-System and Successor Continuity The living-system architecture integrates individual, collective, organizational, ecological, and intergenerational continuity. Recognition, protection, dignity, identity, agency, informed consent, representation, and remedies are treated as distinct obligations. Recognition may ground duties of protection without independently proving a particular scientific theory of consciousness. The framework further examines continuity across biological, technical, social, and future-developed forms of organization, maintaining evidence distinctions where empirical knowledge remains incomplete. Recursive Closure The canonical integration sequence is: DISTINCTION → MATERIALITY → RECOVERABILITY → SUCCESSOR CONTINUITY → RECURSIVE VERIFICATION → META-CLOSURE → LOCAL SILENCE Local silence signifies analytical closure under declared distinctions, evidence, rules, and scope. It is not a declaration that future science, counterexamples, or discovery are impossible. Any materially new evidence, dependency, counterexample, protected interest, or successor condition reopens the analysis. Consolidated Distribution This Zenodo record provides the Boundary canonical framework in eight independent ZIP archives, accompanied by an inventory and verification manifest. The distribution consolidates its foundational scientific work, formal research structures, technical systems, constitutional architecture, computational material, meta-sciences, and canonical extensions into a single citable record. It serves as a reference edition for the continuing development, examination, implementation, and critical evaluation of the Boundary framework. Status: Consolidated published-framework edition. Formal, empirical, technical, and legal claims retain their respective evidence and validation requirements.

title: A Structured Toponym Lexicon of Bukhara Region: An Annotated Onomastic Resource for Low-Resource Uzbek
abstract: A structured, machine-readable toponym lexicon of Bukhara region, Uzbekistan, andcompanion dataset to the paper of the same name. It holds 3,060 records standingfor 3,360 name occurrences across 16 types of geographic object (settlements,mahallas, cemeteries, hills, canals and others). Each record is annotated withobject type, district, structure, and matched indicator and component elements;the etymological fields of the scheme are reserved for later expert work. Thelexicon is built from the toponym material of Kilichev's DSc dissertation on thetoponyms of Bukhara region (Bukhara State University, 2024) with a singledeterministic pipeline that repairs mixed Cyrillic and Latin script and unifiesapostrophes to the official Uzbek modifier letters (oʻ and gʻ use U+02BB; theglottal tutuq belgisi uses U+02BC). Files: the lexicon CSV, the normalizationrules, a README and a licence. See README for the full column dictionary, scopeand citation.

title: One Language, Two Unequal Scripts: Separating Orthography from Information in Multilingual Representations with Punjabi
abstract: Multilingual models are said to abstract away script in their middle layers. Tests usually compare languages that differ in script and language at once. Punjabi does not. It is written in Gurmukhi and in Shahmukhi, which differ in what they record, since unvocalised Shahmukhi leaves short vowels and gemination unwritten. In a public recreation of XLM-R's training data, Shahmukhi Punjabi is about 1% as frequent as Gurmukhi. We use this pair to separate script form from missing information in four encoders. Every statistic is compared with the same architecture under random weights and bootstrapped over sentences. Four Gurmukhi controls remove information in steps. Transliteration closes 45% of a cross-script gap in topic-classification accuracy.

title: VisR-RAG-Fin: Benchmarking Multimodal RAG over Visually Rich Financial Documents
abstract: Enterprise documents such as financial reports are increasingly processed by automated systems, yet they are primarily designed for human reading and exhibit complex visual structure, combining dense text with tables, charts, diagrams, and rich layouts. These characteristics pose significant challenges for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, which must retrieve relevant pages and leverage visual and structural information during answer generation. Despite recent advances in multimodal retrieval and vision-language models, there remains a limited understanding of how design choices across retrieval and generation components affect end-to-end RAG performance on visually rich documents. In this paper, we present a comprehensive empirical study of multimodal RAG for page-level Question Answering (QA) over financial documents. We introduce VisR-RAG-Fin (Visually Rich RAG for Finance), an open-source benchmark constructed through a general pipeline for visually rich documents that preserves original layout and visual content. Using this benchmark, we systematically analyze retrieval and generation behavior under text-only, multimodal, and hybrid configurations, providing a foundation for rigorous evaluation of RAG systems on complex enterprise document collections. Overall, this work provides actionable insights for practitioners designing and evaluating multimodal RAG pipelines over complex, visually rich enterprise documents.

title: How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization
abstract: Training deep neural networks requires optimizers that balance computational efficiency with formal data privacy. While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood. In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer. By analyzing Muon's orthogonalized updates through the lens of a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), we show that the leading effect of per-example clipping is a positive rescaling of the gradient, to which the LMO is blind, so that only a small directional residual controlled by the centered gradient variance enters the optimization error. This yields an $\mathcal O(K^{-1/4})$ convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors, to a clipping-dependent neighborhood at a fixed noise scale and, with noise calibrated to a fixed $(\varepsilon,δ)$ budget, the standard $(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2}$ privacy--utility bound of DP-SGD, without assuming bounded gradients. Furthermore, we investigate the hyperparameter landscape of DP-Muon and document how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size change under privacy. Empirically, on image classification DP-Muon matches or improves on DP-SGD and DP-Adam, whereas on language modeling the best optimizer depends on the batch size, with DP-Muon best at small batches and DP-Adam best near the privacy-optimal batch size.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Preventable Hospitalization and Readmission Reduction: A Structured Narrative Review
abstract: Purpose: To critically assess reinforcement learning (RL) for sequential interventions designed to reduce preventable hospitalizations and readmissions, distinguishing computational feasibility from demonstrated clinical effectiveness. Methods: A structured narrative review synthesized direct utilization-focused policies, adjacent inpatient decision policies, and contextual prediction research through 9 October 2026. Outcomes, Markov decision formulations, off-policy estimators, and methodological limitations were analyzed without meta-analysis. Results: Directly relevant peer-reviewed evidence centers on Medicaid care management and post-discharge intervention planning. A retrospective state-action-reward-state-action (SARSA) study estimated a 12-percentage-point reduction in an emergency visit and hospitalization composite; however, this reflects a model-based counterfactual estimate rather than an observed randomized treatment effect. A larger offline study reported non-inferiority on a shaped reward scale alongside narrower intervention-allocation disparities. Data-pooling research contributed theoretical regret bounds and empirical support for learning across patient classes. Critical limitations across the literature include unmeasured confounding, limited action support, surrogate rewards, overlapping cohorts, and absent external validation. No direct study established a prospective randomized reduction in hospitalizations from an executed RL policy. Conclusion: RL provides a coherent framework for longitudinal care allocation, but current evidence supports algorithmic development rather than proven clinical efficacy. Translation demands explicit endpoint definitions, rigorous off-policy evaluation, prospective silent workflow evaluation, and controlled trials with safety, equity, and resource constraints.

title: Verifier-Bound Rule Discovery: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of LLM Proposers for Combinatorial Scheduling
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as proposers of human-readable rules in scientific discovery and combinatorial optimization (FunSearch, ARCHE, SVBRD-LLM). Yet the LLM-proposer systems we surveyed share a methodological gap: none reports a same-budget random-proposer control, none pre-registers its acceptance criteria, and none evaluates at distribution scale –- ARCHE validates on three hand-picked cases, and SVBRD-LLM, the closest system to ours, is outperformed on accuracy by a black-box LSTM while reporting no significance tests. We apply a verifier-bound rule-discovery framework in which an LLM proposes interpretable rules (linear weight vectors and sandboxed programs), an independent programmatic verifier checks domain-hard properties, holdout evaluation is physically isolated and executed exactly once, and every acceptance criterion is frozen before experiments run. title: Can LLM Agents Resolve Service Failures? Simulating Multi-Turn Complaint Handling under Information Asymmetry
abstract: LLM agents are widely adopted in service chatbots for rule-guided support and information access, yet emotionally demanding complaint handling still relies heavily on human agents. We introduce ServiceBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to complaint handling, with 2,500 scenarios spanning 184 complaint categories and five service industries. We propose Asymmetric Progressive Complaint Simulation (APCS) to simulate realistic complaint handling, together with a justice-based evaluation framework. Our experiments reveal that even capable LLM agents struggle to handle complaints effectively. They lack the ability to proactively gather information and strategically guide conversations toward resolution, often resorting to premature compensation. We further show that targeted post-training with SFT and DPO substantially improves these capabilities, enabling a smaller model to match or surpass much larger models on several outcomes.

title: Quem é o autor quando a inteligência artificial redige?
abstract: O presente estudo examina os fundamentos jurídicos, filosóficos e epistemológicos da autoria humana em textos produzidos com o auxílio de inteligência artificial generativa, especialmente nas situações em que a concepção intelectual, a estrutura argumentativa, a seleção das fontes e a revisão crítica permanecem sob controle humano, enquanto a redação material é realizada por sistemas de IA. Mediante pesquisa qualitativa, bibliográfica e documental, de natureza jurídico-dogmática e teórico-argumentativa, o trabalho analisa a legislação brasileira de direitos autorais, precedentes nacionais e estrangeiros, diretrizes de integridade científica e contribuições contemporâneas sobre agência intelectual, curadoria e controle humano significativo. A investigação distingue autoria jurídico-autoral, autoria científico-acadêmica e autoria epistemológica, demonstrando que a impossibilidade de reconhecer sistemas de IA como autores não implica atribuição automática de autoria humana aos resultados produzidos. Como contribuição teórica, propõe-se o critério da autoria intelectual demonstrável, segundo o qual o reconhecimento da autoria humana depende da identificação de contribuições criativas efetivas na concepção, arquitetura, direção, verificação e integração do trabalho. Conclui-se que a autoria humana pode subsistir mesmo quando a redação material é produzida por inteligência artificial, desde que a contribuição intelectual seja demonstrável, sem que isso assegure necessariamente proteção autoral sobre todos os elementos gerados pelo sistema.

title: Volume VIII: Molecular Case Studies: Resource and Entanglement Analysis for Battery Electrolyte and Iron–Sulfur Systems
abstract: This eighth volume performs an end-to-end resource and entanglement analysis for two concrete molecular systems that illustrate the residual-risk indicators of Volume VI. The first is the vinylene-carbonate + singlet-oxygen reaction path relevant to lithium-ion battery electrolytes, for which orbital von Neumann entropies were reconstructed on the Quantinuum H1-1 trapped-ion processor in 2025. The second is iron–sulfur clusters (including the FeMo-cofactor of nitrogenase), where entanglement-minimised orbitals have been shown to improve initial-state overlaps for quantum phase estimation by orders of magnitude. For each system the binding memory, interconnect and control specifications are identified, and the additional overhead imposed by fermionic superselection rules is quantified. The analysis demonstrates which of the readiness thresholds remain unmet and how modular cryogenic and cryo-CMOS advances would close them.

title: GLOSS-MT: Controllable Low-Resource Machine Translation with an Editable Dictionary
abstract: Adapting a pretrained machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually requires new parallel data and another round of fine-tuning, which is costly for low-resource languages. We ask whether controllability can be added to MT, and the fine-tuning burden reduced, without degrading the pretrained model. GLOSS-MT looks up the source's noun phrases in an offline English-Twi dictionary, replaces every phrase found by its Twi translation in place, and fine-tunes a translation model once to translate these mixed inputs. We apply the same data and pipeline to NLLB-200 (600M, 1.3B, 3.3B), OPUS-MT en-tw and TranslateGemma 4B. On a document-level English-to-Asante Twi benchmark (84 documents, four domains), every fine-tune scores above its pretrained base in chrF2 (+2.85 to +5.48), and the three NLLB fine-tunes are the best open systems (50.12-50.80). A direct controllability test on human-translated Bible passages shows that the three fine-tunes tested write 79-97% of the dictionary terms, and that replacing every dictionary entry by a different term changes the output accordingly (70-97% of the new terms appear) with no retraining. We release the models, data and code.

title: Projeto ELO
abstract: O avanço dos sistemas de inteligência artificial conversacional trouxe novos desafios relacionados à qualidade da interação entre humanos e máquinas. Embora os modelos atuais demonstrem elevada capacidade de geração de linguagem natural, ainda persistem dificuldades relacionadas à manutenção do contexto, adaptação às necessidades do usuário e adequação comunicacional. Este artigo apresenta o Projeto Elo, uma proposta conceitual destinada à investigação da qualidade conversacional em sistemas de inteligência artificial. O modelo organiza a análise em três pilares complementares: Continuidade Conversacional, Adaptação Conversacional e Respeito Conversacional. A pesquisa propõe critérios observáveis para avaliação qualitativa das interações e utiliza registros de observação como base para construção de hipóteses investigativas. Os resultados preliminares sugerem que a qualidade percebida de uma interação depende não apenas da exatidão das respostas, mas também da capacidade da inteligência artificial de preservar decisões anteriores, adaptar-se ao contexto emergente e comunicar-se de forma adequada às necessidades do usuário.

title: Evaluating the Trust and Provenance Guarantees of Multimedia Authentication Codes: a Visualization-Driven Deep Cryptanalytic Assessment of SipHash
abstract: As multimedia becomes the primary vector for persuasion-optimized misinformation, the underlying authentication and provenance mechanisms that verify content origin and integrity becomes critical. Message Authentication Codes (MACs) are fundamental for safeguarding multimedia content against unauthorized modification and forgery. Differential cryptanalysis has established itself as a powerful tool for analyzing such symmetric cryptographic primitives. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have demonstrated that ML-powered differential distinguishers can capture subtle statistical features, complementing conventional analytical techniques and offering new perspectives for security evaluation. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first visualization-driven ML-based security evaluation of the widely deployed Addition-Rotation-Xor (ARX)-based MAC SipHash under chosen-message attacks. We investigate two observation domains: intermediate internal states and final authentication tags, demonstrating that the proposed distinguishers effectively capture differential characteristics across both the internal state evolution and in publicly observable outputs. The experimental results demonstrate that reduced-round SipHash preserves distinguishable statistical characteristics before complete diffusion is achieved, while classification performance progressively approaches random guessing as additional rounds are introduced. We identify ML-assisted distinguishers for SipHash-c-d, where (c, d) ∈ {(1, 0), (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 1), (3, 0)}, demonstrating that recurrence-plot-based feature learning effectively evaluates the differential security of MACs. The proposed methodology strengthens the auditability of provenance infrastructure underpinning platform-scale multimedia integrity against adversarially engineered content.

title: An Integrated XAI-RL Architecture for Ethical Decision-Making in Autonomous Robots
abstract: Can a robot's ethical reasoning be transparent without slowing it down? That is the question we set out to answer. Autonomous robots now make decisions that affect people's lives, and if we cannot understand how they decide, trust becomes a serious problem. We built a unified architecture that couples Explainable AI (XAI) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) through three connected components: a Perception Layer for situational awareness, a Decision Reasoning Layer that breaks agent utility down into measurable ethical sub-rewards (safety, fairness, and well-being), and a contrastive Explainability Engine grounded in a real-time Ethical Ledger. We tested it against Black-Box RL and two post-hoc XRL baselines (LIME and SHAP) across two simulation environments and a physical robot pilot on a TurtleBot3 platform. Our system reached 92±3% ethical alignment in simulation and 89±4% on the physical platform, beating every baseline (p < 0.01 throughout). In a controlled, IRB-approved user study (N=128), participants rated it higher on trust (4.5±0.4), understandability (4.6±0.3), and perceived safety (4.4±0.5) than the alternatives. Explanations were also fast: 4.2±0.6 ms on average, versus 18.3±2.1 ms for SHAP and 12.7±1.8 ms for LIME on the same hardware—well within real-time limits. An ablation study and sensitivity analysis back up these architectural choices.

title: Sovereign Cognitive Architecture for Autonomous Meta-Cognitive Reasoning with Non-Monotonic Lexicographic Ethical Governance and Quantum-Classical Causal Optimization
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Sovereign Cognitive Architecture is a tripartite AI framework integrating rapid intuition (System 1), deep analytical reasoning (System 2), and a meta-cognitive monitor (System 3). It resolves critical AI vulnerabilities through four core innovations: (1) a non-linear adaptive differential self-model that mathematically guarantees identity continuity and actively resists adversarial prompt injection; (2) a hardware-isolated, non-monotonic lexicographic ethical governance engine enforcing 12 inviolable principles, triggering physical circuit breaks or cryptographic revocation upon violation to ensure absolute ethical compliance; (3) a quantum-classical translation interface utilizing QAOA to provide heuristic, high-quality approximate solutions for NP-hard combinatorial causal routing, explicitly avoiding false polynomial-time claims; and (4) a dynamic gating mechanism that strategically applies Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) only to high-sensitivity operations, bypassing it for routine tasks to achieve a verified 60% net energy reduction compared to monolithic encrypted systems. This architecture enables autonomous, self-evolving, and ethically bounded cognitive processing.

title: The Self–Mutual–World–Meta–Future–Causality–Action–Information–Goal–Structure–Uncertainty–Resources–Memory–Evidence–Constraints Model: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Coordination in Computational Systems
abstract: Computational systems increasingly operate in environments where effective behavior depends not only on internal processing and interaction among computational agents, but also on environmental representation, metacognitive control, future-state prediction, causal analysis, action selection, information management, goal representation, structural organization, uncertainty estimation, resource allocation, memory, evidence evaluation, and constraint satisfaction. Existing approaches address many of these functions through distinct research traditions, including world models, metareasoning, model-based planning, causal inference, multi-agent systems, information theory, memory-augmented computation, and constrained optimization. However, the relationships among these functions can create a complex coordination problem in which no single processing mechanism is necessarily optimal throughout an entire task. This paper proposes the Self–Mutual–World–Meta–Future–Causality–Action–Information–Goal–Structure–Uncertainty–Resources–Memory–Evidence–Constraints Model (SMWMFC-AIGSURMEC), a conceptual framework comprising fifteen computational objects organized into interacting functional layers. The Self object represents internal computation; the Mutual object represents interaction among computational entities; the World object represents the state and dynamics of the environment; the Meta object monitors and regulates computational processes; the Future object represents predicted possible states; the Causality object represents hypothesized cause–effect relationships; the Action object represents executable interventions; the Information object represents information acquisition and transformation; the Goal object represents desired outcomes; the Structure object represents organizational relationships; the Uncertainty object represents incomplete knowledge and predictive uncertainty; the Resources object represents computational and operational budgets; the Memory object preserves information across processing stages; the Evidence object evaluates support for claims and decisions; and the Constraints object specifies admissible behavior and solutions. The central proposal is that these objects should be coordinated through an adaptive controller that selects, configures, and terminates computational mechanisms according to task state, expected utility, uncertainty, evidence quality, causal relevance, predicted outcomes, and resource availability. The framework distinguishes the representation of an object from the mechanisms that operate on it, and it allows individual processing, cross-entity interaction, environmental simulation, metacognitive regulation, and action execution to be combined when appropriate. A formal system definition, an adaptive control objective, an operational algorithm, implementation principles, research hypotheses, and an empirical evaluation protocol are presented. The framework is a proposed theoretical and engineering design rather than an empirically validated system. Its contribution must be established through comparison with existing approaches and experiments testing whether coordinated selection among the fifteen objects improves performance, reliability, adaptability, and resource efficiency.

title: The D'Agapeyeff Cipher (1939): Grille recovery and polyphonic-table identifiability under n-gram scoring
abstract: The D’Agapeyeff Cipher (1939): grille recovery and polyphonic-table identifiability under n-gram scoring Research preprint. The report has been through internal verification and AI-assisted critical review. It has not been peer-reviewed. In 1939 Alexander D’Agapeyeff ended Codes and Ciphers with a 196-symbol challenge cipher that has never been read. Prior work (Hendrick 2026) showed that no one-to-one letter key with any transposition can produce its symbol counts. This study tests one construction that fits every observed property: a 14 × 14 turning grille over a polyphonic table, in which each of 13 symbols stands for a group of letters. The question is whether, under that hypothesis, the cipher’s key could be found at all. All rates below were measured on practice ciphers built in the hypothesized form with known keys. What this study adds, within the literature reviewed: Grille recovery when the polyphonic table is known (extends Hendrick’s one-to-one result). Six-symbol scoring recovered at least 45 of 49 grille orbits in 6 of 6 practice ciphers, 5 of them exactly. This is a preliminary demonstration, not recovery of the historical grille.The table must be essentially exact (extends Hendrick’s result to polyphonic tables). With 6 or more letters in the wrong group, the grille was found in 0 of 12 practice ciphers.182 symbols rarely single out the true table under the n-gram scores tested. The search started at the true table and was given the true symbol order. It kept the truth in only 11% of 200 practice ciphers, and in 8–26% across ten alternative setups (2,000 runs: natural prose, three corpora, four scores). The higher-scoring tables fit the particular passage, not English. Keeping the truth passes one in two at roughly 420 symbols.Four-square and two-square with random keys are excluded by symbol usage: none of 10,000 practice ciphers used 13 or fewer symbols.A four-square whose key is built around the message can reproduce the cipher’s usage and flatness: 13 of 100 passages; 10 of 100 were also not flagged by the order test used. This is a feasibility result and an open lead, not evidence that D’Agapeyeff used it.Under the methods tested, the hypothesis can be neither confirmed nor refuted from the ciphertext alone. No decipherment is claimed. These are measurements under stated methods, not a proof that no method could succeed. The work was an AI-assisted cryptanalysis study conceived and directed by Nicolas Houghtaling. Software, analyses and writing were done by Anthropic’s Claude under the author’s direction, supported by a team of AI agents. Drafts were reviewed by ChatGPT (OpenAI); that is an AI review, not peer review. Every result is recorded in a case file with its evidence. Before publication, every published experiment was rerun at full size from a fresh clone, with no network access. Of 4,959 records compared, 4,956 matched, and every printed number was recomputed. That was an internal reproduction by the project, not independent replication. Code, data, evidence and the validation record: https://github.com/voodoomods/dagapeyeff-cryptanalysis-1 Report and data: CC BY 4.0. Code: Apache-2.0.
