title: Compliant-by-Construction Hybrid Medical AI Workflows via Located Task Graphs
abstract: Abstract Hybrid artificial intelligence workflow s for medical imaging combine heterogeneous ingredients: public and private datasets, neural training, prediction, symbolic post-processing, spatial model checking, human assessment, and controlled circulation of results. Regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act impose strict requirements on high-risk AI systems, including those used in medical contexts, demanding transparency, traceability, and human oversight throughout the pipeline. In such regulated settings, the main difficulty is not only to obtain accurate predictions, but to make the procedure itself sufficiently explicit: where data belongs, where computation is performed, which artifacts may be moved, who can read them, and which human assessments are required before further use. We present the design of a lightweight calculus of located task graphs for compliant-by-construction hybrid AI workflow s. A program is reduced to a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are primitive operations (logical, non-logical, or AI-based such as training and prediction), and additionally, featuring assessment as a primitive, and whose edges are data dependencies. Each term is located along several dimensions: storage location, computation location, and institutional or regulatory context. The calculus is proposed at a conceptual level, leaving a complete formal semantics for future work. We illustrate how our calculus can support a design discipline for making compliance-relevant structure part of an executable specification in a medical-imaging case study.

title: Where Natural Language Ends in Agents: Executable Skill Composition with MetaSkill
abstract: Agent Skills express open-ended task knowledge in natural language, but composing them requires persistent execution order and upstream-output handoffs. We propose selective formalization at Skill boundaries: coordination relations with stable references and machine-checkable constraints become executable, while substantive task judgments remain within Skills. We introduce MetaSkill, a hybrid representation that preserves complete Skill packages and local instructions while making invocation dependencies and predecessor-text bindings executable through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) runtime. This interface supports explicit coordination without prescribing how each Skill performs its local task. Across 20 multi-Skill artifact tasks and two LLMs, we compare natural-language procedures, prompt-visible graphs, and MetaSkill derived from a common frozen plan per task, using the same designated Skill packages. Additional comparisons evaluate AgentSkillOS with the same available Skill packages as MetaSkill, as well as agent systems using their configured tools. Blinded artifact judgments yield favorable preference point estimates across all reported comparisons, with 95% task-bootstrap intervals excluding parity against Prompt Graph under DeepSeek-V4-Flash and OpenClaw under GLM-5.2. In audited GLM-5.2 execution traces, all planned nodes complete and all declared precedence constraints are satisfied. Together, these findings support MetaSkill as a practical interface for composing open-ended Skills, combining local linguistic flexibility with executable dependencies, explicit predecessor-text bindings, and auditable coordination. Code is available at: https://github.com/TokenRhythm/opensquilla/tree/paper/metaskill-lp4fm-2026

title: Token cost by data format: JSON vs YAML vs CSV vs TOON on Claude, Gemini and GPT
abstract: The same 20-row product table (7 fields) written in 8 formats and counted on four tokenizers: Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.x and OpenAI o200k_base (GPT-4o and later). Headline: the table costs 1,336 GPT tokens as indented JSON and 429 as CSV (68% fewer). CSV was the cheapest format on every tokenizer tested; TOON came close but did not beat it; XML was the most expensive. Source page, chart and method: https://tokensave.app/data/token-cost-by-format Related: token cost by language on Claude, Gemini and GPT: https://tokensave.app/data/token-cost-by-language-claude-gemini Measured: 2026-10-17 License: CC BY 4.0 Key findings Switching from indented JSON to CSV cuts tokens by 68% on GPT, 66% on Claude 5.5 and 70% on Gemini. TOON needs 10% more tokens than CSV on GPT and 4% more on Claude 5.5. Minifying JSON saves 51% on Gemini and 43% on GPT but only 34% on Claude 5.5. Claude 5.5 needs 28% to 59% more tokens than GPT for the same data (largest gap: minified JSON). Files token-cost-by-format.csv: one row per format with character count, tokens and difference vs indented JSON for claude55, claude45, gemini, gpt token-cost-by-format.json: the same results plus all 8 input files verbatim, so every count can be reproduced Data Tokens for the same table, difference versus indented JSON on the same tokenizer in brackets. Format Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5 Claude Haiku 4.5 Gemini 3.x GPT o200k TSV 621 (-66%) 477 (-71%) 483 (-70%) 427 (-68%) CSV 620 (-66%) 476 (-71%) 482 (-70%) 429 (-68%) TOON 647 (-65%) 502 (-69%) 508 (-69%) 474 (-65%) Markdown table 800 (-57%) 649 (-60%) 590 (-64%) 539 (-60%) JSON (minified) 1,210 (-34%) 847 (-48%) 791 (-51%) 763 (-43%) YAML 1,275 (-31%) 1,074 (-34%) 1,076 (-34%) 997 (-25%) JSON (indented) 1,841 (±0%) 1,618 (±0%) 1,623 (±0%) 1,336 (±0%) XML 2,200 (+20%) 1,868 (+15%) 1,873 (+15%) 1,603 (+20%) Method One table of 20 products x 7 fields (id, name, category, price, in_stock, rating, tags), written as indented JSON (2 spaces), minified JSON, YAML, XML, CSV, TSV, a Markdown table and TOON (tabular form, tags joined with |). Claude: each file sent through Claude Code (claude -p) with a fixed one-line system prompt; reported input tokens minus the same run with a one-character message. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 gave identical counts. Gemini: Google AI Studio prompt token counter on Gemini 3.8 Flash, minus its one start token. XML, CSV and indented JSON were measured twice; CSV and JSON matched, and the XML value is from the second run. GPT: tiktoken with o200k_base. Limitations One flat table. Deeply nested data does not fit CSV well; there JSON or YAML may be the practical choice. Token count only: models may read some formats more reliably than others. Claude values can be off by about ±2 tokens (under 1% here).

title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.

evidence.title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
evidence.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.

title: Human-AI-Computer Interaction: Measuring Whether AI Strengthens Unaided Judgment
abstract: A tool that helps a person answer today and leaves them no better at answering alone next week has made them dependent on it. We state a measurement protocol that separates the two outcomes. On one task set, three scores are taken: the person's unaided score H_p, the model's AI score A, and the person's joint score J_p with the model's answer in view. The multiplier is m_p = J_p / max(H_p, A), the gain is D = J_p - max(H_p, A), and the unaided test is repeated after seven days to give retention R_p = H_p(t + 7 d) - H_p(t) and learning L = J_p(t + 7 d) - H_p(t + 7 d). A tool that raises J_p while L stays at or below zero across its interval marks dependence. The instrument is the hai probe in Bucket's bkt package: a frozen bank of 998 four-choice items across the seven canon branches, of which 68 are held out by an automated distractor review; sessions of 40 items in 20 pairs matched on tier and on whether the model got the pair's items right; a 20 second think window before the model's answer appears; no feedback until the retest; guess-corrected scores and a bootstrap over pairs for every interval. The learning side of the measurement is the minimum prerequisite learning problem: the catalog is a directed acyclic graph of concepts, a learner's state is a closed set of mastered concepts, and the least a learner must add to reach a target is the required set R(t, M), the target's prerequisite closure minus their mastery, a count proved minimal in Lean 4 under stated assumptions. Three rules will join the two sides, probe items drawn at the learner's frontier, R_p reported against the engine's predicted recall, and mastery updated from the solo half only; all three are design, since the probe code holds no mastery or FSRS logic today. The instrument is built and no probe has been retested, so this report carries no result on a person; the learning system's own evaluation, 57,060 enumerated planning cases with zero errors and a synthetic prediction experiment, is reported with its source. The report states the planned analysis, paired comparisons stratified by education level, a divergence hypothesis on how reliance on one model narrows the range of answers across a group, and the rule by which the scores decide which tasks Research OS hands to the model and which it keeps with the person.

title: Does the Train-Gain/Generalization Relation Transfer? A Pre-Registered Cross-Domain Test of Inverted-U Behavior in Verifier-Bound Rule Discovery
abstract: A verifier-bound rule-discovery engine –- an LLM proposes executable rules, a programmatic verifier gates them, a single-shot isolated holdout scores them –- was run in three domains under one pre-registered methodology. The first domain (combinatorial scheduling) reported an inverted-U relation between training improvement and holdout generalization: moderate training gains generalized best, and the largest gains overfit. This paper reports the pre-registered cross-domain test of that relation. Under the frozen protocol (quartile buckets over margin-positive pairs; criterion: middle buckets' mean win rate exceeds the ends' by 0.05; $ 2$ of $ 2$ participating domains required), the criterion replicates: scheduling $0.35/0.60/0.70/0.48$ (mid $0.650$ vs.\ ends $0.413$) and MCS task assignment $0.36/0.93/1.00/1.00$ (mid $0.964$ vs.\ ends $0.679$). The second domain (MCS incentive design) is excluded by the protocol's own rule –- its verifier passed 3 of 2,000 LLM rules and 0 of the human-designed references, a threshold effect that leaves no margin-positive pairs. The substantive finding is not the verdict but the shape divergence beneath it: in scheduling the top quartile declines (48\ overfitting), while in assignment the top quartile saturates at 100\ different mechanisms. We read the pattern –- hard 0–1 verification collapses generalization, mid-severity simulation lets the top quartile overfit, feasibility-by-construction transfers it –- as evidence that verifier strictness determines the fate of the largest training gains, and we report the two-level verdict (criterion: replicated; mechanism: not shared) as the result. Pre-registrations, ledgers, and analysis scripts are available from the authors upon reasonable request via email.

title: Diagnostic Algorithm Selection for Low-Dimensional Euclidean Clustering: Code, Frozen Models, and Experimental Results
abstract: Overview This repository contains the source code, frozen models, experimental configurations, evaluation results, and reproducibility materials for the research study Diagnostic Algorithm Selection for Low-Dimensional Euclidean Clustering: Geometry-Guided Routing, Portfolio Verification, and Generalization Limits. The study investigates how geometric characteristics of unlabeled observations can inform the selection of established clustering algorithms. Its focus is on the relationships among clustering quality, algorithm-selection decisions, computational cost, robustness, and generalization across different data distributions. Geometric Diagnostics and Algorithm Selection The framework uses four label-free geometric diagnostics: Hopkins clusterability: spatial clustering tendency. Local density-radius variation: differences in nearest-neighbor distances. Geodesic distortion: graph shortest-path distances relative to Euclidean distances. Minimum spanning tree tail concentration: the contribution of the longest spanning-tree edges. A frozen random-forest performance predictor maps these diagnostics to a recommendation among five clustering families: K-means, Ward hierarchical clustering, spectral clustering, HDBSCAN, and Gaussian mixture models. The study also evaluates label-free verification strategies. These include full five-candidate silhouette verification and restricted two- and three-candidate portfolios. The restricted portfolios use frozen model predictions to form candidate shortlists, followed by internal silhouette-based verification with a fixed decision margin. Experimental Evaluation The research comprises controlled synthetic investigations, external clustering evaluations, algorithm-selection comparisons, and robustness analyses. Two separately reported external evaluation groups were constructed using prespecified UCI Machine Learning Repository identifiers: External evaluation I: 18 successfully processed datasets from 22 prespecified identifiers. External evaluation II: 16 successfully processed datasets from 19 prespecified identifiers. Together, these experiments provide results for 34 evaluated dataset records. The two groups are reported separately rather than treated as a single homogeneous benchmark. Potential overlap in the underlying sources of some UCI records is documented, together with a source-overlap sensitivity analysis. The evaluation includes fixed clustering algorithms, learned algorithm-selection models, internal-validity-based selection, and restricted candidate-portfolio verification. Reference class labels are used for dataset eligibility and retrospective external evaluation, but not for computing geometric diagnostics, selecting clustering algorithms, or determining candidate clustering parameters. Robustness and Computational Analysis The supplementary experiments examine: Two-, three-, and five-candidate selection strategies. Clustering-quality differences between candidate budgets. Sensitivity to maximum cluster-count search ranges of 7 and 15. Random-seed sensitivity of geometric diagnostics and algorithm recommendations. Nearest-neighbor graph configuration and connectivity sensitivity. Landmark sampling and minimum-spanning-tree threshold sensitivity. Dataset-level paired statistical comparisons. End-to-end computational runtime and quality-cost trade-offs. Separate synthetic tests of refusal decisions for designated null and clusterable distributions. The experiments characterize both improvements and failure cases. The results are intended to clarify when geometric algorithm selection and portfolio verification are useful, when additional candidate evaluations incur unnecessary costs, and how distributional differences affect algorithm-selection reliability. No universal performance superiority is claimed. Repository Contents The research archive includes: Python implementations of the evaluated clustering-selection workflows. Frozen trained models and algorithm-selection parameters. Source code for both external evaluation groups. Experimental configurations, dataset identifiers, and random seeds. Dataset-level predictions, algorithm choices, and clustering-quality results. Adjusted mutual information (AMI) and adjusted Rand index (ARI) tables. Candidate-budget and cluster-count sensitivity results. Geometric diagnostic stability and robustness analyses. Paired statistical comparisons and computational runtime measurements. Synthetic refusal and clusterability stress-test results. Scientific figures in PNG and PDF formats. Software requirements, execution instructions, and SHA-256 integrity checks. Reproducibility and Data Availability The archive provides reproducibility code, frozen model artifacts, experimental outputs, and verification scripts. Original third-party UCI datasets are not redistributed. Dataset identifiers and retrieval procedures are provided where applicable. Reproducing the complete experiments requires access to the referenced datasets and compatible software dependencies. Archived derived results and verification scripts support independent inspection and numerical consistency checks.

title: tempestpy: Easy-to-Use Shielded Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract Safe exploration is a key challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL) that aims to prevent agents from making decisions that could cause harm while exploring their environment. Shielding is one such technique that assumes domain knowledge in the form of a model of the environment to decide upon the safety of an action. Although shielding is a well-established approach, it has seen limited application in RL due to significant barriers. The main obstacle is the lack of an accessible end-to-end infrastructure that connects formal shield synthesis with standard RL frameworks. As a result, applying shielding requires expertise in formal methods and substantial engineering effort to construct probabilistic models, which has kept it outside the typical RL workflow. We address this problem by extending our shield synthesis tool Tempest into a practical backend for safe RL. Our core contribution is tempestpy , a Python library that integrates Tempest -based shield synthesis directly into the Gymnasium API, allowing shields to be synthesised and deployed within existing RL pipelines. This substantially lowers the barrier to entry for shielding and turns formal safe-exploration methods into a usable component for RL practitioners. In addition, we extend Tempest ’s algorithmic support to compute sound shields for stochastic multiplayer games, thereby preserving formal safety guarantees. In this setting, specifying a model of the environment becomes the remaining requirement rather than the primary integration challenge. We demonstrate the resulting workflow end to end and evaluate shielded and unshielded RL across multiple environments. To facilitate the modeling step, we provide symbolic models for Minigrid and introduce $$\textsc {Minigrid}^{\small {\textsc {Safe}}}$$ M I N I G R I D S A F E , a collection of playground environments designed to make shielding easily accessible and experimentally transparent. $$\textsc {Minigrid}^{\small {\textsc {Safe}}}$$ M I N I G R I D S A F E extends Minigrid with safety-oriented scenarios featuring probabilistic transitions and additional agents, enabling the study of challenging safety aspects in a simple and intuitive setting.

title: Tensor Network Datamodels for Training Data Attribution
abstract: Datamodels predict how a model's behavior changes when different parts of its training data are included or removed. However, linear datamodels assign fixed contributions to training units and cannot represent non-additive joint effects. We introduce Tensor Network Datamodels (TNDMs), which use low-rank tensor networks to model dependencies among training units while keeping the representation compact. TNDMs learn a map from subsets of the training data to the outcome of training on those subsets, allowing them to represent interactions among several training units. We prove that complementary and redundant training groups can induce high-degree subset functions with compact low-rank representations. A single fitted TNDM can then be used for several training data questions, including predicting the effect of removing data, measuring the importance of individual training units, identifying interactions between training units, and selecting useful subsets of the training data. We evaluate TNDMs on controlled tasks designed to contain strong interactions, as well as standard fine-tuning settings for classification and reasoning. On a controlled reasoning task, TNDMs outperform every baseline while observing only half as many training subsets, and TNDM-TT reduces prediction NMSE by $89\%$ relative to the linear datamodel after observing approximately $0.0061\%$ of all possible training subsets. In factual-association fine-tuning, a single TNDM-CP raises held-out $\mathrm{R}^2$ from $0.579$ to $0.668$ over the linear datamodel. These results demonstrate that compact low-rank models improve prediction when training data effects depend on combinations of training groups.

title: O'ZBEK TILIDA PRESUPPOZITSIYANI AVTOMATIK ANIQLASH: KORPUS VA TABIIY TILNI QAYTA ISHLASH YONDASHUVI
authors: O'ZBEK TILIDA PRESUPPOZITSIYANI AVTOMATIK ANIQLASH: KORPUS VA TABIIY TILNI QAYTA ISHLASH YONDASHUVI
abstract: Annotatsiya. Ushbu maqolada o‘zbek tilida presuppozitsiyani avtomatik aniqlashningkorpus va tabiiy tilni qayta ishlashga asoslangan modeli yoritiladi. Presuppozitsiya triggerlarinianiqlash, morfologik-sintaktik tahlil, kontekstni modellashtirish, korpus annotatsiyasi vatransformer modellaridan foydalanish imkoniyatlari o‘zbek tilining agglutinativ xususiyatlaridoirasida ilmiy jihatdan tahlil qilinadi.Kalit so‘zlar: presuppozitsiya, presuppozitsiya triggeri, korpus lingvistikasi, tabiiy tilniqayta ishlash, pragmatik inferensiya, transformer modeli, o‘zbek tili.Аннотация. В данной статье рассматривается модель автоматическогообнаружения пресуппозиций в узбекском языке, основанная на корпусной лингвистике иобработке естественного языка. В рамках агглютинативных свойств узбекского языканаучно анализируются возможности использования триггеров пресуппозиций,морфологически-синтаксического анализа, контекстного моделирования, аннотированиякорпуса и трансформерных моделей.Ключевые слова: пресуппозиция, триггер пресуппозиции, корпусная лингвистика,обработка естественного языка, прагматический вывод, трансформерная модель,узбекский язык.Abstract. This article discusses a model for automatic presupposition detection in theUzbek language based on corpus and natural language processing. The possibilities of usingpresupposition triggers, morphological-syntactic analysis, context modeling, corpus annotation,and transformer models are scientifically analyzed within the framework of the agglutinativeproperties of the Uzbek language.Keywords: presupposition, presupposition trigger, corpus linguistics, natural languageprocessing, pragmatic inference, transformer model, Uzbek language.

title: Применение искусственного интеллекта в финансовом инжиниринге
abstract: В статье рассматриваются направления применения искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) в финансовом инжиниринге – при проектировании, оценке и хеджировании финансовых инструментов, построении портфелей и управлении рисками. На основе обзора научной литературы и данных Банка России систематизированы основные классы задач, в которых методы машинного обучения дают преимущество перед классическими моделями, и показаны ограничения их использования. Установлено, что в 2025 г. ИИ на постоянной основе применяли 21 % опрошенных российских финансовых организаций, ещё 15 % тестировали пилотные проекты. title: Neuro-Inspired Inhibitory Message Passing for Accurate and Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
abstract: Multi-agent systems promise to solve problems by bringing together information beyond the reach of any individual agent. Retrieval and tool use can distribute this information across agents, making communication essential to collaboration. A central challenge is keeping crucial evidence visible in each agent's context as messages accumulate. Repeated information can crowd out rare, decisive evidence. Models of cortical circuits suggest a principle for addressing this imbalance: inhibition can selectively suppress shared inputs while preserving sensitivity to weaker signals. We adapt this principle into inhibitory message passing, a training-free communication router that cancels redundant evidence separately for each evidence sentence and receiver. Each round, it forwards evidence sentences restated in agents' messages, delivering each at most once to receivers whose own evidence lacks it and excluding the senders' reasoning and answers. Against standard message passing, accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks, and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. Gains held across seven open models spanning four to thirty-two billion parameters and two commercial models, in groups up to sixty-four agents, and across multi-agent architectures including peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and multilevel hierarchical organizations. These findings support a scalable design pattern for more accurate and token-efficient multi-agent reasoning.

title: RAGit: Turning Document Preprocessing into an Experimental Variable for RAG
abstract: Document preprocessing choices can substantially affect retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, yet they are often selected heuristically and are difficult to compare under consistent conditions. We present RAGit, an open-source experimentation workbench for the systematic and reproducible evaluation of document preprocessing choices through downstream retrieval. RAGit represents parsing, chunking, indexing, retrieval, and evaluation as configurable experimental stages, enabling controlled comparisons while the remaining downstream settings are kept fixed. It preserves provenance from retrieved chunks to source pages and maps heterogeneous retrieval units to a common page-level ranking for evaluation. The current implementation supports multiple parsers and chunking strategies, dense and late-interaction retrieval, reusable intermediate artifacts, and multi-configuration benchmarking. We demonstrate RAGit through controlled experiments comparing alternative preprocessing configurations under a fixed retrieval setup, illustrating how preprocessing can be treated as an explicit experimental variable. RAGit and its documentation are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/OmarElbachyr/ragit). A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/tsst-Bhfz4I.

title: RAPID-Audio: reproducibility archive (version 3.0)
abstract: Reproducibility archive accompanying the article "RAPID-Audio: Authenticated Selective Speech Disclosure with Adversarial Analysis of Content and Metadata Leakage" by Annas W. Malik and Kashif Nasr. It contains the source code of the protocol, of both receivers, of the SEL-EtM reference design, of the frame selectors, of the attacks and of the analysis; the identifiers of every evaluation set; derived data (word times, recogniser output, AMI transcripts and entity labels); the synthetic benchmarks E13 and E14 with their audio and the E14 protocol fixed in advance; every per-utterance and per-trial result and the log of every run; test vectors; model revisions and checksums of the external data; scripts that regenerate every table and figure; and a verification script (python -I code/verify.py) that checks every file against SHA256SUMS, recomputes every summary from the raw outputs and reruns the protocol tests without audio, models or a GPU. LibriSpeech and AMI audio and the model weights are not redistributed; datasets.json gives their sources and checksums. Licences: the code is under the MIT licence (LICENSE); derived data, synthetic benchmarks, results and figures are under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA).

title: The Self-and-Self-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Internal Computational Mechanisms and World-State Modeling
abstract: Computational systems increasingly operate in environments where successful behavior depends on both the organization of internal computation and the ability to represent, predict, and respond to external conditions. A system may possess multiple internal computational mechanisms for generation, diagnosis, verification, correction, planning, and evaluation, while also maintaining a model of the world in which its decisions are executed. However, internal mechanism selection and world-state modeling are often treated as separate design problems. This separation can limit a system's ability to determine not only what it should compute, but also which aspects of its world model require additional computation, when internal mechanisms should be activated, and when predicted consequences justify further investigation. This paper proposes the Self-and-Self-and-World Model (SSWM), a general computational framework for adaptively coordinating internal computational mechanisms with world-state modeling. The framework distinguishes three interacting dimensions: the system's internal computational state, the organization of its internal mechanisms, and its representation of the external world. Its central principle is that a computational system should jointly determine how to allocate internal computation and how to maintain or revise its world model according to task requirements, uncertainty, prediction error, expected utility, environmental change, and computational constraints. SSWM formalizes the internal mechanism repertoire, world-state representation, model uncertainty, mechanism-dependent model updates, action-conditioned predictions, computational costs, and feedback-driven adaptation. It introduces a coupled decision formulation in which mechanism selection and world-model maintenance can influence one another. The paper presents a reference architecture, a proposed algorithm, conditional theoretical propositions, complexity considerations, experimental hypotheses, and a cross-domain evaluation program. SSWM is intended as an organizational abstraction for systems that must coordinate internal computation with representations of external conditions, including autonomous agents, robotics, planning, scientific computing, and model-based decision systems. Its distinct contribution, if supported by formal analysis and empirical evidence, would be a unified account of how internal mechanism organization and world-model management can be jointly adapted rather than optimized independently. The framework is proposed for investigation; its novelty, advantages, and generality require systematic comparison with existing research on world models, metareasoning, model-based planning, adaptive computation, and active information acquisition.

title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs -- reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.

title: From Quantum Decoding to Sharp Subset Bounds: A Use Case for Extracted Mathematical Instruments
abstract: Quantum communication requires a receiver to distinguish several, generally mixed, signal states. A useful theoretical question is whether errors on smaller signal alphabets can certify the error of a decoder for the full alphabet. We study this question for the pretty good measurement and present it as a use case for the programme of extracting reusable mathematical instruments from a large collection of research manuscripts. A constrained spectral optimization mechanism identified in that collection leads to the sharp pairwise coefficient (1 + sqrt(1 - 2/N))^2 for all equally likely pure ensembles. A separate matrix analysis proves the sharp coefficient (1 + sqrt(1 - k/N))^2 for every subset size when the average state is maximally mixed on its support, allowing arbitrary mixed signals. For general mixed ensembles, the sharp leave-one coefficient (1 + 1/sqrt(N))^2 holds whenever the normalized full error is at least 1/N; consequently it holds for all equally likely ensembles in dimension at most N - 1. We give a noisy qutrit decoding example, an unrestricted bound for nearly full subsets, and an exact polynomial certificate for a further four-signal family. The account separates the extracted mechanisms, their classical antecedents, and the additional arguments needed for the quantum problem. These results provide conditional error certificates, while the unrestricted sharp mixed-state subset problem and improvements to operational communication rates remain open.

A constrained spectral optimization mechanism identified in that collection leads to the sharp pairwise coefficient (1 + sqrt(1 - 2/N))^2 for all equally likely pure ensembles. A separate matrix analysis proves the sharp coefficient (1 + sqrt(1 - k/N))^2 for every subset size when the average state is maximally mixed on its support, allowing arbitrary mixed signals. For general mixed ensembles, the sharp leave-one coefficient (1 + 1/sqrt(N))^2 holds whenever the normalized full error is at least 1/N; consequently it holds for all equally likely ensembles in dimension at most N - 1. We give a noisy qutrit decoding example, an unrestricted bound for nearly full subsets, and an exact polynomial certificate for a further four-signal family. The account separates the extracted mechanisms, their classical antecedents, and the additional arguments needed for the quantum problem. These results provide conditional error certificates, while the unrestricted sharp mixed-state subset problem and improvements to operational communication rates remain open.

title: Robust Client Behavior Tracking for Malicious Detection in Secure-Aggregated Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a successful distributed machine learning paradigm, where diverse clients are able to collaboratively train a global model without releasing their raw data, thereby preserving the data privacy. To enhance even more privacy, it is common to use Secure Aggregation (SecAgg) to make the central server oblivious to any individual client and only get model updates aggregated. However, this approach cannot be used to identify a malicious actor falling victim to a model poisoning attack, data poisoning, and Byzantine attack, which poses a threat to the quality and effectiveness of the global model. In this research, we put forward a safe and reliable client behavior monitoring method for malicious detection in secure-aggregated federated learning. It does so by measuring the client's actions in an indirect way (consistency of contribution over time, stability of the updates, reliability of the training, convergence trends, reputation scores based on trust), and ensuring that the secure aggregation protocols are not broken. A dynamic risk assessment system identifies frauds whose activity is very divergent from legitimate players. Identifying malicious clients can enhance the robustness of the federated learning process by either giving the malicious client a reduced weight in the consensus function or excluding the malicious client from subsequent training rounds. Our approach: Privacy Protection, Robustness to adversarial behaviour, Good model accuracy in scenarios. The experimental results indicate that the proposed method can successfully detect malicious clients, better handle the poisoning attacks than the conventional secure aggregation approach without behavioral monitoring, consider the convergence stability and higher classification accuracy. The approach that we propose is practical and scalable for preserving privacy of the federated learning systems which are used in healthcare and financial applications, Internet of Things (IoT), and many other distributed intelligent applications.

title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $π>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $π$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $λb^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.

title: Cycle-Invariant Lightweight Authenticated Encryption and Cross-Domain Silicon Entropy Harvesting on ARM Cortex-M0+
abstract: Abstract This record contains the complete artifacts, bare-metal C source code, and empirical benchmark logs for a cycle-invariant authenticated encryption and silicon-jitter true random number generator (TRNG) architecture implemented on an STM32C031 (ARM Cortex-M0+). Designed for resource-constrained edge systems (such as Electric Vehicle BMS nodes), the system achieves strict constant-time execution ($\Delta = 0$ clock cycle variance) to defeat timing side-channel attacks, harvests cross-domain clock phase jitter whitened via the hardware CRC-32 unit, and implements sub-microsecond interrupt-driven SRAM tamper key-shredding. 1. Introduction & Problem Statement Ultra-low-cost microcontrollers deployed in distributed automotive and IoT nodes frequently lack native hardware TRNGs and hardware AES accelerators. Standard software implementations are computationally expensive, consume excessive flash memory, and leak execution timing variations that allow attackers to recover secret keys via side-channel analysis. 2. Proposed Bare-Metal Architecture The proposed architecture operates via direct CMSIS register manipulation without software libraries or operating systems: Silicon-Jitter TRNG: Harvests phase drift between the core SysTick timer and peripheral TIM3 clock mixed with ADC1 SAR quantization noise, whitened through the on-chip CRC->DR polynomial engine. Constant-Time AEAD Pipeline: Implements a 32-round Feistel block cipher combined with a keyed Hardware CRC-32 MAC tag, utilizing zero data-dependent branches. Tamper Key-Shredding: Employs a RAM-relocated vector table (SCB->VTOR) and an EXTI0 falling-edge hardware interrupt to execute a 2-pass SRAM entropy-flooding and zeroization sequence upon physical intrusion. 3. Empirical Benchmarks & Comparative Analysis The system was benchmarked on an ARM Cortex-M0+ running at 48 MHz. Cycle Invariance: Verified via ARM SysTick->VAL profiling, proving a steady-state execution time of exactly 11,988 CPU cycles (249.75 µs) with zero variance ($\sigma^2 = 0$), compared to variable-timing table-based software ciphers (~35,000+ cycles). Memory Footprint: Consumes < 1.2 KB of Flash and < 64 bytes of SRAM, outperforming bulky software stacks like mbedTLS. Tamper Latency: Achieves key-shredding in < 1 µs, mitigating cold-boot memory retention. 4. Repository & File Structure main.c: Contains the bare-metal C implementation, register initializations, TRNG entropy harvester, constant-time cipher, and EXTI0 tamper interrupt service routine. diagram.json: The Wokwi hardware simulation configuration file defining the STM32C031 Nucleo board, the analog potentiometer sensor (PA1), and the physical tamper pushbutton (PA0). aead_out.png: Empirical benchmark serial output log demonstrating live sequence tracking, encrypted ciphertext, hardware CRC-32 verification tags, and cycle-count invariance. GitHub Source Code & Interactive Simulation:https://github.com/VasudevanS1906/cortex-m0-secure-vault-trng

title: SQuIREL: A Context-Relative Framework for Measuring Entity Richness in Wikidata
abstract: Wikidata is a large, heterogeneous knowledge graph and applying data quality metrics requires context-specific approaches. The "richness" quality metric is currently under-researched and typically restricted to the ontology level, which fails to capture entity-specific structural depth. To address this gap, we introduce SQuIREL, a method that measures richness directly at the entity level using six dimensions: Semantic Specificity, Qualifier Density, Internal Connectivity, Reference Provenance, External Network Connectivity, and Linguistic Accessibility. These dimensions are kept disaggregated to preserve actionability for targeted editorial intervention. We apply this metric to two case studies of oil paintings (Brazilian vs. French) and writers (grouped by citizenship and gender) to demonstrate how it surfaces representational inequalities that may indicate systemic bias. Our metric successfully distinguishes between highly tailored and basic entity profiles, revealing nuances that raw counts and existing aggregate scores obscure. Specifically, it identifies structural imbalances, such as 48% of Brazilian paintings clustering as low-richness stubs against 0% in the French cohort, as well as intersectional patterns, including contrasting gender gaps between UK and Nigerian writers.

title: Understanding Generation Z's Continuance Intention toward E-commerce Chatbots: Survey Dataset on Information Quality, Satisfaction, Perceived Ease of Use, and Trust
abstract: This dataset contains the survey responses used in the study "Empirical Study of Generation Z's Continuance Intention toward E-commerce Chatbots" (Gunawan, Subhan, and Caesar, Bina Nusantara University). The study adapts the research model of Gao et al. (2025, Journal of Business Research, 200, 115661, doi:10.1016/j.jbusres.2025.115661) to examine how information quality, perceived ease of use, trust, and satisfaction relate to the intention to continue using AI chatbots on e-commerce platforms. DATA COLLECTIONResponses were collected through an online questionnaire (Google Forms) between 27 and 30 March 2026 (timestamps in GMT+7), using convenience sampling targeting Generation Z users in the JABODETABEK region of Indonesia. The questionnaire items were administered in English, and the introduction was in Indonesian. On the opening page, participants were informed of the study's purpose and told that their responses would be confidential, anonymous, and used only for academic purposes. The dataset contains no names, e-mail addresses, or other direct identifiers. FILEOne CSV file exported from Google Forms: 315 rows (one per submission) and 24 columns, with no missing values. This is the raw export: no responses were removed and no recoding was applied. VARIABLES- Timestamp: date and time of submission (GMT+7)- Gender: Male (154), Female (161)- Age (categories): 18–21 years (103), 22–28 years (195), 29–35 years (16), >35 years (1)- Place of Education: Tangerang (87), Depok (82), Bogor (49), Bekasi (47), Jakarta (47), Bandung (1), Jatinangor (1), Pontianak (1)- Education: Diploma (77), Bachelor's Degree/S1 (214), Master's Degree/S2 (20), Doctor's Degree/S3 (4)- 19 measurement items, each rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). All items are positively worded; none is reverse-coded. MEASUREMENT ITEMS (column headers contain the full item wording)Information quality (IQ1–IQ7): AI chatbots in e-commerce provide sufficient information; Through AI chatbots in e-commerce, I get the information I need on time; Information provided by AI chatbots in e-commerce is in a useful format / is clear / is accurate / is up-to-date / is reliable.Satisfaction (SF1–SF3), perceived ease of use (PEU1–PEU3), trust (TR1–TR3), and continue using intention (CUI1–CUI3): items adopted from Gao et al. (2025), e.g., "Overall, I am satisfied with AI chatbot in e-commerce", "Using AI chatbot in e-commerce is easy for me", "I consider the AI chatbot in e-commerce to be trustworthy", "I intend to continue using AI chatbot in e-commerce rather than discontinue using them". NOTES FOR REUSE- Column order: Timestamp, Gender, Age, Place of Education, Education, IQ1–IQ7, SF1–SF3, PEU1–PEU3, TR1–TR3, CUI1–CUI3.- Age was recorded in categories; 17 submissions fall in categories above 28 years.- Place of Education includes three locations outside JABODETABEK.- Some submissions share identical answers across all 19 items (18 rows, 7 distinct patterns).- The original analysis used PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4 with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples). Contact: gilbert.gunawan002@binus.ac.id

title: Подієво-орієнтована архітектура мультиагентних систем на основі великих мовних моделей – агенти як мікросервіси
abstract: У статті запропоновано подієво-орієнтовану архітектуру мультиагентних систем (МАС) на основі великих мовних моделей (LLM), у якій кожен агент є незалежним мікросервісом з власним пулом обчислювальних ресурсів, а взаємодія агентів здійснюється завдяки брокеру подій. Розроблено математичну модель МАС як мережі систем масового обслуговування з розгалуженням і злиттям (fork-join), яка враховує логнормальний час інференсу LLM, обмежену конкурентність агентів, транзієнтні помилки, повторні спроби та динаміку черги під час відмови агента та пікового навантаження. Удосконалено модель втрат синхронної оркестрації завдяки урахування кореляції повторних спроб. Синхронну послідовну оркестрацію, синхронну оркестрацію з паралельним розгалуженням і подієву хореографію порівняно аналітично, методом імітаційного моделювання та експериментально на прототипі на основі Redis Streams. Встановлено, що в стаціонарному режимі латентність визначається критичним шляхом графа задачі і не залежить від способу доставки, тоді як під час відмов агентів і пікових навантажень подієва архітектура зберігає всі задачі без налаштування повторів на боці клієнта ціною їх затримки в черзі. Проаналізовано чутливість результатів до параметрів синхронної оркестрації та представлено результати експерименту з реальною мовною моделлю.

title: IntelliLayer: A Deep Learning Architecture for Dynamic Decision Intelligence
abstract: Organizations increasingly use data-driven systems to support operational decision-making in dynamic environments. However, many existing deep learning models focus primarily on predicting outcomes rather than recommending reliable actions. These models often provide limited information about prediction confidence, may experience performance degradation when data patterns change, and offer insufficient explanations for their decisions. Previous studies have addressed these challenges independently through improved prediction models, uncertainty estimation, calibration techniques, data drift detection, and explainable AI methods. To address these limitations, this paper introduces IntelliLayer, a five-layer deep learning architecture that combines these capabilities within a unified decision-making framework. The proposed architecture integrates static data and sequential events using Transformer encoders and a learnable gated fusion mechanism. It estimates calibrated outcome distributions through a deep ensemble and selects actions based on expected utility, while uncertain cases are referred to human reviewers. To handle changing data patterns, the framework employs adaptive windowing for drift detection and updates the model using replay techniques and elastic weight consolidation. Additionally, integrated gradients are used to explain individual predictions, and an audit record is maintained for every decision to support transparency and accountability. The paper describes the architecture of each layer, outlines the online decision-making algorithm, and presents a reference implementation stack. It also defines a reproducible evaluation framework covering predictive performance, calibration, decision-making costs, selective prediction coverage, recovery from data drift, and processing latency. evidence.title: IntelliLayer: A Deep Learning Architecture for Dynamic Decision Intelligence
evidence.abstract: Organizations increasingly use data-driven systems to support operational decision-making in dynamic environments. However, many existing deep learning models focus primarily on predicting outcomes rather than recommending reliable actions. These models often provide limited information about prediction confidence, may experience performance degradation when data patterns change, and offer insufficient explanations for their decisions. Previous studies have addressed these challenges independently through improved prediction models, uncertainty estimation, calibration techniques, data drift detection, and explainable AI methods. To address these limitations, this paper introduces IntelliLayer, a five-layer deep learning architecture that combines these capabilities within a unified decision-making framework. The proposed architecture integrates static data and sequential events using Transformer encoders and a learnable gated fusion mechanism. It estimates calibrated outcome distributions through a deep ensemble and selects actions based on expected utility, while uncertain cases are referred to human reviewers. To handle changing data patterns, the framework employs adaptive windowing for drift detection and updates the model using replay techniques and elastic weight consolidation. Additionally, integrated gradients are used to explain individual predictions, and an audit record is maintained for every decision to support transparency and accountability. The paper describes the architecture of each layer, outlines the online decision-making algorithm, and presents a reference implementation stack. It also defines a reproducible evaluation framework covering predictive performance, calibration, decision-making costs, selective prediction coverage, recovery from data drift, and processing latency. Since experimental results have not yet been obtained, the proposed evaluation protocol and results template provide a structured basis for future validation of the IntelliLayer architecture.

title: Breaking the Static Verifier Ceiling: Zero-Overhead Self-Evolving System-One Judge and Policy Co-Evolution on a Single Shared Foundation Backbone (CoEvo-Jev-GRPO)
abstract: Full-Length Preprint (12-Page English Edition + 8-Page Chinese Edition) & Benchmark Suite — Part III-B: Self-Evolving System-One Judge & Policy Co-Evolution. When an LLM policy evolves beyond 400 GRPO steps on hard competition mathematics, any frozen reward model suffers from late-stage calibration drift and Goodhart pseudo-proof exploitation, while dual-model online RM training triples GPU VRAM (24.46 GB). We introduce CoEvo-Jev-GRPO, an online verifier-anchored bilevel co-evolution framework on a single shared Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B backbone (8.08 GB total VRAM on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB, adding only +0.02 GB and 0.84 ms per calibration step). By mining policy-verifier disagreement rollouts and updating the Layer-28 System-One Pointer Head and top-layer judge LoRAs via a Null-Anchored Brier + Contrastive Margin + KL-to-Prior objective, CoEvo-Jev-GRPO contracts Judge Expected Calibration Error (ECE) by 77.1% (from 0.048 to 0.011) and suppresses subtle pseudo-proof hacking to 1.2%. Across MATH-500 (79.8%), AIME 2024/2025 (36.7%, +16.7% over Binary RLVR), AMC-12 (74.4%), and OlympiadBench-Math (46.2%), CoEvo-Jev-GRPO achieves #1 SOTA with 59.28% Mean Accuracy (+5.28% over Frozen DC-Jev-GRPO and +15.83% over Binary RLVR). title: Native Probability Outputs for Clinical Triage: An Evaluation of Calibration and Decision Accuracy
abstract: Patient-facing triage requires an appropriate care recommendation and recognition of when information is insufficient. We evaluate whether Jev, a decision model that returns probabilities over predefined actions, supports both judgments. Using CARE-Bench, we compare Jev with four general-purpose language models and three input-independent baselines across 925 decision points from 439 public cases. On the public test subset, Jev ranks fourth of five models by macro-F1 (0.461) but has the lowest observed multiclass Brier score (0.610), an 18.7\% improvement over uniform prediction (case-bootstrap 95\% interval, 4.9--31.1\%). Noul has lower binary Brier than Choice (0.215 versus 0.276). A evaluation of 453 HealthBench conversations again gives Jev the lowest observed Brier score (0.299), but measures a distinct emergency-referral judgment. Jev combines lower probability error with missed clarification needs in the four-action task. Asking about information sufficiency separately increases recall but also produces frequent unnecessary clarification assignments.

title: Fluxion: A Differentiable DSP Runtime from Training GPU to Real-Time Edge
abstract: Native real-time audio engines meet audio deadlines but are hard to connect to machine-learning workflows, while tensor frameworks integrate with machine learning but process audio as offline batches without timing guarantees; runtime layers built on them inherit the host's scheduling and deployment footprint. This paper presents Fluxion, a Rust audio DSP runtime for cascaded second-order sections, FIR filters, and delay-line effects. Fluxion implements the parts that are specific to DSP: closed-form filter design, forward kernels, analytic adjoints for the recursion, and stability checks. It relies on existing libraries for the autodiff graph, GPU code generation (tested here on CUDA), and array interchange. One graph algebra is lowered to a differentiable training engine and to an allocation-free real-time engine; between them, a trained graph is checked for stability and frozen into a versioned artifact that an edge device checks again before playback. We compare Fluxion with six framework-hosted and native baselines under one float32 protocol. Among the systems that compute the exact recursion, Fluxion has the highest GPU throughput when data stays on the device and the highest throughput on most CPU workloads, while its CPU training step is slower than those of torchaudio and GRAFX. Its test suite checks the audio thread for allocations with an instrumented allocator, and we report measured latency tails. Fluxion is open source at https://github.com/matteospanio/fluxion.

title: Capability-as-Infrastructure: Software on Demand
abstract: Capability-as-Infrastructure (CaI) proposes that the durable unit of a software system is no longer the application but the declared capability, together with the data, history, decisions and authority it operates on. Applications, interfaces, synchronization logic and much of the executable code become compiled, replaceable outputs of an agentic environment that builds them when a need appears and maintains them while they are useful: software on demand. Where Methodology-as-Infrastructure compiles how to think, Intent-as-Infrastructure compiles what to reach into, and Governance-as-Infrastructure compiles what must be true, CaI compiles what must be possible, opening a duration axis alongside GaI's upstream terminus. Four properties are required: Capability-declared, Implementation-compiled, Continuity-sovereign (observation, interpretation and accepted state kept distinct), and Human-as-primitive at authority. CaI extends local-first software (the sync protocol itself becomes a compiled capability) and malleable software. This is a concept paper: its two central claims, continuity under replacement and autonomous capability growth, are stated as hypotheses with a validation protocol, and a companion document describes a reference architecture on Cloudflare (Workers, Durable Objects, Agents SDK, Workflows).

title: 枯れ葉から大樹へ:AIエコシステムにおける構造改革のための戦略的提言 — データ配当(Data Dividend)プロトコルとオンデバイス動画生成AI(Veo Nano)アーキテクチャによる共生的未来の設計 (From Leaf to Tree: A Strategic Proposal for Structural Reform in the AI Ecosystem)
abstract: Author: Yoko Hasebe (長谷部 洋子) | Original Manuscript Date: November 2025 現在、生成AIエコシステムは「熱力学的限界(クラウド推論の電力・コスト・遅延)」と「情報学的限界(有機的学習データの枯渇と自己回帰的モデル崩壊:Model Collapse)」という二つの存亡に関わる壁に直面している。本論文(2025年11月起案・第212編アーカイブ版)は、対価なき一方的データ抽出パラダイムが長期的には基盤モデル自身の品質劣化とクリエイター離反を招くことを指摘し、以下の2つの技術的・経済的解決策を提言する。(1) 経済的解決策(Data Dividend / GDDプロトコル):C2PA来歴証明規格とシャープレイ値(Shapley Value)/影響関数に基づく貢献度算定を結合し、人間が創出した高エントロピーな「有機的データ(Organic Data)」へマイクロ・ロイヤリティを自動還元するサプライチェーンを確立する。(2) 技術的解決策(オンデバイス動画生成AI「Veo Nano」アーキテクチャ):クラウドGPU(H100等)の推論コストと通信レイテンシを解消するため、敵対的蒸留(1ステップ推論化)と拡散トランスフォーマー(DiT)の4ビット量子化(W4A8)および連合学習(Federated Learning)を統合し、モバイル・エッジNPU上で完結するプライバシー保護型リアルタイム生成アーキテクチャを設計する。 (English Abstract): Generative AI confronts a dual existential bottleneck: thermodynamic scaling limits (cloud GPU inference energy, cost, and network latency) and information-theoretic degradation ("Model Collapse" induced by training on recursive synthetic data while alienating human creators). Originally authored in November 2025, this 212th monograph proposes a two-pillar structural reform: (1) a C2PA and Shapley-Value Data Dividend (GDD) Protocol that distinguishes human-created "Organic Data" from synthetic outputs and automates micro-royalty attribution; and (2) an On-Device Video Diffusion ("Veo Nano") Architecture combining single-step adversarial distillation, 4-bit Diffusion Transformer quantization (W4A8KV4), and GDPR-compliant Federated Learning on mobile NPUs. title: Analysis of Information Degradation and Reliability Transitions via Structured Noise Injection in Multisensor Localization
abstract: This study investigates information degradation and reliability transitions in multisensor localization systems using a structured noise injection approach. A five-sensor localization scenario is considered, where range measurements are intentionally corrupted by Gaussian perturbations, intermittent burst disturbances, and positive measurement biases. Target coordinates are estimated using a weighted nonlinear least-squares method, while localization performance is evaluated through root mean square error (RMSE), Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), Cramér–Rao Lower Bound (CRLB), and failure rate metrics. Experiments are conducted under signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) levels ranging from −5 dB to 25 dB using 600 Monte Carlo realizations for each operating condition. The results show that increasing perturbation levels progressively reduce localization accuracy and information content while increasing theoretical uncertainty. A distinct reliability transition region is observed between 5 dB and 10 dB, where localization failures rapidly decrease as measurement quality improves. The findings demonstrate that controlled noise injection provides a practical means of exposing information-deficient operating conditions and reliability boundaries in multisensor localization systems.

title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.

title: Prune Early, Verify Deep: Single-Backbone System-One Prefix Tree-GRPO and Speculative Noul Pruning for Long-Horizon Reasoning and Theorem Proving (Tree-Jev-GRPO)
abstract: Full-Length Preprint (12-Page English Edition + 7-Page Chinese Edition) & Benchmark Suite — Part III-C: Long-Horizon Prefix Tree-GRPO & Formal Theorem Proving. Standard flat-sequence GRPO wastes 70%+ of decoding FLOPs regenerating shared reasoning prefixes and continuing to decode 1,500+ tokens after a chain hits an early algebraic contradiction. We introduce Tree-Jev-GRPO, which exploits Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B’s hybrid Gated-DeltaNet linear-attention architecture (3.81x lower prefix-tree KV memory, 14.20 GB vs. 54.10 GB on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB) and co-located jaredpalmer/kev-4b incremental node probing (14.80 ms/node). By immediately pruning dead-end branches where g_noul < 0.30 and computing sibling-relative branch advantages across shared-prefix forks (-61.5% gradient variance), Tree-Jev-GRPO cuts wasted dead-end FLOPs by 66.0% (2.94x compute speedup) and achieves #1 SOTA across 4 Formal & Long-Horizon Reasoning Benchmarks: MiniF2F-Lean4 (64.8%, +20.2% over Flat Binary RLVR), ProofNet-Formal (52.4%), MATH-500 Level-5 Hard (68.7%, +26.9% over Binary RLVR), and GPQA-Diamond (56.1%), reaching 60.50% Mean Accuracy. We introduce Tree-Jev-GRPO, which exploits Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B’s hybrid Gated-DeltaNet linear-attention architecture (3.81x lower prefix-tree KV memory, 14.20 GB vs. 54.10 GB on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB) and co-located jaredpalmer/kev-4b incremental node probing (14.80 ms/node). By immediately pruning dead-end branches where g_noul < 0.30 and computing sibling-relative branch advantages across shared-prefix forks (-61.5% gradient variance), Tree-Jev-GRPO cuts wasted dead-end FLOPs by 66.0% (2.94x compute speedup) and achieves #1 SOTA across 4 Formal & Long-Horizon Reasoning Benchmarks: MiniF2F-Lean4 (64.8%, +20.2% over Flat Binary RLVR), ProofNet-Formal (52.4%), MATH-500 Level-5 Hard (68.7%, +26.9% over Binary RLVR), and GPQA-Diamond (56.1%), reaching 60.50% Mean Accuracy. title: TwinLens: an interpretability digital twin for LLMs
abstract: TwinLens builds a transcoder-based digital twin of a language model, predicts the effect of feature interventions, and checks each prediction against the real model. Across 8,064 interventions on GPT-2 small (56 prompts), the linear twin that attribution graphs describe ranks real effects poorly (Spearman rho 0.20). The error traces to two dropped derivatives, the LayerNorm scale and the attention pattern. Restoring both keeps the graph exactly linear and raises rho to 0.53, matching the nonlinear replacement model (0.52), and cuts catastrophic misses from 2.2% to 0.05%. The fix replicates on Qwen3-0.6B (2,304 edits). A trust model predicts in advance, from the clean run alone, when a prediction will hold (AUROC 0.93).

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Mechanisms and Mutual Mechanisms Under Uncertainty: A General Framework for Uncertainty-Aware Coordination in Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) operate under multiple forms of uncertainty, including uncertainty about the correctness of generated answers, the completeness of available evidence, the validity of intermediate reasoning, the interpretation of task requirements, and the reliability of feedback. Individual-model mechanisms, such as self-reflection, self-evaluation, self-diagnosis, self-correction, and self-verification, provide ways to inspect and revise outputs. Mutual mechanisms, including cross-model evaluation, mutual diagnosis, collaborative reasoning, cross-model verification, and information exchange, provide additional perspectives that may reveal errors overlooked by an individual model. However, neither individual processing nor multi-model collaboration is universally optimal under uncertainty. Individual processing may preserve computational efficiency but remain trapped in persistent errors, whereas collaboration may introduce correlated judgments, misleading consensus, additional computational costs, and uncertainty that is transferred or amplified through interaction. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching Between Self-Mechanisms and Mutual Mechanisms Under Uncertainty (ASSM-MM-U), a conceptual framework that treats uncertainty as a central state variable for dynamically selecting and coordinating individual-model and cross-model processing mechanisms. The framework distinguishes uncertainty associated with incomplete evidence, model limitations, ambiguous task specifications, conflicting information, and uncertain evaluation signals. It represents uncertainty through a multidimensional state that includes estimated magnitude, source, calibration quality, persistence, propagation, and reducibility. A cost-sensitive controller estimates the expected value of candidate mechanisms in reducing relevant uncertainty and improving task outcomes. It can retain an individual mechanism, activate a mutual mechanism, return to individual processing, or transition between mechanism families according to the evolving uncertainty state. The paper formalizes the problem, presents an uncertainty-aware architecture and reference algorithm, identifies reliability safeguards, and proposes research questions, hypotheses, and an experimental protocol. The framework is a research proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Its potential contribution is the explicit integration of uncertainty characterization, uncertainty reduction, mechanism selection, and resource-aware coordination within a common control framework. The novelty and effectiveness of this integration require systematic comparison with existing uncertainty-estimation, adaptive reasoning, and multi-agent collaboration methods.

title: The Collider Beacon: Certified Public Randomness from Symmetry and Quantum Measurement
abstract: We propose particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider as a shared cryptographic resource. The construction rests on a division of labor between symmetry and quantum measurement: rotational invariance fixes the azimuthal distribution to the Haar measure, while each event is an unpredictable quantum draw. We give a formal source model, a master bound decomposing the distance-to-uniform into named physical terms, and a pre-commitment protocol turning embargoed datasets into time-capsule beacons. On 5,211,771 CMS ZeroBias events (Run 2016G open data) we measure h_inf = 7.8413 of 8 bits per event, with the bound closing exactly on its measured parameters; NIST STS reports zero flags. A cross-detector check on ATLAS open data (597,965 events) finds the CMS acceptance seam absent (local band ratio 1.0024 +/- 0.0072; excluded at 14.1 sigma), while ATLAS exhibits a distinct broad modulation -- the seam is a per-device geometric fingerprint. Code and evidence: https://github.com/qBucker/collider-beacon (tag phase0-v1.0).

title: Geometry-Aware Interpolation for Inverse Problems
abstract: Recovering missing visual information from incomplete or degraded images remains a challenging problem, particularly when spatial variations and complex image structures affect reconstruction accuracy. Although Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs) facilitate spatial feature alignment, their reliance on conventional linear or bilinear interpolation limits their ability to capture the underlying geometric characteristics of image data. Furthermore, interpolation based on a restricted set of neighbouring pixels can introduce inconsistencies in gradient propagation, potentially affecting optimisation stability. To address these limitations, we propose a Geometry-Aware Interpolation Network (GAIN), a variational autoencoder-based framework that incorporates manifold geometry into spatial transformation and image reconstruction. Rather than estimating pixel intensities solely from fixed spatial neighbours, GAIN exploits the local tangent structure of the data manifold to construct geometry-informed intensity approximations. An entropy-based regularisation mechanism further guides the estimation of spatial transformation parameters, promoting more adaptive interpolation. In addition, a convolutional normalisation strategy is introduced to regulate the magnitude of non-zero activations and improve gradient stability during training. Extensive experiments on challenging image completion and classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GAIN in improving predictive accuracy while reducing computational cost compared with existing methods.

title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning
abstract: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.

title: Cost Per Correct: benchmark tasks for cost-per-correct-answer evaluation of LLM agents
abstract: Cost Per Correct is a small benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on cost-effectiveness rather than accuracy alone. Instead of asking only whether a model produces a correct answer, it prices the run and reports the cost of each correct answer: total spend in USD divided by the number of correct answers, so a cheap model that is usually right can beat an expensive model that is always right. Version 1.0.0 contains the 5 easy-tier tasks (arithmetic, extraction, classification) that are live in the hosted benchmark. Each task is a self-contained prompt with a deterministic grading assertion (regular-expression match on the response; no LLM judge). The benchmark was created by Karmendra Pandey and first published as a public benchmark on Kaggle Benchmarks on 11 October 2026 (Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge entry), where the live leaderboard remains: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/karmendra8386/cost-per-correct In the first hosted run (11 October 2026), Gemini 2.5 Flash passed all 5 tasks (leaderboard score 100.00) and GPT-OSS 120B failed one extraction task; three runs on the second task show as errors because the Kaggle platform would not register swapped-in models - platform errors, not model answers, disclosed in the accompanying README (hosted-results-2026-10-11.csv) and in the entry write-up at the time. Costs are accounted with tokenecon (software DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23427025), the token-economics library that decomposes per-task spend into prompt, completion, tool-call, and retrieval tokens priced per model tier. The underlying cost model is described in the companion preprint "Token-Economics for Agentic AI" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23195511). This Zenodo record mirrors the benchmark off Kaggle so the task set and methodology carry a permanent, citable DOI independent of any single platform. Provenance: the hosted benchmark was never exported from Kaggle; the task definitions were transcribed verbatim from the local source code used to build it and cross-checked against the entry-day record written from the live task pages. Only tasks e1-e5 of the author's 24-task local suite are live on Kaggle, so only those 5 are in this dataset.

title: SwinMask-Cyto: Supporting Experimental Data and Evaluation Results
abstract: This repository contains supporting experimental data for the research manuscript entitled “SwinMask-Cyto: A Swin Transformer-Enhanced Mask R-CNN Framework for Multi-Class Cervical Cell Instance Segmentation.” The research investigates a Swin Transformer-enhanced Mask R-CNN framework for automated detection and instance segmentation of five cervical cytology cell categories: Superficial-Intermediate, Parabasal, Metaplastic, Koilocytotic, and Dyskeratotic. The repository contains available experimental training logs, validation and test evaluation results, model configuration files, training metric histories, prediction outputs, and supporting numerical data. The experiments investigate different training durations, data augmentation strategies, and model regularization configurations. The best recorded 36-epoch experiment achieved a bounding-box mAP@0.5 of 0.7230 and a segmentation mAP@0.5 of 0.7280 on the held-out test set. These materials are provided to support transparency, reproducibility, and further research in artificial intelligence-assisted cervical cytology analysis. Dataset sources, file descriptions, and applicable data-sharing restrictions are documented in the accompanying files. Original private clinical images are not included in the public research data collection.
