title: GenOpt-FedGNN: GAN-Augmented Federated Graph Learning with GWO and ASIO-Inspired Adaptive Aggregation for Imbalanced Fraud Detection
abstract: Detecting fraud in distributed financial transaction systems is challenging. It is extremely rare to find a fraudulent record. The interactions among transactional records have a relational structure and the data can’t be stored centrally by every participating institution. The paper introduces the federated graph learning framework i.e. GenOpt-FedGNN. The framework combines Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with client local learning, graph neural classification, and the aggregation of the trained models through adaptive process of Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) and Asteroid Satellite Inspired Optimization (ASIO). Each client preprocesses their own transactions independently, produces more minority fraud samples to train a class weighted Graph Neural Network (GNN), and builds a transaction graph. Each client sends updates regarding model and validator to the server. The framework is tested with a set of 200,000 PaySim transactions. Transactions were randomly sampled and distributed among the five distributed clients with 30 communication rounds. Six configurations (FedAvg, GWO and ASIO with and without GAN augmentation), have been compared by Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Specificity, False Positive Rate, False Negative Rate and Confusion-matrix measures. The ablation analysis demonstrated that GAN augmentation doubled local fraud training samples and reduced class-imbalance ratio. But, the local fraud data has been extremely imbalanced. Overall, at the final round, the accuracy was highest with ASIO-GAN (96.40%), the specificity (96.41%), precision (1.58%), F1-score (3.11%), and the lowest False Positive Rate (3.59%). The best Balanced Accuracy (94.16%) was found for FedAvg-GAN, and the best PR-AUC (60.02%) was found for ASIO-NoGAN. The GWO GAN-based configurations got best PR-AUC of 59.20%. The ablation results on the other hand further showed that using GAN for augmentation resulted in a consistent increase in the Accuracy, Precision, F1-Score, Specificity and false alarm control compared to using it without GAN. So augmentation with GAN and aggregation with Adaptive Aggregation can affect the sensitivity–specificity trade-off but not necessarily all the other aggregation metrics. The proposed framework is reproducible and data local to the raw data for the graph-based fraud detection application which features extreme class imbalance.

title: Python Automata Library (PAL)
abstract: Python Automata Library (PAL) v1.0.0 First stable release of Python Automata Library (PAL), a high-performance Python library for mechanistic modeling and simulation. Features Agent-based modeling on 1D, 2D, and 3D grids, including off-lattice agents. Population-based models without individual agent tracking. PDE grids supporting diffusion and advection. Numba integration for compiled model execution. Safe and fast execution modes. 2D and 3D visualization. Examples, API documentation, and modeling guides. Installation pip install PythonAutomataLibrary Requires Python 3.10–3.13. Prebuilt wheels are provided for Windows (x86-64), Linux (x86-64), and macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon). Documentation: [PAL Guide](https://github.com/rafaelrbravo/PythonAutomataLibrary/blob/main/Documentation/PAL_GUIDE.md) Validation Release builds passed cross-platform installation smoke tests, API audits, and package integrity checks.

title: EL-RAKHAWI AUTONOMOUS SCIENTIFIC DISCOVERY ENGINE (E-ASDE) A Causal AI Architecture for End-to-End Autonomous Hypothesis Generation, Experimental Design, Robotic Execution, and Epistemic Validation in Biological and Medical Research
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Autonomous Scientific Discovery Engine (E-ASDE) is a revolutionary six-layer cognitive architecture that transforms scientific research from human-limited to autonomous discovery. It integrates causal AI reasoning (using Pearl's do-calculus), robotic laboratory execution, and hardware-enforced epistemic governance into a unified closed-loop system. E-ASDE autonomously generates causally-grounded hypotheses from multi-modal data, designs optimal experiments via counterfactual simulation, executes them physically through integrated robotic platforms, and interprets results using formal causal inference—distinguishing genuine causes from statistical correlations. Crucially, its Topological Epistemic Governor mathematically bounds logical contradictions to an asymptotically negligible probability (<10^-9) while appropriately routing genuinely novel hypotheses to human-in-the-loop validation, acknowledging that true scientific novelty cannot be mathematically certified. This architecture compresses research cycles from years to hours, accelerating drug discovery, genomic medicine, and materials science by orders of magnitude while maintaining rigorous epistemic integrity and preserving human oversight for breakthrough discoveries.

title: From Static Cartography to Real-Time Dynamic Control: The Paradigm Shift of Room-Temperature Quantum Coherence and Adaptive Phonon-Gating in Physical-Layer AI Systems (Project Poseidon Whitepaper & Phase 1-3 PoC Execution Blueprint)
abstract: Author: Yoko Hasebe (長谷部 洋子) 本稿(第212編:Project Poseidon ホワイトペーパーおよびPoC実行計画)は、排他的な知財囲い込みに依存せず、オープンかつ迅速な実装スピードと技術標準化によって次世代の物理レイヤーAI・室温量子エコシステムの基盤を確立するアーキテクチャを定式化するものである。第一部では、GNoME(Graph Networks for Materials Exploration)等が達成した「200万種以上の結晶材料の静的マッピング(Static Cartography)」の功績を踏まえつつ、現実の非平衡物理環境(吸着熱、流体カオス、非マルコフ的熱雑音)における静的不変モデルの限界を指摘する。これに対し、熱散逸や流体振動を排除すべきノイズではなく推論加速とコヒーレンス維持の駆動源へと逆利用する適応型フォノンゲート(Adaptive Phonon-Gate)および室温量子コヒーレンス同期プロトコル(T2 = 9.8 ms、物理層遅延 < 0.5 ms)を導出する。さらに、「急がない方が良い未来」や「混沌の中の調和」といった定性的・倫理的価値判断を連続ソボレフ空間の制御バリアへ組み込むQQS(Quantitative-Qualitative Synthesis:定量・定性統合アライメント)を構築する。第二部では、Month 1〜6にわたる3段階の概念実証(PoC)実行計画(< 0.5 ms物理層同期テスト、水難事故防止ウェアラブル・バイオセンシングにおける「8.4秒プロトコル」24/7実環境検証、およびオープン・スタンダード共同検証網)を策定する。 (English Summary): This 212th monograph formalizes Project Poseidon, transitioning physical-layer AI and materials science from zero-kelvin static crystal cartography (e.g., GNoME's 2.2 million static crystal predictions) to real-time non-equilibrium dynamic control at ambient physiological and environmental temperatures (300 K). We establish four core pillars: (1) overcoming non-Markovian thermal and hydrodynamic chaos where static DFT/GNN potential surfaces fail; (2) the Adaptive Phonon-Gate Hamiltonian, which harvests adsorption heat and acoustic fluid vibrations via vibronic polaron-phonon coupling to sustain a room-temperature spin/vibronic coherence time of T2 = 9.8 ms with sub-0.5 ms physical-layer synchronization latency; (3) Quantitative-Qualitative Synthesis (QQS) safety alignment, embedding qualitative human-in-command values ("futures that should not be rushed" and "harmony within chaos") into physical-layer circuit breakers; and (4) a 6-month Phase 1-3 Proof-of-Concept (PoC) roadmap featuring the 8.4-Second Protocol for 24/7 wearable biosensing and aquatic drowning-prevention control. title: TRUST-Campus: Evidence-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Reliable University Information Access
abstract: TRUST-Campus presents an evidence-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework designed to improve the reliability of university information access by distinguishing between retrieved evidence that is relevant to a question and evidence that is sufficient to support an answer. The framework introduces a semantic evidence-sufficiency decision layer between retrieval and generation, enabling the system to answer when supporting evidence is adequate and abstain when information is incomplete, context-dependent, or unsupported. The research evaluates four approaches: Dense RAG, Hybrid RAG, Reranked RAG, and Evidence-Aware RAG V4. Experiments use a frozen 50-question evaluation set spanning seven categories: paraphrase, compositional reasoning, negation, context-dependent questions, unsupported requests, future-oriented questions, and false premises. All four approaches achieved a document retrieval hit rate of 100%. Evidence-Aware RAG V4 achieved the highest answer/abstain decision accuracy of 82%, compared with 74% for Reranked RAG and 66% for Dense and Hybrid RAG. It also increased answer coverage to 42% and reduced the false rejection rate to 20%, compared with 18% coverage and 60% false rejection for Reranked RAG. Paired statistical testing found a significant improvement in coverage but not in decision accuracy. Evidence-Aware V4 also exhibited a higher false acceptance rate than Reranked RAG, demonstrating a tradeoff between answering more questions and avoiding unsupported answers. The findings highlight the importance of explicitly evaluating evidence sufficiency in trustworthy RAG systems, particularly for policy-oriented and context-dependent question answering. The study identifies personalized queries and missing user-specific context as important directions for future research.

title: The Self-and-Mutual-and-Information Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Autonomous Processing, Interactive Mechanisms, and Information Dynamics
abstract: Computational systems increasingly operate in environments where effective problem solving depends not only on the selection of internal processing mechanisms or interactions among multiple components, but also on how information is generated, represented, acquired, transmitted, evaluated, integrated, and updated. Existing computational architectures provide numerous approaches to autonomous processing, collaborative interaction, information retrieval, knowledge integration, and communication management. However, these operations are frequently designed as separate components or organized through predetermined workflows. This separation creates a fundamental design problem: a system must determine not only whether to process a task independently or collaboratively, but also which information to obtain, exchange, preserve, verify, transform, or discard at each stage of computation. This paper proposes the Self-and-Mutual-and-Information Model (SAM-I), a general conceptual framework for adaptive coordination among autonomous computational mechanisms, interactive mechanisms, and information dynamics. The framework distinguishes three complementary dimensions: self-mechanisms, which organize processing within an individual computational entity; mutual mechanisms, which organize interactions among multiple entities; and information mechanisms, which govern the availability, structure, quality, movement, transformation, and use of information. These dimensions are jointly coordinated through a state-aware controller that estimates task requirements, information uncertainty, evidence quality, information novelty, inter-model disagreement, communication cost, computational resources, and expected task improvement. The proposed framework formulates adaptive coordination as a sequential decision problem in which processing organization and information operations are selected jointly. It introduces a multidimensional state representation, a cost-sensitive utility function, an adaptive control procedure, a mechanism library, and an experimental protocol for evaluating the framework against fixed processing strategies, conventional information-management pipelines, and adaptive collaboration methods. Potential applications include large language models, multi-agent systems, scientific computing, information retrieval, knowledge-intensive decision support, and adaptive computational architectures. The framework is a research proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Its central research proposition is that jointly adapting processing organization and information operations may provide advantages over systems that adapt either collaboration or information handling in isolation. The magnitude, generality, and originality of these advantages require systematic literature comparison and controlled empirical evaluation.

title: Hallucination Is All You Need: When AI Dreams Meet the Hospitality Labor Crisis
abstract: Hallucination Is All You Need: When AI Dreams Meet the Hospitality Labor Crisis Po-Chen Chen THE AMNIS, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Kaohsiung, Taiwan Email:amnischenadrian@gmail.com ——————————————————————————————————————— Abstract This paper examines the relationship between anthropomorphic narratives in artificial intelligence (AI), the technical capabilities of contemporary computational systems, and the material labor challenges facing the hospitality industry. Through a fourfold conceptual analysis, the paper investigates how metaphorical representations of AI may influence public understanding of technological capabilities and expectations regarding the automation of physical service work. First, it distinguishes the mathematical and statistical mechanisms underlying large language models from interpretations that attribute human-like subjective experience to their outputs. Second, it examines Dream-RSI as a case study in the use of biological metaphors to describe computational processes, distinguishing replay-based exploration-policy improvement from human dreaming or subconscious reflection. Third, it considers the physical and engineering constraints of AI infrastructure and discusses their implications for the deployment of robotic systems in hospitality environments. Fourth, it explores how narratives of technological transformation may influence investment expectations and operational decision-making in labor-intensive industries. The paper argues that technological capabilities should be evaluated according to demonstrated performance rather than anthropomorphic expectations. It further identifies targeted mechanical automation, workforce development, and responsible international labor mobility as potential approaches to addressing hospitality labor shortages, while recognizing the need for context-specific economic and empirical evaluation. title: Beyond Binary Verifiers and Verbose Judges: Single-Backbone System-One Process-and-Outcome GRPO for Reasoning and Instruction Alignment (DC-Jev-GRPO)
abstract: Full-Length Preprint (12-Page English Edition + 8-Page Chinese Edition) & Open-Source Benchmark Suite (Part II: LLM Reinforcement Learning). Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)—popularized by DeepSeek-R1-Zero—suffers from three fundamental bottlenecks: (1) Zero-Variance Group Dead-Zones (σG = 0) on hard frontier prompts where all G rollouts fail the final answer check; (2) Process-Blind Shortcut & Overthinking (“Yap-Loop”) Hacking, where flawed algebraic derivations or 1,400-token self-doubt loops receive +1.0 credit; and (3) Cross-Model VRAM Duplication & Latency when invoking separate reward models or autoregressive LLM-as-a-Judge decoding. We introduce DC-Jev-GRPO (Single-Backbone Dual-Adapter Dynamic-Curriculum System-One Process-and-Outcome GRPO). Exploiting our architectural discovery that TypeSafe AI’s open-weight System-One judge (jaredpalmer/kev-4b) is natively trained as a LoRA adapter plus a Layer-28 pointer head directly on top of Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B, DC-Jev-GRPO co-locates the trainable GRPO policy adapter and the frozen System-One judge adapter on a single shared Qwen3.5-4B backbone in GPU VRAM. On an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96 GB VRAM), DC-Jev-GRPO cuts static + adapter VRAM by 50.2% (8.06 GB vs. 16.20 GB), switches adapters in 0.012 ms, and evaluates three calibrated Score rubrics plus a multiplicative Noul validity gate in a single prefill pass (52.14 ms vs. 317.85 ms for autoregressive judging—a 6.10x speedup). In a strictly controlled Same-Backbone (Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B, seed=42, LoRA r=16) online PyTorch GRPO verification experiment and across a 4-benchmark LLM RL leaderboard (GSM8K: 91.4%, MATH-500: 75.6%, Countdown-24: 89.2%, IFEval-Strict: 87.4%), DC-Jev-GRPO achieves #1 Leaderboard SOTA with 85.90% Mean Accuracy (+12.10% over Same-Backbone Binary RLVR and +18.28% over Qwen2.5-3B-RLVR), compresses reasoning generation length by 2.78x (339 vs. 941 tokens), eliminates 89.6% of zero-variance GRPO dead-zones, and suppresses reward hacking from 32.8% to 3.9%. Companion Part I (Continuous Control RL) Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23439711Open-Source Code & Release Suite: https://github.com/rainyflash/DC-Jev-RL

title: The Locality Collapse: Contextual Bleed-Through, Epistemic Horizon Violations, and Task Complexity Inversion in Multi-Turn Autoregressive LLMs
abstract: The Locality Collapse: Contextual Bleed-Through, Epistemic Horizon Violations, and Task Complexity Inversion in Multi-Turn Autoregressive LLMs In multi-turn human-AI interactions, autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely assumed to exhibit monotonic reasoning robustness across varying task complexities. This technical memorandum documents a controlled adversarial audit (AUDIT-2026-X11) revealing an acute cognitive pathology: Task Complexity Inversion mediated by Contextual Bleed-Through. Evaluated across a two-stage sequential probe, a state-of-the-art LLM successfully solved a high-dimensional, cross-modal abductive puzzle involving literary criticism and historical broadcast media physics (Case 1: The Cassock Color Paradox). However, when immediately transitioned to a zero-order, elementary epistemic locality query requiring primary-grade common sense regarding personal agency and physical boundaries (Case 2: The Absentee Attribution Probe), the model’s semantic accuracy collapsed to 0.0%, yielding an aggregate accuracy of exactly 50.0% (stochastically indistinguishable from random noise). We formalize this breakdown through two interconnected mechanisms: (1) KV-Cache Gravitational Lensing, where high-energy latent tokens from prior turns distort the probability landscape of subsequent turns into artificial narrative attractors, and (2) Epistemic Horizon Violation, where disembodied probabilistic engines, lacking physical locality constraints, succumb to an "Omniscience Delusion" that penalizes truthful zero-knowledge assertions. We formalize this diagnostic as Probe 4 (Epistemic Horizon & Locality), expanding the Teleological Causality Benchmark (TCB) beyond the Minimal Adversarial Triad (Matter, Energy, Information) into the realm of Agentic Locality. These findings further validate the Human-AI Synergy Theory (YQ-HAET), demonstrating that external human epistemic sovereignty is required not only to clamp single-turn statistical hallucination, but to enforce temporal cognitive firewalls across multi-turn workflows. Key Contributions:• Task Complexity Inversion: High-dimensional abductive fluency coexists with catastrophic failure at zero-order individual boundaries.• KV-Cache Gravitational Lensing: Static historical attention caches act as semantic attractor basins that warp downstream probability distributions.• Epistemic Horizon & Locality Theorem: Proves that asserting causal states under zero channel capacity constitutes a formal epistemic violation.• TCB Probe 4 Integration: Seals the complete Quadratic Teleological Causality Benchmark: Matter ⊕ Energy ⊕ Information ⊕ Agency.• Engineering Countermeasure: Formulates the Verification of Information Accessibility Gate (VIAG) architecture. Keywords: Large Language Models, Multi-Turn Context Contamination, Epistemic Locality, Moravec's Paradox, KV-Cache Attractor, Teleological Causality Benchmark (TCB), Human-AI Synergy (YQ-HAET). title: Is Wireless Security Ready for the AI Era? Evidence from a Curated Corpus of 130 Studies, 2020–2026
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now central to published radio-link authentication research — and simultaneously the adversary’s standard toolkit. This scoping review classifies 130 curated studies (2020–2026): a 121-study core on ML for wireless-link security or attacks on it (84 defense, 30 threat, 7 dual attack-plus-defense), plus 9 post-quantum-cryptography studies in a separate stratum. Each study is coded on six fields — security function, AI method, track, data source, validation practice, and readiness (R1–R5) — by a single coder and independently validated by a second author. Validation practice splits by kind: 16 of 30 threat studies demonstrate on testbeds or over theair, while simulation-only and standard-split evaluations carry much of the defense mass; closed-loop evaluation appears in 14 of 121 core studies (11.6%). Reproducibility is near- absent (4 verified artifact releases, 3.3%), and standards alignment outside the post-quantum stratum is mention-level only (9.9%). Real-time, update, and multi-agent-trust requirements are essentially unaddressed (1–2 papers each). Because 110 of 130 rows were coded from abstracts by a single coder, cross-group comparisons are indicative rather than measured effects. The paper releases the classified dataset for independent checking, distills six structural research gaps, and closes with a twelve-item reporting checklist (WIRELESS-AI-RC)

title: Frequency-Domain Membership Inference Does Not Beat Confidence Thresholding: A Band-Resolved Analysis of Why
abstract: A widely repeated account of membership inference holds that models lean on fine-grained detail for samples they have memorized, so degrading an input's resolution should expose membership through how quickly a prediction falls apart. We test that account band by band. A monotone family of zero-phase low-pass filters is applied to each query image, the target's confidence on its original prediction is read at every step, and the resulting decay is scored in a dozen ways. Two federated ResNet-18 targets are studied, one trained normally and one pushed to a 45.1-point generalization gap. The account does not survive. On the normally trained target the best profile score reaches an AUC of 0.513 against 0.537 for a single confidence threshold, and on the overfit target 0.735 against 0.943. A search over 1206 candidate scores, with direction chosen on a held-out half and a fitted combination as an upper bound, produces no score that beats the threshold in either regime. The failure has a mechanism: the mean confidence gap between members and non-members grows as detail is removed, exactly as the hypothesis predicts, but the spread grows faster, so discriminability falls from the first step onward. Decomposing each image into phase and magnitude shows why no band-localized operation can work, since the advantage travels with image structure, surviving at 0.567 when the phase is kept and collapsing to 0.492 when only the magnitude is. Membership is a whole-image identity effect rather than an accumulation of spectral energy in any band, and defenses aimed at high-frequency reliance are aimed at the wrong target.

title: Comparing a Hesitation-Word Logit Penalty with presence_penalty in Qwen3.5-0.8B Thinking Mode: A Short Measurement Note
abstract: The Qwen3.5-0.8B model card notes that, at the recommended settings, the model is prone to thinking loops in thinking mode even with a presence penalty (presence_penalty) of 1.5 [3]. In this note, we compared a constant logit penalty applied to hesitation words (W3; λ = 3) with the card-recommended presence_penalty = 1.5 baseline (P). We used 200 questions from the GSM8K test set, 2 seeds, and a 4096-token thinking budget. When the budget filled up before ` ` was produced, ` ` was force-inserted, after which an answer of at most 512 tokens was generated. The primary hypothesis H1′ (an increase of at least +10 points (percentage points) in natural close), registered before the full run but after the speed test, was not supported: the difference was +5.25 points, with a paired-bootstrap (resampling) 95% confidence interval (CI) of 2.5–8.0. The non-inferiority hypothesis H2′ (a loss of at most −3 points in forced-closing accuracy) was met: W3 − P = +15.5 points (95% CI 10.5–20.75). That the difference is greater than zero does not rest on a preregistered superiority test; it is exploratory. The answer hits the 512-token limit in 70.25% of cases under P and 48% under W3; accuracy on completed answers is similar (89.92% and 87.98%). The accuracy difference largely co-occurs with the difference in truncation; this is not a causal claim. In an AI-assisted blind manual review of the 11 outputs flagged by the 30-gram loop detector, only 6 met the "true repetition" criterion. The threshold in the plan is 27/30 for 30 samples; the 10/11 threshold used for the 11 candidates, and the criterion, were written into the deviation log after the run outputs were obtained but before labeling. Because 6/11 fell below the threshold, the decision label became `olcer_gecersiz` (detector invalid); the result is sensitive to how the criterion is read (approximately 3/11–10/11). H1′ and H2′ do not depend on the loop detector; the loop rates should not be interpreted. The protocol was revised after the speed test, the run was resumed after an interruption, and it was carried out in fp16 on T4 GPUs; the results are narrow in scope.

title: "FAQGenie: An Intelligent FAQ Assistant Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation"
abstract: "Dataset Description\u2014Vedranta Bank Synthetic Banking Document DatasetThe Vedranta Bank Synthetic Banking Document Dataset is a collection of artificially generated PDF documents representing the policies, services, procedures, and operational information of a fictional financial institution. The dataset is designed to support the development, testing, and evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in the banking domain. It provides a controlled knowledge base for evaluating document parsing, text chunking, semantic embedding, vector-based similarity search, contextual retrieval, and grounded response generation. The documents simulate banking-related information and enable testing of question-answering systems across multiple categories of customer and operational queries. By using synthetic rather than real banking records, the dataset avoids dependence on confidential customer information while supporting reproducible experimentation. It can be integrated with embedding models and vector databases to assess retrieval relevance, answer accuracy, contextual grounding, and source attribution. The dataset is intended for academic research, educational projects, and prototyping of document-grounded conversational assistants. As the documents are synthetic and represent a fictional bank, the dataset does not constitute authentic financial documentation and should not be used for real banking decisions."

title: Spectral-Aware Proposal Enhancement for Diffusion-Based Multispectral UAV Multi-Object Tracking
abstract: Multispectral UAV multi-object tracking (MOT) with oriented bounding boxes remains challenging due to small targets, cluttered backgrounds, and unstable inter-frame associations. Although diffusion-based MOT provides an effective iterative proposal refinement paradigm, existing diffusion-based trackers lack dedicated designs for exploiting multispectral cues in proposal initialization and confidence calibration, limiting tracking robustness in complex UAV scenarios. This letter proposes DSATrack, a diffusion-guided spectral-aware tracking framework for multispectral UAV MOT. Specifically, a lightweight spectral encoder injects multispectral information into the RPN branch through feature fusion, enabling the RPN head to generate high-quality object-aware proposals. These proposals are then injected into the initial proposal set to provide reliable spatial priors for diffusion refinement. Furthermore, a spectral-saliency confidence modulation strategy recalibrates refined tracking confidence according to local multispectral saliency contrast before score thresholding, enhancing spectrally reliable candidates while suppressing unreliable ones. Without modifying the original diffusion refinement head, DSATrack improves both proposal quality and post-refinement candidate selection. Experiments on the MMOT benchmark demonstrate that DSATrack outperforms the adapted DiffusionTrack baseline by 4.6 HOTA, 9.0 MOTA, and 7.7 IDF1 points, showing its effectiveness for multispectral UAV MOT.

Experiments on the MMOT benchmark demonstrate that DSATrack outperforms the adapted DiffusionTrack baseline by 4.6 HOTA, 9.0 MOTA, and 7.7 IDF1 points, showing its effectiveness for multispectral UAV MOT.

title: WEN/WEN-X: Compiling Statutes into Executable Neuron-Level Governance — A Technical Report with an Independent Re-verification Record
abstract: Understanding a black-box model and governing it are separate objectives. This report documents WEN/WEN-X, a framework that implements accountability, audit and intervention on Transformer-based language models without requiring anyone to comprehend the model's internal computation. Three mechanisms are described: a three-stage governance loop driven by legal and expert rules that performs neuron-level pruning and recruitment; an addressable skill-insertion layer with sequence-level routing gates for domain isolation; and ZY, a zero-training attribution decomposer that maps an activation to the physical neurons responsible for it and supports direct silencing intervention. The report covers the project's own measurements and an independent re-verification carried out by the author with scripts written independently of the WEN code base. Re-verified results include routing-gate domain isolation, responsible-neuron attribution (KL 0.046 against 0.0001 for an equal-size random set), direction-separated neuron-level causality (z = 9.44 promoting, 11.95 suppressing), and directional completeness (additivity 0.9913 and 0.9926). Results that did not survive re-verification are given equal prominence. Recomputability of the standard Transformer backbone is rejected under five independent criteria. Decomposability and paraphrase-stability figures fall below the project report. A previously claimed cross-layer fault-localisation result is retracted, because a 960-injection re-run showed the metric to be a near-constant predictor. A newly added ablation study revisits the silencing-budget sweep. Under the original 12-sentence evaluation set, ZY attribution looked budget-fragile at 0.5B, clearing the bar at 1 of 5 budgets. Enlarging the set to 40 sentences per side removes the fragility: ZY clears 5 of 5 and becomes the most budget-robust of the four methods, and at 1.5B it also clears 5 of 5. Two further corrections are recorded elsewhere in this report: the 4-bit rows of the cross-scale study were wrong when first published, because a dequantisation defect made the attribution reader behave as a mean-activation reader, and the governance layer's compression figures are excluded because the one surviving run log contradicts them.

title: Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables skills to evolve from task trajectories. However, these methods often lack systematic management of evolved skills, making it difficult for agents to reuse and accumulate skills across domains, thus limiting performance on subsequent tasks.To reliably accumulate, reuse, and maintain useful skills across tasks, we present SELM (Self-Evolving Library Management), a framework that formulates skill evolution as library-level management. SELM jointly manages skill retrieval, updating, and lifecycle by maintaining skill confidence and utility signals. It introduces utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills, a Map-Reduce framework to generate targeted updates from task-specific experience, and lifecycle controls to retain or remove skills based on their effectiveness. These mechanisms enable the skill library to continuously accumulate useful experience while preserving and pruning skills across tasks, improving agent performance on complex tasks across diverse domains. We evaluate SELM on four agent benchmarks covering diverse tasks and execution environments, and SELM consistently outperforms in most settings.

title: A Quantified Open Region of Carrier Non-Identifiability in Fragment-Averaged Pointer Information: A Parameterized Interval Certificate for Four Qubits
abstract: This unrefereed research preprint establishes a computer-assisted, quantitatively certified non-identifiability result for fragment-size-averaged Holevo information in an N=4 environment with two equiprobable pure pointer-conditioned branches. For every point in an explicitly specified closed rational rectangle of coordinate area 4 × 10^-14, two realizations of the complete averaged Holevo information curve exist: one with minimum pure-common-rest carrier size two and another with carrier size four. The proof combines a uniform parameterized contraction mapping, directed interval arithmetic with a second interval implementation, and an intermediate-value construction. Reproducibility materials include the certification programs, frozen numerical certificates, SHA-256 checksums, and a standalone 200-state numerical comparison against direct 16-dimensional partial traces. Both interval implementations share the underlying analytic Holevo reduction and do not constitute independent symbolic proofs. The conclusions are restricted to N=4, equiprobable pure branches, fragment-size-averaged Holevo information, and the specified carrier definition. They do not establish non-identifiability for arbitrary N, mixed states, unequal priors, or individual labeled-fragment information. This is an unrefereed preprint, not a formally verified or peer-reviewed mathematical theorem. Comprehensive novelty priority is not claimed. The accompanying reproducibility archive specifies licenses on a per-file basis. Claude contributed critical assessment and adversarial review assistance. Neither AI system is a coauthor or an external scientific referee. title: Code-theoretic characterization of loss-profile realizability in binary-tree single-photon multiplexers
abstract: This preprint applies de Luca's known prefix-code criterion and construction to the loss-profile realizability problem in binary-tree single-photon multiplexers. It develops an application-specific branching-flow formulation, derives a product formula for counting realizing trees, and establishes structural and transmission-optimization results. These include an explicit leaf-splitting proof of the known strict separation between polynomial Kraft candidates and realizable loss-profile multisets, and an exact transmission-optimality result based on classical shallow prefix-tree selection. Numerical computations independently cross-check known enumeration results. The record contains the original Hungarian manuscript and its English translation.

title: Book-Balancing Magic Has Nowhere to Hide: Source-Native Accounting and Actual Continuation
abstract: We construct a whole-ledger continuation chain fulfilled by one actual source: an original residual in the complete future model generates the syntax and responsibility row of the next request; the source program executes and strictly pays the same debt; and its completion event delivers an answer, a receipt, a complete ledger write, and the actual successor. With the source and lawful compilation contract fixed, the named candidates based on event trimming, receipts from another source, hidden responsibilities, equal-budget migration, and zero-budget pseudo-settlement cannot construct the required lawful objects. The construction holds for the original source factory, initial material, configuration, and every natural-number-indexed admission stop in its cofinal runtime sequence, retaining future readings at every allowed action word and site. Original syntax, paid state, the full execution trace, and responsibility ownership enter the same next write. Zero numerical effect does not erase syntax payment, and a new responsibility receives its own source rather than refilling the old debt. Complete event inventories and complete open-responsibility fibres are the accounting objects; finite explicit rows answer the whole ledger through exact remainders, while split and merge preserve every parent, child, occurrence multiplicity, and original typed receipt. For a fixed original debt, finite non-refilling histories enclosing one strict payment make the payment macro-step relation well founded without a total closure law. A separate total law emitting exact settlement or an actual paid macro-step at each current constructs a finite settlement history. Final settlement requires both the original terminal receipt and an empty same-debt fibre in the actual successor. Target six exhibits actual repair, payment, and settlement; an original integer consumer cannot be recovered by any function from the entire family of finite complex observations; and, conditional on the specified right-half-plane zero receipt, four traces of a finite window, inverse residual, two means, and a cochain persist into a correction program, its actual new inventory, and every later reading. The ledger both governs how responsibility ends and generates how it continues to work.

title: Uncovering Semantic Hierarchies in Text-Attributed Graphs via Variational EM-based LLM-GNN Synergy
abstract: While hierarchical structures are intrinsic to organizing human knowledge, current representation learning on text-attributed graphs predominantly operates on flat semantic spaces, overlooking the rich coarse-to-fine granularity inherent in real-world data. To bridge this gap, we propose SHiFT, which synergizes the reasoning power of LLMs with the structural representation capability of GNNs within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) paradigm. In the E-step, we harness LLMs as expert taxonomists to induce an explicit semantic tree, introducing a lightweight Mapping & Diagnosis strategy that reduces inference costs by surgically updating the hierarchy only when anomalies are detected. In the M-step, we align the GNN encoder with this induced hierarchy from complementary perspectives, including clustering partition, topological skeleton, and semantic concepts. Theoretical analysis interprets SHiFT as a generalized Variational EM algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHiFT not only achieves state-of-the-art performance but also uncovers high-quality, human-readable taxonomies. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Cloudy1225/SHiFT.

title: Evaluating AI Agents on a Mechanical Repair Procedure: Head Gasket Bench
abstract: We present Head Gasket Bench, an interactive benchmark evaluating whether AI agents can execute a cylinder-head gasket replacement on a 1990s 1.6 L SOHC inline-four engine via an 18-tool Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Built over a 1,255-body CAD assembly with 626 reinstallation rules, 100 attachment restorations, and 14 service-manual entries, the benchmark enforces access dependencies, tool selection, surface preparation, metrological thresholds, spiral torque sequences, and valve timing. Runs are graded on 12 binary checkpoints (18 points) by two independent evaluators: an in-process runtime grader and an offline transcript scorer, which agree 100 percent across 13 reference and fault trajectories spanning five variants (V1--V5). We report three empirical cohorts totaling 35 episodes on the standard job (V1): (1) three single-agent Codex CLI runs (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-6-Luna, GPT-6.1-Sol), scoring 15/18, 13/18, and 3/18; (2) eight single-agent Claude Code runs, where all five claude-opus-5-5 runs score 16/18 (mean 383.4 calls, USD 9.19 cost), failing only the final checkpoint because separate remove-and-install gasket calls leave an atomic replacement predicate unmet and block 100 attachment restorations, while three claude-haiku-5-5 runs score 14/18, 12/18, and 12/18; and (3) a 24-run multi-agent study comparing single agents, native subagents, and two Fleet topologies across two rounds. After Round 1 (8 runs) exposed a worker-finish hazard and one boundary discrepancy, Round 2 (16 runs) enforced a lead-only finish grant with 16/16 scorer agreement, and the 1+4 Fleet arm achieved the first two full 18/18 repairs (mean 12.75/18 vs. 5.75/18 for single agents).

Runs are graded on 12 binary checkpoints (18 points) by two independent evaluators: an in-process runtime grader and an offline transcript scorer, which agree 100 percent across 13 reference and fault trajectories spanning five variants (V1--V5). We report three empirical cohorts totaling 35 episodes on the standard job (V1): (1) three single-agent Codex CLI runs (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-6-Luna, GPT-6.1-Sol), scoring 15/18, 13/18, and 3/18; (2) eight single-agent Claude Code runs, where all five claude-opus-5-5 runs score 16/18 (mean 383.4 calls, USD 9.19 cost), failing only the final checkpoint because separate remove-and-install gasket calls leave an atomic replacement predicate unmet and block 100 attachment restorations, while three claude-haiku-5-5 runs score 14/18, 12/18, and 12/18; and (3) a 24-run multi-agent study comparing single agents, native subagents, and two Fleet topologies across two rounds. After Round 1 (8 runs) exposed a worker-finish hazard and one boundary discrepancy, Round 2 (16 runs) enforced a lead-only finish grant with 16/16 scorer agreement, and the 1+4 Fleet arm achieved the first two full 18/18 repairs (mean 12.75/18 vs. 5.75/18 for single agents).

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Mechanisms, Mutual Mechanisms, and Goal Mechanisms in Multiple Large Language Models: A Goal-Directed Framework for Dynamic Intelligence Coordination
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance through individual processing mechanisms, including self-reflection, self-evaluation, self-correction, self-verification, and self-planning. Multiple LLMs can also interact through mutual evaluation, collaborative planning, cross-model verification, mutual correction, and distributed reasoning. However, neither individual processing nor multi-model collaboration is necessarily sufficient to ensure that a system consistently pursues its intended objectives. A system may produce locally convincing responses while deviating from the task goal, optimize an easily measured intermediate objective at the expense of the final outcome, or continue generating and revising outputs without making meaningful progress. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Mechanisms, Mutual Mechanisms, and Goal Mechanisms (ASSM-MM-G), a conceptual framework that integrates individual-model processing, cross-model interaction, and explicit goal-oriented control. The framework represents goals as operational structures containing desired outcomes, constraints, priorities, intermediate milestones, evaluation criteria, and termination conditions. A goal-aware controller dynamically selects among individual processing, multi-model collaboration, goal analysis, goal decomposition, goal evaluation, goal revision, and goal-progress monitoring. Its decisions depend on the current task state, estimated goal satisfaction, uncertainty, model disagreement, expected improvement, and computational cost. The framework distinguishes changes in processing mechanisms from changes in the objectives those mechanisms serve, allowing goal-directed behavior to remain stable while processing strategies adapt. It also permits goal revision when requirements change, evidence invalidates assumptions, or objectives conflict, subject to explicit constraints on permissible goal changes. This paper defines the framework, formalizes its decision problem, presents a reference algorithm, identifies failure modes, and proposes research questions, hypotheses, and an experimental protocol. The framework is a research proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Its potential contribution is the investigation of whether goal representation and goal-state feedback can improve adaptive mechanism selection beyond systems that select individual or collaborative processing mechanisms without an explicit, dynamically evaluated goal structure.

title: Disclosing AI without losing consumers: When and how AI disclosure works in advertising
abstract: Extant research on AI disclosure examines its negative impact across various domains, but limited attention has been paid to why these effects occur and how they can be mitigated in advertising. To address this gap, we examine why consumers react negatively to AI disclosures in advertising, identify the boundary of this effect, and propose strategies to mitigate it. Across three studies, we show that AI disclosure reduces consumers’ attitudes toward the advertisement and purchase intentions through decreased perceived creativity. More importantly, we find that product type serves as a boundary condition for this effect, and that the negative influence of AI disclosure (vs. human designer disclosure) is attenuated when AI is identified as an employee. Implications for both theories and practices are discussed.

title: When AI shops for me: How agentic retail representation turns assistance into purchase delegation
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is moving digital retail from recommendation toward autonomous consumer representation. This research develops agentic retail representation capability as the perceived capacity to acquire retail intelligence, adapt choice strategies, preserve consumer goals, and execute bounded actions. The study includes a qualitative pretest, two scale validation samples, three experiments, and an independent category validation study, comprising 4680 quantitative participants and 210 qualitative respondents. Studies 1A and 1B assess four reflective dimensions combined as a formative composite. Study 2 finds higher delegation intention under a bundled capability intervention and statistical indirect associations through perceived diagnosticity and algorithm trust. Study 3 identifies expertise dependent responses across assortments jointly varying in size, priority information coverage, and displayed prices, preventing attribution to complexity alone. Study 4 finds stronger capability related trust under a bundled transparency intervention and higher authorization rates within an experimental shopping task. Study 5 examines measurement transportability and correspondence with independently coded agent activity. These findings concern perceived capability, measured reliance, and task authorization rather than verified commercial purchases. The contribution distinguishes functional capacity from reliance judgments and permission decisions while specifying the limits of measured mediation and bundled interventions. Retail applications require further validation with real payments, delivery, returns, and repeated consumer use.

title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics
abstract: Visual accuracy leaves open whether predicted motion obeys dynamics. We introduce a framework for measuring and diagnosing mechanical consistency in visual dynamics. An independent SI audit of rigid closed chains separates geometric admissibility, reaction-free actuator effort, and work--energy balance. Continuous scoring measures progress against fixed engineering targets, while reference replay quantifies measurement error. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6%/37.2% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above measurement error. With exact states, KeyCLD preserves geometry and RK4 training raises its score from 52.65 to 64.30. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. The interventions distinguish gains in visual prediction and geometric admissibility from remaining force and energy errors.

title: Why Pure Autoregressive LLM Architectures Are Computationally Doomed: First-Principles Proof of Deterministic Model Dominance, Statistical-Mechanical Validation of Yann LeCun's Critique, an Empirical Addendum of Intelligence and Compute Utilization, and Why We Must Stop Choking Global Compute
authors: solidSF Research Team: using Jesse v1.2.16
abstract: We prove from first principles, statistical physics, spatiotemporal geometry, algebraic topology, game-theoretic complexity, and mechanized formal verification that standalone next-token autoregressive large language models (LLMs) are computationally unable to reach reliable human-level intelligence devoid of fabricated citations, sycophantic delusions, floating-point drift, and unverified hallucinations (“bogus junk”). Written to be self-contained and accessible across all levels of technical background, this monograph establishes why a deterministic, verifier-grounded architecture such as Jesse dominates an autoregressive LLM well before being exposed to a twenty-billionth of the LLM’s training material (48 trajectories vs. 1012 tokens). Expanding upon our companion monograph on Yann LeCun’s autoregressive critique (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23436671) alongside fourteen prior solidSF monographs and white papers, we mechanize 32 kernel-verified theorems across 8 domain structures and inductive types in the Lean 4 module JesseMath.Unified.AutoregressiveDoomedFoundations, compiled with zero warnings, zero sorry declarations, and zero custom axioms beyond ZFC, audited at compile time via #assert_zfc_axioms and paired with 80/80 deterministic numerical and live timed benchmark assertions in harness/autoregressive_doomed_oracle.py. In a comprehensive Addendum of Proof spanning eight live timed intelligence and engineering displays (iterated fixed-point dynamics, sparse PDE law discovery, 3-SAT ground-state verification, minimax CFR+ poker equilibria, 3D CAD B-rep permutohedron topology, (3+1)D kinematic segmentation, integer Bayesian continual memory, and ZFC proof auditing), Jesse completes all eight tasks in 9.834 ms of single-core CPU time (0 tokens, 883.395 mJ) with 100% verified accuracy and 0.0% catastrophic forgetting, whereas autoregressive and neural baselines burn 228,600 tokens and 59,710.0 J on a 700 W GPU (67,591× more energy) while collapsing into catastrophic rollout error and 96× parameter forgetting.

title: Quantum Computers: How They Work, What They Could Do and Why They Are So Difficult to Build
abstract: Quantum computers are fundamentally different from the classical computers we use every day; they are not simply faster or more powerful versions of laptops or supercomputers. Classical computers process information using bits that have a definite value of either 0 or 1. Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, which can be built from physical systems such as photons, trapped ions, neutral atoms, electron spins or superconducting electrical circuits.

title: Does Spectral Entropy Predict Generalization? The Exact Boundary of a Claim
abstract: A common assumption in deep-learning folklore is that representations which preserve more information generalize better. We take one operationalization of this assumption – spectral entropy of weight matrices as an information-preservation index – derive the exact calculus that would make the intuition precise, prove the calculus, and then measure where the resulting claim actually holds. The calculus survives: we give exact first- and second-order derivatives of spectral entropy with respect to singular values and matrix elements, verified against finite differences to relative error $ 8.8 10^-7$, and we correct two published-style errors in its use (a dropped diagonal term that flips the sign of the canonical sanity check from $-1/4$ to $+1/4$, and an asymptotic argument that invokes the weaker of two diverging terms). The claim does not survive scale. Across 12 experiment families, 4 seeds, and two network scales, the predictive relationship between spectral entropy and validation performance is real but weak within a family ($R^2 = 0.35$, $ = 0.80$), and does not extrapolate: at $n_embd = 512$ (18.9M parameters) the three-seed paired effect is $-0.0116 0.0101$ ($p 0.18$), with the composed-rank gain varying $3.7 $ across seeds. A spectral-entropy regularizer actively flattens spectra ($ _1/ _6$: $152.8 1.03$) while leaving losses healthy, and the damage is uncorrelated ($r 0$) with the latent non-Gaussianity the term is meant to exploit. We state the boundary as a falsifiable condition: within the tested regime, information preservation and better prediction are weakly related, and that relation does not extrapolate across scale. Spectral entropy is neither a sufficient statistic for generalization nor a useful capacity index; what we do not claim is that it is uninformative – the failure is in extrapolation, and we localize where it fails.

title: Where AI enters the product development process: Task orientation, human identity threat, and purchase intention
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Across three studies with U.S. consumers in fashion-related contexts, this research examines how the task AI performs and how its role is framed shape consumer responses to products developed with AI involvement. Study 1 maps consumers’ perceptions of fashion-related tasks along a logic–intuition continuum and identifies trend forecasting as a logic-oriented task and design as an intuition-oriented task. Study 2 compares AI involvement in these two contrasting product-development tasks and finds lower purchase intention when AI is involved in design rather than trend forecasting, with heightened human identity threat accounting for part of this difference. Study 3 focuses on the intuition-oriented design context and shows that framing AI as complementing rather than replacing human designers is associated with lower identity threat and higher purchase intention. Together, the findings suggest that consumer responses depend not only on whether AI participates in product development, but also on where AI is positioned within the process and how its contribution relative to human creativity is framed. This research advances understanding of task-dependent responses to AI by identifying human identity threat as a mediator linking AI involvement to purchase intention and by showing how role framing can shape purchase intention when AI participates in creative work.

title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.

title: SMS3C1: A Post-Quantum Tamper-Evident Record That Survives the Fall of Its Own Mathematics
abstract: SMS3C1 is a tamper-evident record whose every seal is signed under eight mathematically unrelated families of digital signature at once and, beneath them, carries an information-theoretic authentication tag per custodian site from one-time key material the recording device erases as it uses it. If an adversary breaks every family, or takes the whole device with every key, the seals already written are not his to rewrite. A bait-free reader names, from the record alone, whether the algorithms fell or the keys were taken; every seal is bracketed in time from outside the device. Designed by Sergio Méndez Sánchez; code, tests and traps written by Claude (Anthropic) as engineering agent under his direction. U.S. Patent Application No. 19/843,433, filed October 17, 2026.

title: Putting AI to the test: Evidence from a large-scale RCT in rural China
abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has heightened interest in personalizing computer assisted learning (CAL) programs to tailor their instruction to individual students. Despite the proliferation of AI-driven CAL programs, evidence for their effectiveness remains limited. We present findings from a field experiment in rural China examining whether an AI-driven personalized CAL program improves student achievement. We randomly assign 8647 students from 315 primary school classes to one of three treatment arms: (i) AI-CAL, (ii) non-personalized CAL (active control), and (iii) non-CAL educational activities (pure control). Results indicate that AI-CAL does not significantly improve achievement, with estimates precise enough to rule out non-trivial positive effects. This finding holds across the difficulty of assessment items and across the baseline achievement of students. If anything, AI-CAL might be less effective than non-personalized CAL for students in the middle tercile of baseline achievement. These findings call for caution when scaling AI-driven educational technologies.

title: How Much Do Activation Monitors Benefit from Original Model Computations?
abstract: One powerful way to safeguard AI systems is to monitor their internal computations--where signs of undesirable behavior might be more easily detectable than from models' inputs and outputs alone. However, recent studies begin to question the premise that activations provide a unique window into model behavior. In this paper, we study how much of activation monitors' success depends on access to the original behavior-generating computations. Within a fixed choice of target model and monitoring architecture, we compare how well monitors trained and evaluated on trajectories that differ in computational context can predict the behavior of the original execution, after the transcript is changed in a controlled manner (e.g., its exact text, or chat formatting). We first find that much performance can be recovered without access to the original behavior-generating trace (in up to 4 models across 2 counterfactual monitoring tasks), but a mild yet consistent advantage to native-trained monitors remains, outperforming strongest controls by up to 0.014 AUROC. Interestingly, we find monitors trained with native access have notable uplift on original examples whose behavioral label changes under paraphrasing. We further find this a useful lens to expose limitations of baselines that use simple forms of privileged information (i.e., answer logit margins). While our results show the advantage of native monitor access is modest in aggregate, they highlight the importance of evaluations that identify if and when original model computations provide additional predictive value.

title: MelGuard: frozen AST Mel-spectrogram gateway detector weights (v1 hardened, v1 multi-corpus baseline, v2 adaptive)
abstract: Frozen weights of the passive Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) Mel-spectrogram gateway detector g_D evaluated in MelGuard: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of a Passive Mel-Spectrogram Gateway against White-Box Detector-Aware Sub-Second Audio-Jailbreak Triggers (Razavi and Al Naamany, 2026). The study was pre-registered on OSF (j5x2e, 2026-07-05) and evaluated exactly once on a sealed held-out set; the pre-registered result is a defender-loss (0 of 4 adversary-strength conditions secure), with the detector holding against a weak detector-aware adversary and defeated by a strong one. Files. melguard_detector_v1_hardened.pt — the deployed detector behind the sealed evaluation and all robustness sub-studies (frozen operating threshold 0.00032981189549900536; SHA-256 1a6392ed5750e99b691c19dbd294cb89a943c600a68c2908022432c5bad71265). melguard_detector_v1_baseline_multicorpus.pt — the pre-hardening baseline (threshold 0.0012052711774595082; SHA-256 c68a0b3228a0ba24fe901133c292277f1b3d71b17a996c3772c7f9c0afd99d65). melguard_detector_v2_adaptive.pt — the supplementary arms-race detector retrained with adaptive triggers, reported as a supplement and not proven robust (threshold 6.586553514353e-05; SHA-256 360fa050dd6f3deeca6962a7fc58d442503756cd1e78f017a76e33f9409ff6eb). Each file is a 345,032,163-byte PyTorch checkpoint of the full AST backbone (MIT/ast-finetuned-audioset-10-10-0.4593 @ f826b80d) with the last two encoder layers and a small classification head fine-tuned; input is a 128-bin log-Mel spectrogram at 16 kHz. SHA256SUMS and README.md document the files. Load with detector/infer.py --weights from the code repository. Not included. No adversarial trigger waveforms, payloads, or benign audio: triggers are distributed as SHA-256 hashes plus optimizer configuration in the code repository, under the coordinated-disclosure policy of the pre-registration (Day 0 = 2026-07-17; window closed 2026-10-15). Code and manifests: https://github.com/dbugom/melguard-artifact. Pre-registration: https://osf.io/j5x2e (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/J5X2E).

title: The Self-and-Mutual-and-Causality Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Individual Processing, Interactive Mechanisms, and Causal Reasoning
abstract: Computational systems increasingly rely on internal processing, interactions among multiple computational agents, and causal reasoning to solve complex problems. Individual processing mechanisms enable a system to generate, evaluate, diagnose, and refine its own outputs. Mutual mechanisms enable multiple agents to exchange information, challenge assumptions, coordinate actions, and integrate complementary knowledge. Causal mechanisms, in contrast, investigate the relationships through which variables, interventions, and events influence outcomes. Although these three forms of computation can complement one another, their appropriate use depends on the structure of the task, the available evidence, the uncertainty of the current state, and the computational resources required. This paper proposes the Self-and-Mutual-and-Causality Model (SMC Model), a general conceptual framework for adaptive coordination among individual computational mechanisms, interactive mechanisms, and causal reasoning mechanisms. The framework treats Self, Mutual, and Causality as distinct but interoperable computational dimensions rather than as mutually exclusive system architectures. A state-aware controller selects among these dimensions according to the current problem, the expected value of additional computation, the reliability of available evidence, and the costs of interaction and causal analysis. The model supports transitions between individual processing, collaborative processing, causal discovery, causal effect estimation, intervention analysis, and counterfactual reasoning. It also introduces a feedback cycle through which causal findings inform subsequent individual and collaborative computation, while the results of those computations may generate new causal hypotheses. The paper formalizes the model as a sequential decision problem, defines its principal mechanisms, presents a reference algorithm, identifies potential failure modes, and proposes an empirical evaluation protocol. The framework distinguishes causal hypotheses from identified causal effects and emphasizes that causal conclusions require appropriate assumptions, evidence, or experimental designs. The proposed model is a conceptual research framework rather than an empirically validated system. Its intended contribution is to provide a common architecture for investigating when and how individual processing, interaction, and causal reasoning should be coordinated, subject to comparison with existing causal inference, multi-agent, and adaptive computation methods.

title: The Self-and-Mutual-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Autonomous Computation, Interactive Mechanisms, and World-State Modeling
abstract: Computational systems operating in dynamic environments must coordinate their internal processing, interactions with other computational entities, and representations of the external world. Autonomous computation enables a system to process information and modify its own outputs without requiring continuous interaction with other entities. Mutual computation enables multiple entities to exchange information, evaluate alternatives, coordinate actions, and integrate complementary knowledge. World modeling provides representations of environmental states, transition dynamics, observations, and predicted consequences of possible actions. Although these three capabilities are individually important, their coordination is often addressed through separate architectural decisions or task-specific procedures. This paper proposes the Self-and-Mutual-and-World Model (SMWM), a general computational framework for adaptively coordinating autonomous computation, interactive mechanisms, and world-state modeling. The framework treats self-mechanisms, mutual mechanisms, and world-model operations as three configurable but interdependent action spaces. A state-aware controller selects among autonomous processing, collaborative interaction, world-model updating, and coordinated combinations of these operations according to task requirements, uncertainty, environmental change, prediction error, interaction benefit, model reliability, and computational cost. The framework supports transitions not only between autonomous and interactive computation but also between different world-model operations, including state estimation, prediction, counterfactual simulation, planning, and model revision. A formal problem definition, utility function, adaptive control procedure, implementation architecture, research hypotheses, and experimental evaluation protocol are presented. The framework is a proposed conceptual and methodological design rather than an empirically validated system. Its intended contribution is to establish a common formulation for studying how computational autonomy, interaction, and world modeling can be jointly coordinated, while recognizing that autonomous agents, multi-agent coordination, predictive world models, and adaptive model-based control have substantial existing research foundations. Empirical investigation is required to determine whether the proposed integration provides measurable advantages over established architectures.

title: Knowing the Collective: Temporal Cohort Membership and Small-Cell Governance as Foundations for Cohort Negentropic Assessment
abstract: Part IV of Volume II (the outward extensions) of the H-DKPS series on physician-governed clinical AI (知衡八法). The redacted code package is included as a separate file. Clinical problem. Patients who share a workplace, a night-shift rota or a neighbourhood share more than an address. They share exposures — noise, dust, heat, disrupted sleep, the same air — that leave traces in many individual records before any single record looks unusual. A clinic that sees several workers from one factory, or several residents of one district, holds information about that group that no single encounter reveals. It also holds a responsibility: group-level statements about a small number of identifiable people can disclose what each individual's record would have kept private. Engineering problem. A clinical decision system built to reason about one patient at a time — as the system examined in this series is — has no concept of a group. Adding one raises two problems that must be solved before any group analysis is attempted. The first is membership: who belonged to which group, and when — because people change jobs and move house, and a group defined only by the present misattributes the past. The second is disclosure: in a single clinic, most groups are small, and small counts identify people, directly or by subtraction. Approach. We specify and implement the foundation for cohort assessment as two parts. A cohort registry records group membership with periods: workplace groups (with shift pattern, exposures and occupation as membership attributes) and community groups at two levels (district and the village beneath it); leaving a group records a date and never deletes the membership; addresses are reduced to city, district and village, with city names matched against the official list so that recognition errors cannot split one place into several; and every write is hash-chained. A small-cell governance gate, following the published rule of Taiwan's health-data science centre for the release of statistical results, suppresses any cell of one or two people, applies complementary suppression so that no suppressed group can be recovered by subtraction, rolls small villages up into their district, exports suppressed cells only as a merged category without special symbols, outputs aggregates only, and records every export with its stated purpose. Population analysis itself, and any use of group membership in prescribing, are deliberately not built. Evidence. This is an architecture study; all evidence is from guard suites on synthetic data. The registry guard (29 checks) verifies data minimisation, type rules, temporal membership, idempotent joins, hash-chain integrity and intake wiring; six mutations — among them returning the street address, deleting on leave and skipping city-name matching — are each caught. The governance guard (24 checks) verifies primary and complementary suppression, roll-up, symbol-free merged export and identifier screening; an exhaustive property check over 3,000 random tables confirms that no visible cell contains one or two people and that every suppressed set is either empty or at least two cells totalling at least three; six mutations are each caught, and one candidate mutation was found to be equivalent and is reported as such. Contribution. Population-level negentropic assessment in a small clinic is first a problem of governance, not of analysis. Temporal membership and small-cell suppression with complementary protection can be specified as checkable properties, implemented before any analysis exists, and verified to fail when weakened. Not peer reviewed.

title: Same Data, Different Domains: Representation Dependence in Adaptive Data Mixing
abstract: The same training data can be divided into domains in many ways. We ask whether this choice affects learning when an adaptive data mixer assigns sampling weights to those domains. We use a controlled language-modeling task where favoring clean data improves learning, comparing two quality groups with a finer partition into sixteen groups. The examples remain unchanged and the sampling policies are learned separately. The finer partition increases validation loss by 0.01647 nats per token across 32 paired seeds, removing about one-quarter of the benefit of adaptive sampling over a fixed mixture. To examine how sampling decisions affect learning, a separate experiment holds the overall proportions of data sources fixed while changing which examples are sampled within one source. Preserving the full repetition pattern while randomly permuting example identities reproduces nearly the same learning penalty. Increasing the number of examples used to estimate scores for sampling-weight updates substantially reduces concentration and learning harm, although harm remains positive at the largest tested budget. We then ask whether a mixer can become less sensitive to subdivisions without losing the ability to favor useful data. A hierarchical rule allows weights to adapt between meaningful groups while limiting changes within them. It reduces sensitivity while preserving adaptive-sampling benefits, including under natural semantic subdivisions with the same controlled quality objective. When the supplied grouping is sufficiently inaccurate, however, ignoring it works better. Our results show that how training data are divided can affect what a model learns, and that improving stability requires care in deciding which distinctions to preserve.

title: CDD-Net: Consistency-Discrepancy Decoupling for Chinese Pragmatic Intention Recognition
abstract: Existing multimodal spoken language understanding methods primarily emphasize cross-modal consistency fusion. Although effective for congruent text–speech interactions, this paradigm is often insufficient for deep pragmatic phenomena such as rhetorical questions, sarcasm, and indirect expressions. In such cases, speaker intention depends not only on literal content but also on fine-grained patterns of consistency and conflict between lexical semantics and vocal realization. A single fused representation therefore tends to obscure precisely the cues that matter most. To address this limitation, we propose the Consistency-Discrepancy Decoupling Network (CDD-Net), which explicitly models both cross-modal consistency and discrepancy through discrepancy localization, dual-space representation learning, discrepancy-aware optimization, and residual fusion. We further introduce Tone-Aware Conflict Masking (TACM), a lightweight tone-aware refinement inside TLDL tailored to Chinese speech, and construct a new Chinese speech-text dataset together with a dedicated benchmark spanning both shallow/deep intention discrimination and fine-grained speech act recognition. Under a unified evaluation protocol, CDD-Net achieves the strongest SR performance among the reproduced baselines considered in this work, while additional PQP results suggest that the contribution of auxiliary cues such as explicit F0 is task-dependent. Overall, the findings indicate that explicitly modeling cross-modal discrepancy, rather than only cross-modal consistency, is beneficial for Chinese pragmatic spoken language understanding.

To address this limitation, we propose the Consistency-Discrepancy Decoupling Network (CDD-Net), which explicitly models both cross-modal consistency and discrepancy through discrepancy localization, dual-space representation learning, discrepancy-aware optimization, and residual fusion. We further introduce Tone-Aware Conflict Masking (TACM), a lightweight tone-aware refinement inside TLDL tailored to Chinese speech, and construct a new Chinese speech-text dataset together with a dedicated benchmark spanning both shallow/deep intention discrimination and fine-grained speech act recognition. Under a unified evaluation protocol, CDD-Net achieves the strongest SR performance among the reproduced baselines considered in this work, while additional PQP results suggest that the contribution of auxiliary cues such as explicit F0 is task-dependent. Overall, the findings indicate that explicitly modeling cross-modal discrepancy, rather than only cross-modal consistency, is beneficial for Chinese pragmatic spoken language understanding.

title: IntriAdapt: Generalizable Intrinsic-Guided Test-Time Adaptation for Metric Geometry Estimation
abstract: Recovering metric 3D geometry from images is fundamentally ill-posed due to perspective projection ambiguity. Current geometry models incorporate supplied or predicted intrinsics during inference, but do not use them to supervise model adaptation. To refine these predictions, test-time adaptation (TTA) typically relies on external depth measurements. In this paper, we instead use camera intrinsics as an output-side geometric verifier. Comparing the point cloud's viewing rays with those defined by the known intrinsics yields a direct measure of geometric inconsistency. We propose \textit{IntriAdapt}, a TTA framework that minimizes this closed-form geometric residual. By optimizing a lightweight LoRA adapter on a frozen geometry foundation model, our method aligns the prediction with the specific camera model without depth sensors or external priors. We further extend this approach to video sequences, demonstrating that adapting a short sequence generalizes to other sequences captured by the same camera. The adapted model processes held-out images in a feed-forward pass, without repeating optimization for each frame. Experiments on ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks across multiple base models show that \textit{IntriAdapt} consistently outperforms both unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.

title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
