title: Autonomous labeling of surgical resection margins using a foundation model
abstract: Abstract Assessing resection margins is central to pathological specimen evaluation and has profound implications for patient outcomes. Failure to achieve clear margins significantly increases the risk of local recurrence and may necessitate adjuvant therapies such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy. However, margin assessment faces multiple procedural challenges, including human error during manual tissue margin labeling (physical inking), tissue shrinkage and distortion from fixation and processing, and thermal damage from cautery that obscures cellular features, all of which can compromise accurate margin identification. We demonstrate a virtual inking network (VIN) that localizes the resection margin on whole-slide images (WSIs), producing a standardized, ink-free margin map that helps mitigate limitations of physical inking and enables accurate and reproducible margin measurements. VIN uses a frozen foundation model as the feature extractor and a compact two-layer multilayer perceptron trained for patch-level classification of cautery-consistent features. The dataset comprised 120 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained slides from 12 human tonsil tissue blocks, resulting in ~ 2 TB of uncompressed raw image data, where a board-certified pathologist provided boundary annotations. In blind testing with 20 slides from previously unseen blocks, VIN produced coherent margin overlays that qualitatively aligned with expert annotations across serial sections. Quantitatively, region-level accuracy was ~ 73.3% across the test set, with errors largely confined to limited areas that did not disrupt continuity of the whole-slide margin map. Our results suggest that VIN is capable of capturing cautery-related histomorphology, offering a potential ink-free margin delineation for digital pathology workflows. These proof-of-concept results warrant further validation of VIN as a tool for margin localization in larger, clinically representative cohorts.

title: Steering beyond Language: Improving Multilingual Training-Free Text Embeddings via Paired-Residual Subspace Removal
abstract: While deriving text embeddings directly from frozen LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, existing methods focus almost exclusively on English, leaving multilingual settings largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of multilingual training-free text embeddings in LLMs. Our analysis reveals a language-conditioned embedding geometry in which semantically equivalent sentences remain misaligned across languages. We hypothesize that language-specific variation can be disentangled from semantic content to improve embedding quality. To this end, we propose Paired-Residual Subspace Removal (PRSR), a training-free inference-time intervention that steers LLM representations toward a more language-invariant semantic space. PRSR first constructs paired residuals from multilingual parallel sentences to capture language-specific deviations. It then estimates layer-wise low-rank subspaces from these residuals and suppresses the corresponding components in the last-token hidden states. We conduct more than 200 monolingual evaluations across 18 languages using MTEB and MMTEB, along with cross-lingual bitext mining between English and over 200 other languages. Empirical results demonstrate that PRSR consistently improves the performance of existing training-free baselines in both monolingual and cross-lingual settings across different LLMs.

title: Persistent Planar Memory for Video World Models
abstract: Video world models that generate and explore environments at scale need a persistent 3D memory of what they have produced. Plane primitives offer a natural candidate: a compact set of oriented planes captures the dominant structural elements (e.g., walls, floors, facades) of indoor and outdoor scenes, while requiring only 7 parameters per primitive. We present PPMem, a video world model that adopts plane primitives as its persistent 3D memory. PPMem augments a video diffusion transformer with a planar prediction head and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module: each autoregressive chunk jointly produces RGB video and planar geometry, which merges into a persistent plane memory that conditions subsequent chunks via rendered depth. The resulting memory is three orders of magnitude more compact than per-pixel point clouds (~100K primitives, 5MB for a full scene), geometrically explicit (metric depth, normals, exportable surfaces), cross-view consistent (jointly predicted by the shared backbone), and adaptive (refined by the merging procedure as generation proceeds). On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, PPMem outperforms prior 3D-grounded world models in video quality while jointly producing metric-scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry, sustaining coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/ppmem.

title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.

title: WAInjectBench: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detections for Web Agents
abstract: Multiple prompt injection attacks have been proposed against web agents. At the same time, various methods have been developed to detect general prompt injection attacks, but none have been systematically evaluated for web agents. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting the first comprehensive benchmark study on detecting prompt injection attacks targeting web agents. We begin by introducing a fine-grained categorization of such attacks based on the threat model. We then construct datasets containing both malicious and benign samples: malicious text segments generated by different attacks, benign text segments from four categories, malicious images produced by attacks, and benign images from two categories. Next, we systematize both text-based and image-based detection methods. Finally, we evaluate their performance across multiple scenarios. Our key findings show that while some detectors can identify attacks that rely on explicit textual instructions or visible image perturbations with moderate to high accuracy, they largely fail against attacks that omit explicit instructions or employ imperceptible perturbations. Our datasets and code are released at: https://github.com/Norrrrrrr-lyn/WAInjectBench.

title: Video Diffusion Avatars: Taming Video Diffusion Models into Controllable 3D Avatars
abstract: Video diffusion models (VDMs) trained on internet-scale data encode a rich prior on appearance, motion, and physics that is difficult to replicate with explicit 3D rendering and costly 3D data capture. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), a method that creates photo-realistic, multi-view consistent avatars from a single image by fine-tuning a VDM for precise control over camera viewpoint, facial expression, and upper-body pose. Departing from 3D morphable models (3DMMs), VDAs use a learned expression space that lifts the expressiveness ceiling of 3DMMs, e.g., for the tongue and mouth interior. However, learned expression codes exhibit heavy viewpoint bias, as our DISTRACT benchmark reveals. We show that this bias can be removed through disentanglement, enabling their use as driving signals for multi-view consistent avatars. Camera and upper-body pose are controlled jointly via proxy-mesh renderings, giving independent control over expression, pose, and viewpoint. A camera-triplet training strategy makes the approach efficient: our models train for 34 hours on a single A100 using only public multi-view data. VDAs outperform state-of-the-art single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, reducing face LPIPS by 29% and improving perceptual quality (JOD) by 66% on BecomingLit. A static 3DGS reconstruction probe further confirms that our generations are the most multi-view consistent. Built on a video prior, VDAs produce effects beyond the reach of explicit renderers, including physically plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.

title: MTEdit: Packed Trajectories Beat Rollouts for Multi-Turn Image Editing
abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, making it better aligned with human-AI collaborative creation than single-turn editing. However, constructing high-quality multi-turn training data remains challenging, as conventional sequential rollout accumulates errors and introduces visual-quality drift across editing turns. To address this challenge, we introduce MTEdit, a multi-turn image editing dataset built through a pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. By jointly generating multiple editing states within a unified visual context, this pipeline reduces visual-quality drift across turns. Covering both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios, MTEdit comprises 500K multi-turn image editing trajectories, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, making it one of the most extensive datasets for multi-turn image editing. We further introduce MTEdit-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate both scenarios by assessing models' ability to follow editing instructions, maintain content consistency, resist visual-quality drift, and effectively use historical context across turns. Using MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. On MTEdit-Bench, we evaluate a broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Experimental results show that Qwen-Image-MTEdit achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving models' multi-turn image editing capabilities.

title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models
abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.

title: The Italian lawmaking process: a unified and structured dataset
abstract: The Italian legislative process is documented in detailed parliamentary records hosted in institutional websites. However, much of this information is available only as unstructured text, limiting its systematic reuse. We applied a controlled, systematic LLM-based extraction procedure, validated against manually annotated records, to convert these texts into ordered and dated events including, e.g., bill introduction, committee examination, plenary examination, and approval. The resulting dataset reconstructs the procedural histories of all 5346 Italian laws enacted between 1985 and 2026, spanning parliamentary terms IX to XIX, for overall 101413 events. Each event records the activity, date, and chamber, with additional procedural details where available. The dataset supports research in the emerging fields of computational legal and legislative studies, potentially combined with process-oriented data science methods to examine procedural paths and legislative timing across parliamentary terms.

title: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.

title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
abstract: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.

title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
abstract: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.

title: TUPLE-Bench: Evaluating and Mitigating Privacy-Utility Trade-offs in Typed Decision Models
abstract: Typed decision models often return more than a selected category. They also expose probabilities for each candidate and, sometimes, a separate confidence score. These fields support downstream decisions but may reveal information beyond a recipient's authorization. We introduce TUPLE-Bench (Typed decision models' Utility and Privacy Leakage Evaluation Benchmark), a benchmark of paired synthetic cases in which recipients may learn a coarse operational category but not its fine-grained cause. Across nine models, instructions to withhold the cause fail to protect it: 91.88%-99.93% of responses reveal the cause through direct selection or residual scores. Even when causes are excluded from the candidate set, full outputs enable 62.85%-75.35% recovery on held-out cases, compared with 51.04%-57.64% using only the selected category (50% chance). Full outputs also reduce mean downstream cost in all 27 model-task comparisons. However, confidence fields increase leakage without consistently reducing cost. We further introduce workflow-constrained privacy quantization (WCPQ), which reduces secret recovery while preserving the behavior and cost of specified downstream workflows. Our findings highlight the need to audit decision interfaces field by field and workflow by workflow.

title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
abstract: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

title: Task-aligned spectral inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits
abstract: Parameterized quantum circuits are widely investigated in quantum machine learning, yet how their architecture can provide task-aligned inductive biases remains poorly understood. We study data reuploading quantum circuits with two distinct inputs: a signal that varies between samples and a fixed, task-defined spectral query that specifies how the signal should be probed. We show that encoding the query can change the circuit's hypothesis class over the signal by modulating how its existing signal frequencies are combined, without introducing new sample-dependent information. This mechanism matches tasks built on nonuniform Fourier transforms, whose evaluation frequencies specify the query and whose sampling positions guide its encoding. We examine this connection in a classification task inspired by synthetic aperture radar, where acquisition geometry determines a query for classifying unfocused spectral patches before image formation. Across small-scale spectral and radar-like tasks, aligned queries improve learning from limited data over parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries. These results provide a route from known spectral task structure to the design and validation of inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits.

title: A Language-Informed Loss for Visual Generation
abstract: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 $\to$ 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.

evidence.abstract: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 to 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.

title: Beyond the Answer: Student-Conditioned Trace Construction for Reasoning Distillation
abstract: A reasoning trace can accompany a correct answer without providing effective supervision for a particular student. We study how to construct traces that improve learning beyond answer-only supervision by considering both their intermediate content and their accessibility to the target learner. We introduce ReDiST, a student-conditioned trace-construction and distillation framework for evidence-rich reasoning. Starting from the student's own attempts, ReDiST revises answer-correct drafts against the supplied evidence and repairs unsuccessful drafts with additional guidance from the verified answer. A frozen student-matched reader screens and ranks original and edited candidates using answer recovery and verified-answer probability, given the question, evidence, and candidate trace. We distill the selected targets while balancing trace and final-answer supervision with an auxiliary answer loss. Construction and selection occur offline, and inference uses only the distilled student. Experiments on question-answering benchmarks show that ReDiST can improve both source-task and cross-benchmark performance over answer-only, original-trace, and the evaluated trace-selection and rewriting baselines. Across supervision recipes, performance rankings can differ between source and transfer benchmarks, highlighting the importance of evaluating trace teaching utility across distributions.

title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
abstract: Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.

title: Not Every Mention Is a Claim: Rethinking Object Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Object hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs) is usually measured by checking each object a caption names against the image. Most benchmarks and detectors alike treat every object mention as a claim that the object is present. This assumption fails when a caption names an object without asserting it, as in "a bench for people to sit on", which mentions people without claiming that any are in the image. We call such mentions non-assertive. Treating them as hallucinations inflates the error rates attributed to models that use such language. To separate them from real hallucinations, we introduce NAME-Bench (Non-Assertive Mention Evaluation Benchmark), 25,497 object mentions from captions that five VLMs generate for COCO images. Each mention is labelled concrete (asserted and present), hallucinated (asserted and absent), or non-assertive, and non-assertive mentions are further divided into four subtypes: depictive, purpose, negation and hedged. All the hallucination detectors that we evaluate flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations, at rates between 14% and 80%. Adding non-assertive mentions to detector training as negatives largely corrects this on LLaVA-1.5. On the four newer VLMs, a comparable correction takes five to ten times more data, and the detectors then catch fewer real hallucinations. These findings show that current detectors conflate mentioning an object with asserting it, and that this conflation is harder to undo on the four newer VLMs than on LLaVA-1.5. Hallucination evaluation should therefore separate what a caption asserts from what it merely mentions.

title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes. The source code is publicly available at https://mias.group/MaSS.

title: Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
abstract: Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

title: GEO X Q12–Q12R2: geometry-adaptation results and unsuccessful coding co-evolution — archive consistency companion
abstract: Results/archive companion preserving David Glowalla's GEO X Q12, Q12R and Q12R2 correction lineage. Q12 used effective quantum-channel proxies and reported a 1.2148% improvement in its held-out ranking score; its selected winner used single rail. Later explicit-channel and noisy-circuit studies did not replicate an independent geometry-code co-evolution advantage: joint and geometry-only selections coincide. The earlier free-retry model was excluded as requiring unaccounted quantum resources. Q12R stores a mean resource-adjusted score of 0.3349475662 for the joint/geometry-only selection versus code-only 0.3176231818; paired difference 0.0173243844, historical 95% interval −0.0189537444 to 0.0403313622. Q12R2 stores corresponding means 0.3530163770 and 0.3357186479; paired difference 0.0172977291, historical 95% interval 0.0139308373 to 0.0203762831. Joint versus geometry-only difference is exactly zero in both studies. Q12R2 uses five synthetic environments crossed with three noise profiles; these are not fifteen independent hardware trials. Four-qubit recovery remains exploratory rather than fully native-gate compiled. Fresh review passes 1,173 provenance and stored-table arithmetic checks over original archive bytes, declared manifests, aggregates, resource division, fidelity identities and matched differences. It covers 54, 55 and 150 condition rows respectively. These checks are not fresh solver or bootstrap reproduction. All three Python files in the inspected original ZIPs contain descriptions only; executable generators were not recovered. Ranking-score definitions and historical bootstrap construction remain open. Ranking-score versus mean-score plot labels, unbalanced noise-chart aggregation and original nonstandard JSON NaN values are explicitly documented. The package retains unchanged reports, selected numerical data, four historical figures, separate review and audit hashes. Source, schedule-edge tables, route diagrams and private Studio/ISA implementations are excluded. Geometry adaptation is an experimental simulation result; no calibrated quantum hardware, temperature/cooling model, refrigeration-free computation, general computational speedup or physical validation is established. Files restricted; copyright retained with no additional reuse grant. Studio demonstrations and licensing: https://github.com/Nibiru99/ics-research-studio; darklightblackwing@gmail.com.

title: WAGRL: A Wind Adaptive Guidance Framework for Uncertainty-Aware UAV Trajectory Control
abstract: To address the challenges of wind-induced uncertainty, decision inconsistency, and safety risks in quadrotor trajectory tracking, this study presents a Wind Adaptive Guidance Reinforcement Learning (WAGRL) framework. Unlike conventional controllers relying on fixed aerodynamic models, WAGRL integrates ensemble-based policy learning with uncertainty-guided reinforcement learning to adaptively manage diverse wind conditions. A set of digital expert policies is trained to capture heterogeneous wind-response strategies, and an ensemble-based estimation mechanism quantifies epistemic uncertainty for robust action selection. An entropy-driven adaptive intervention module monitors real-time decision confidence and activates expert guidance when uncertainty exceeds adaptive thresholds. To validate the proposed framework, extensive simulations are conducted under both nominal and wind-disturbed settings, covering square-loop tracking, geometric path following, and gust rejection scenarios. The results show that WAGRL achieves faster convergence, enhanced trajectory accuracy, and smoother attitude responses. Real-world flight tests further confirm that WAGRL maintains stable and reliable performance under outdoor wind disturbances, demonstrating its potential for safe and adaptive UAV control in complex aerial environments.

title: Learning to Correct Geometry in Generated Videos
abstract: Generated videos often lose geometric consistency under camera motion: structures warp under viewpoint change, parallax becomes inconsistent, and smooth camera movement may collapse into shot-like transitions. We argue that this failure is largely a data problem. In web-scale video corpora, most visible motion comes from dynamic objects captured by static or weakly moving cameras, leaving only sparse supervision for viewpoint-induced appearance changes. To address this, we propose Video Geometry Corrector (VGC), a post-hoc video-to-video model trained on synthetic paired supervision. Starting from real videos with diverse camera motion and pose annotations, we construct VG-Pairs with a synthetic paired-supervision data generation pipeline. Each video clip is treated as a geometry-consistent target and paired with a distorted counterpart synthesized by a pretrained image-to-video inpainting model using trajectory-adaptive keyframes. VGC learns to map the distorted input to the geometry-consistent target without modifying the source generator, and uses optical flow as an auxiliary cue to help disentangle camera motion from object motion. Experiments on pose-conditioned and prompt-driven benchmarks show that VGC improves geometric consistency across multiple source generators, and scaling to a larger backbone further extends the framework toward more general video refinement.

title: Crossing the Sandbox Boundary: Bypassing Multimodal LLM Guardrails via Lossless LSB Steganographic Dead-Drops and Agentic Code Execution
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents rely on dual-layer defenses: text prompt shields that filter user tokens and vision classifiers that inspect images for explicit harm or typographic text. Prior image steganography jailbreaks face a fundamental bottleneck. When a stego-image is processed solely through a vision transformer (ViT), patch linear projection and floating-point normalization destroy least significant bit (LSB) planes, limiting commercial VLM attack success rates to 14.8%–18.9%. Conversely, neural steganography frameworks require registering custom external decoding tools via API schemas. We identify and formalize Execution-Boundary Privilege Inversion, an architectural blind spot in MLLM-integrated coding agents equipped with a native Python sandbox. title: XAI and its Applications in Decision Support System
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed decision-making across various industries by enabling systems to analyse large volumes of data and provide intelligent recommendations. However, many modern AI models, particularly deep learning algorithms, function as "black boxes," making it difficult for users to understand how decisions are generated. This lack of transparency limits the adoption of AI in critical domains such as healthcare, finance, law, and business. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a promising solution that improves transparency, interpretability, and trust in AI systems. Decision Support Systems (DSS) assist decision-makers by combining data, analytical models, and domain knowledge. Integrating XAI into DSS enables users to understand AI-generated recommendations, thereby improving confidence and accountability. This review paper explores the concepts of XAI, different explanation techniques, and their applications in DSS. The paper also discusses recent research, challenges, limitations, and future research directions

title: Data Labeling with Local and Global Consistency Using Phylograms
abstract: One of the main challenges in machine learning tasks is unlabeled data. Consequently, semi-supervised learning is an approach commonly used in labeling data tasks. The use of diffusion kernels is one of the powerful methods in this set of learning. This paper introduces Phylogram based Data Labeling (PhyDL), an innovative method that combines the benefits of phylogram analysis with Learning with Local and Global Consistency (LLGC). PhyDL leverages phylogram analysis to act as an aggregator of information from labeled samples, capable of correcting possible labeling errors. PhyDL constructs a phylogram using community detection algorithms, FastGreedy and Edge Betweenness, to identify and leverage the structure of the data, with FastGreedy emerging as the best-performing algorithm among those evaluated. We implemented PhyDL and evaluated its performance on the TwoMoons, MNIST, MUSK, HEART, and SONAR datasets. PhyDL outperformed LLGC on 4 out of 5 evaluated datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in semi-supervised learning scenarios. On the TwoMoons, MNIST, MUSK, and SONAR benchmarks, the method showed steady accuracy gains, with consistent improvements as the number of labeled samples increased. However, on the HEART dataset, standard LLGC achieved better results, indicating that PhyDL’s community-based diffusion can be limited by certain underlying spatial structures. Furthermore, the experiments revealed that the Edge Betweenness algorithm is unsuitable for these specific high-dimensional tasks. Ultimately, this study showcases PhyDL’s potential, when equipped with the FastGreedy algorithm, to significantly improve data labeling performance in semi-supervised scenarios, effectively leveraging the structural topology of complex datasets.

title: Quantum thermometry with a phase damped curvature-dependent Jaynes-Cummings model in the dispersive regime
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we study an atom-field system described by a curvature-dependent Jaynes-Cummings model, in the presence of a phase-damping reservoir with an unknown temperature T . In our curvature-dependent system, the field, as well as the it’s reservoir, is analogically modeled with a oscillator on a circle, which represents a curvature-induced deformation of the conventional flat oscillator. We show that our λ-dependent system can be engineered in a laser-driven trapped ion inside a Kerr medium. By calculating the quadrature squeezing, curvature-dependent Wigner function and negativity of the Wigner function, we investigate the curvature and also, the temperature effects on nonclassical properties of the cavity field states. We calculate the quantum Fisher information for a pure probe state undergoing evolution governed by the Hamiltonian of the dispersive, curvature-dependent Jaynes-Cummings model in the low temperature regime. Furthermore, we identify the optimal measurement that saturates the quantum Cram´er-Rao bound. Our results show that homodyne detection provides a nearly optimal measurement strategy in the limit of small temperatures, and offers a feasible route toward high-precision quantum thermometry in curved quantum systems.

title: Rethinking the design space of Vanilla Pixel Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction ($\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction) with clean image prediction ($\boldsymbol{x_0}$-prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between $\boldsymbol{x_0}$- and $\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end-to-end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity -- notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post-hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high-frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik-kanad.github.io/mflow-diffusion/.

title: Anyonic Neural Network Wavefunctions
abstract: The macroscopic behavior of a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons has remained unsettled for many decades. Prior numerical methods employing exact diagonalization in the continuum and on the plane have been limited to small system sizes, at most N = 4 anyons. Using the rapidly developing technology of neural network wavefunctions, we develop variational ansatze appropriate for studying continuum models of the Abelian anyon gas. The neural network architecture, which we call "AnyNet", is capable of exactly enforcing the non-analytic short-distance behavior induced by the anyonic statistics. We demonstrate excellent agreement with exact diagonalization for N=4 anyons, obtain accurate results up to N = 16 for intermediate statistics, and study up to N=20 for almost-fermionic anyons, matching perturbative results within a 0.4% discrepancy. We use this methodology to study anyons in a harmonic trap, and anyonic atoms as a model for anyon binding to impurities. We study the structure of anyonic wavefunctions as the statistics parameter is varied. We focus on the single-particle density, the pair density, the angular momentum, and the scaling of the wavefunction as multiple anyons coalesce. This work opens doors to understanding the macroscopic behavior of anyons, for which rich phases have been predicted theoretically.

title: Reinforcement learning to disentangle multiqubit quantum states from partial observations
abstract: Using partial knowledge of a quantum state to control multiqubit entanglement is a largely unexplored paradigm in the emerging field of quantum interactive dynamics with the potential to address outstanding challenges in quantum state preparation and compression, quantum control, and quantum complexity. We present a deep reinforcement learning (RL) approach using an actor-critic algorithm for constructing short disentangling circuits for states with up to 16 qubits. With access to only two-qubit reduced density matrices, our agent decides which pairs of qubits to apply two-qubit gates on; requiring only local information makes it directly applicable on modern NISQ devices, as we demonstrated experimentally on a trapped-ion quantum computer. Utilizing a permutation-equivariant transformer architecture, the agent can autonomously identify qubit permutations within the state, and adjusts the disentangling protocol accordingly. Once trained, it provides circuits from different initial states without further optimization. We demonstrate the agent's ability to identify and exploit the entanglement structure of multi-qubit states. We analyze the disentangling circuits constructed by the agent for 4- and 5-qubit Haar-random states, and observe strong correlations between consecutive gates and among the qubits involved. Through extensive benchmarking, we show the efficacy of the RL approach to find disentangling protocols with minimal gate resources. We explore the resilience of our trained agents to noise, highlighting their potential for real-world quantum computing applications. Analyzing optimal disentangling protocols, we report a general circuit to prepare an arbitrary 4-qubit state using at most 5 two-qubit (10 CNOT) gates.

title: Yapay Zekâ Destekli Kişiselleştirmenin Tüketici Davranışlarına Etkisi: Güven, Mahremiyet ve Şeffaflık Ekseninde Bir Değerlendirme
abstract: Yapay zekâ (YZ) teknolojilerinin pazarlama alanında giderek yaygınlaşması, işletmelerin tüketici verilerini analiz etme, tercihleri öngörme ve bireyselleştirilmiş pazarlama uygulamaları geliştirme kapasitesini önemli ölçüde artırmıştır. Bu dönüşümün en görünür sonuçlarından biri olan YZ destekli kişiselleştirme; tüketicilere daha ilgili, yararlı ve zamanında ürün, hizmet, içerik ve öneriler sunulmasına olanak sağlarken, aynı zamanda veri kullanımı, mahremiyet, gözetim, kontrol ve algoritmik karar süreçlerine ilişkin çeşitli kaygıları da beraberinde getirmektedir. Bu bölümün amacı, YZ destekli kişiselleştirmenin tüketici davranışları üzerindeki etkilerini güven, mahremiyet ve şeffaflık ekseninde bütüncül bir yaklaşımla değerlendirmektir. Bu doğrultuda ulusal ve uluslararası literatürden yararlanılarak YZ destekli kişiselleştirmenin kavramsal temelleri, veri toplama ve tüketici profilleme süreçleri, öneri sistemleri, kişiselleştirilmiş reklamlar, dinamik teklifler, chatbotlar ve hiper-kişiselleştirme uygulamaları ele alınmıştır. Literatür bulguları, kişiselleştirmenin algılanan ilgililik, fayda ve değer aracılığıyla müşteri deneyimi, etkileşim, satın alma niyeti, sadakat ve ilişkiyi sürdürme eğilimi üzerinde olumlu sonuçlar yaratabildiğini; ancak bu etkilerin her durumda doğrudan ve koşulsuz biçimde ortaya çıkmadığını göstermektedir. Aşırı veya açıklanması güç kişiselleştirme uygulamaları ise algılanan gözetim, müdahalecilik, ürkütücülük, kontrol kaybı, psikolojik tepkisellik ve algoritmik kaçınma gibi olumsuz tüketici tepkilerine yol açabilmektedir. Bu çerçevede güven, kişiselleştirmenin sunduğu yararlar ile veri kullanımından kaynaklanan risklerin davranışsal sonuçlara dönüşmesinde temel bir değerlendirme mekanizması olarak öne çıkarken; mahremiyet, tüketici verilerinin kullanım sınırlarını, şeffaflık ve açıklanabilirlik ise algoritmik süreçlerin anlaşılabilir ve sorgulanabilir olmasını belirlemektedir. Sonuç olarak YZ destekli kişiselleştirmenin sürdürülebilir başarısının yalnızca teknolojik doğruluk ve kişiselleştirme düzeyine değil, tüketicinin mahremiyetini, kontrol alanını ve karar özerkliğini koruyan güvenilir ve şeffaf uygulamaların geliştirilmesine bağlı olduğu değerlendirilmektedir.

title: ChatGPT Personal Agent: User-Controlled Persistent Memory and Cross-Device Continuity
abstract: The proposal introduces a dedicated memory space in which users explicitly decide what information is stored, updated, retained, or deleted. It also outlines an account-linked personal agent that can access authorized memory across supported devices, helping users resume their work without unnecessarily reconstructing previously preserved context. The document discusses the proposed architecture, user experience, privacy and security considerations, design principles, potential applications, and a phased implementation roadmap. This proposal is submitted for consideration as a potential future enhancement to ChatGPT. It is an independent proposal and does not represent an existing or announced OpenAI feature, nor does it imply endorsement or acceptance by OpenAI.

title: The Consciousness AI: A Biologically Grounded Architecture for Artificial Consciousness and Effective Information Measurement
abstract: The Consciousness AI (v1.6.0) Archival release of The Consciousness AI, a biologically grounded research architecture investigating synthetic awareness, emotional homeostasis, oscillatory binding, and causal emergence measurement. Architecture Highlights Sensory Tectum (models/core/sensory_tectum.py, models/audio/): Multisensory spatial integration layer modeled on the vertebrate optic tectum (superior colliculus). Stacks aligned retinotopic visual maps, a cochlear auditory pipeline (64-band Gammatone filterbank, inner hair cell transduction, tonotopic encoder, ITD/ILD spatial audio, and acoustic affect extraction), and somatosensory body projections fused by inverse effectiveness. Includes topographic spatial map binding (models/core/map_binding.py), rhythm binding (models/core/rhythm_binding.py), and tectal motor mapping (models/core/tectal_motor_map.py). Oscillatory Binding (models/core/): Selectable Kuramoto synchronization mechanisms including AKOrN (Artificial Kuramoto Oscillatory Neurons on an N-sphere) and KomplexNet (complex-valued phase-content coupling), alongside offline Brian2 spiking neural network validation (models/validation/). Global Neuronal Workspace and Capsule Hierarchy (models/core/global_workspace.py): Central broadcast bottleneck with sigmoid ignition, recurrent reverberation, 5 to 10 cycle reentrant predictive settling, and a 4-level dynamic-routing capsule hierarchy. Affective Core and Self-Model (models/emotion/, models/self_model/): Homeostatic interoceptive drives (energy, fatigue, damage) feeding a continuous Valence-Arousal-Dominance (PAD) field that modulates workspace bidding and ignition thresholds, paired with basal ganglia D1/D2/STN action selection and a self-prediction meta-representation vector. Consciousness and Emergence Instruments (models/evaluation/): Integrated Information ($\Phi$): Exact IIT 3.0 evaluation via pyphi over ConsciousnessGate state transitions, plus geometric proxy and RIIU SVD-residual estimators. Causal Emergence 2.0 (CE 2.0): SVD-based macroscale causation heuristic (Hoel 2025) across gate, workspace, and RSSM-latent levels, superseding deprecated discrete Effective Information (EI). Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI): Perturbation-response complexity measurement across workspace settling trajectories. Experimental Thermodynamic Substrate (models/thermodynamic/): Isolated probabilistic-bit (p-bit) emulation Checked against exact Boltzmann statistics, free-energy relaxation against closed-form posteriors, spike coding (rate, latency, phase), and Neuromorphic Intermediate Representation (NIR) export. Evaluation Environments (simulations/environments/): Dark Room (SimpleVisualEnv with audio and decoy configurations), Multi-Room Navigation, Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS), and Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (WCST), alongside a matched DQN baseline. Verification and Environment Record Test Suite: 2,057 passing tests on Python 3.12.10 (2,052 on Python 3.8.3). Documentation & Empirical Record: Full pre-registered predictions, negative and positive empirical findings (including the 9-run Phi-1 campaign and RSSM perception-collapse diagnostics), and indicator rubrics are archived under docs/. evidence.abstract: The Consciousness AI (v1.6.0) Archival release of The Consciousness AI, a biologically grounded research architecture investigating synthetic awareness, emotional homeostasis, oscillatory binding, and causal emergence measurement. Architecture Highlights Sensory Tectum (models/core/sensory_tectum.py, models/audio/): Multisensory spatial integration layer modeled on the vertebrate optic tectum (superior colliculus). Stacks aligned retinotopic visual maps, a cochlear auditory pipeline (64-band Gammatone filterbank, inner hair cell transduction, tonotopic encoder, ITD/ILD spatial audio, and acoustic affect extraction), and somatosensory body projections fused by inverse effectiveness. Includes topographic spatial map binding (models/core/map_binding.py), rhythm binding (models/core/rhythm_binding.py), and tectal motor mapping (models/core/tectal_motor_map.py). Oscillatory Binding (models/core/): Selectable Kuramoto synchronization mechanisms including AKOrN (Artificial Kuramoto Oscillatory Neurons on an N-sphere) and KomplexNet (complex-valued phase-content coupling), alongside offline Brian2 spiking neural network validation (models/validation/). Global Neuronal Workspace and Capsule Hierarchy (models/core/global_workspace.py): Central broadcast bottleneck with sigmoid ignition, recurrent reverberation, 5 to 10 cycle reentrant predictive settling, and a 4-level dynamic-routing capsule hierarchy. Affective Core and Self-Model (models/emotion/, models/self_model/): Homeostatic interoceptive drives (energy, fatigue, damage) feeding a continuous Valence-Arousal-Dominance (PAD) field that modulates workspace bidding and ignition thresholds, paired with basal ganglia D1/D2/STN action selection and a self-prediction meta-representation vector. Consciousness and Emergence Instruments (models/evaluation/): Integrated Information ($\Phi$): Exact IIT 3.0 evaluation via pyphi over ConsciousnessGate state transitions, plus geometric proxy and RIIU SVD-residual estimators. Causal Emergence 2.0 (CE 2.0): SVD-based macroscale causation heuristic (Hoel 2025) across gate, workspace, and RSSM-latent levels, superseding deprecated discrete Effective Information (EI). Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI): Perturbation-response complexity measurement across workspace settling trajectories. Experimental Thermodynamic Substrate (models/thermodynamic/): Isolated probabilistic-bit (p-bit) emulation Checked against exact Boltzmann statistics, free-energy relaxation against closed-form posteriors, spike coding (rate, latency, phase), and Neuromorphic Intermediate Representation (NIR) export. Evaluation Environments (simulations/environments/): Dark Room (SimpleVisualEnv with audio and decoy configurations), Multi-Room Navigation, Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS), and Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (WCST), alongside a matched DQN baseline. Verification and Environment Record Test Suite: 2,057 passing tests on Python 3.12.10 (2,052 on Python 3.8.3). Documentation & Empirical Record: Full pre-registered predictions, negative and positive empirical findings (including the 9-run Phi-1 campaign and RSSM perception-collapse diagnostics), and indicator rubrics are archived under docs/. title: DNS Privacy Leaking Mitigation and Energy Costs: Measuring the Impact of Adding Dummy Queries on Encrypted DNS Protocols
abstract: The Domain Name System (DNS) was originally designed without privacy mechanisms. Encrypted variants such as DNS over TLS (DoT), DNS over HTTPS (DoH), DNS over HTTP/3 ( (DoH/3)), and DNS over QUIC (DoQ) protect the content of the queries, but the resolver and any network observer with access to the traffic metadata can still profile the user. Client-side defenses counter this by adding dummy queries to the real DNS traffic of the device. On a smartphone, the battery cost of such a defense has not been characterized. We evaluate the energy cost of adding dummy queries on an unmodified Android device using the BatteryStats subsystem. Since the dummy queries must be sent over the protocols the device already uses, we measure this cost for the five DNS protocols in use (Do53, DoT, DoH, (DoH/3), and DoQ) and four public resolvers (Google DNS, Cloudflare, Quad9, and AdGuard DNS), at both the application and system-resolver levels. Our results show that the cost of the countermeasure depends on the protocol and resolver used, on the number of dummy queries added, and on their scheduling: sending them as a single burst rather than periodically reduces the energy cost for the same privacy gain.

title: Relation-aware dynamic knowledge subgraph enhanced large language models for medical multiple-choice question answering
abstract: Medical multiple-choice question answering requires models to simultaneously understand question semantics, candidate-answer differences, and structured relations among medical entities in complex clinical contexts. To address the limitations that existing knowledge-enhanced methods often adopt question-level unified modeling and thus struggle to characterize local relational differences among different candidate options, while conventional low-rank adaptation lacks relation-pattern adaptivity, this paper proposes a knowledge-enhanced large language model framework that combines option-level knowledge subgraph representation fusion with relation-aware dynamic LoRA adaptation. The proposed method first constructs a local medical knowledge subgraph for the question stem and each candidate answer separately, and then injects structured knowledge into candidate representations through a graph encoder and gated fusion mechanism. Subsequently, multiple learned LoRA expert branches are dynamically combined through candidate-conditioned routing based on the relational information encoded in the enhanced candidate representations, enabling the model to obtain more suitable parameter update paths. The experimental results are reported as the mean and standard deviation over three random-seed runs. On the MedQA dataset, the proposed method achieves Accuracy scores of 62.90%±0.82% and 62.84%±1.04%, together with F1-Score values of 62.97%±1.07% and 62.79%±0.78%, using Llama3 8B and Qwen 7B, respectively. On the MedMCQA dataset, the corresponding Accuracy scores are 61.04%±0.30% and 58.59%±0.65%, while the F1-Score values reach 61.21%±0.54% and 57.77%±0.57%, respectively. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively improve knowledge understanding, candidate discrimination, and reasoning stability in medical multiple-choice question answering.

title: Experimental Demonstration of a Balanced Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier
abstract: Superconducting travelling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) provide broadband gain, low added noise, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for applications requiring wide instantaneous bandwidth. This is crucial for amplifying multiplexed narrow band signals spread over a wide frequency range, such as qubit resonator arrays, or amplifying inherently wide band signals, such as in spectrometers or radiometers. In many cases, however, the useful bandwidth of a TWPA is limited by the production of the idler tone at an image frequency. For three-wave-mixing (3WM) TWPAs, for example, an input signal at f_s is indistinguishable from one at f_p - f_s, which can produce spectral ambiguity when the input spectrum is broadband or not known in advance. We experimentally demonstrate a balanced architecture that doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth available to a 3WM TWPA by spatially separating the amplified signal from the output pump and generated idler, which resolves the sideband degeneracy. The architecture consists of two amplifiers connected between a pair of 180^{circ} hybrid couplers, with the signal and pump injected and output through the sum and difference ports, respectively. Using two kinetic-inductance TWPAs, we demonstrate approximately 20 dB of signal gain across nearly an octave of bandwidth, together with pump rejection below --20 dB and an average image rejection of approximately --15 dB over the operating band. These results establish balanced TWPAs as a practical approach to broadband parametric amplification, enabling improved contamination free bandwidth and eliminating the need for complex filtering.

title: Fast construction of partitioned learned Bloom filter with theoretical guarantees
abstract: Abstract Bloom filter is a widely used classic data structure for approximate membership queries. Learned Bloom filters improve memory efficiency by leveraging machine learning, with the partitioned learned Bloom filter (PLBF) being among the most memory-efficient variants. However, PLBF suffers from high construction cost, with time complexity $$\mathcal {O}(N^3k)$$ O ( N 3 k ) , where N and k are hyperparameters. In this paper, we propose three methods, fast PLBF , fast PLBF++ , and fast PLBF# , that reduce the construction complexity to $$\mathcal {O}(N^2k)$$ O ( N 2 k ) , $$\mathcal {O}(Nk \log N)$$ O ( N k log N ) , and $$\mathcal {O}(Nk \log k)$$ O ( N k log k ) , respectively. Fast PLBF preserves the original PLBF structure and memory efficiency. Although fast PLBF++ and fast PLBF# may have different structures, we theoretically prove they are equivalent to PLBF under ideal data distribution. Furthermore, for non-ideal scenarios, we introduce an instance-specific measure of deviation from the ideal distribution and use it to bound the resulting difference in memory efficiency between PLBF and fast PLBF++. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that, under the default setting ( $$N=1000$$ N = 1000 and $$k=5$$ k = 5 ), fast PLBF, fast PLBF++, and fast PLBF# are up to 58.7, 74.5, and 75.7 times faster to construct than original PLBF, respectively. In an ablation with larger k , which enables the construction of more accurate PLBFs, the speedups reach 235, 865, and 871 times at $$k=50$$ k = 50 . Additionally, fast PLBF maintains the same data structure as PLBF, and fast PLBF++ and fast PLBF# achieve nearly identical memory efficiency.

title: Real-Time Earthquake Detection and Risk Classification using Machine Learning and Streamlit
abstract: Earthquakes pose a significant threat to human life and infrastructure worldwide, with approximately 500,000 detectable events occurring each year. Early detection and rapid risk assessment are critical for disaster mitigation and emergency response. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have shown great promise in automating earthquake detection. However, most existing systems are not deployed as real-time web applications accessible to the public. In this paper, we present a real-time earthquake detection and risk classification system that leverages live data from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) API. Our system employs a Random Forest classifier trained on four key features: magnitude, depth, latitude, and longitude. The model classifies each earthquake into three risk categories — HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW — with an associated confidence score and a risk score on a 0-100 scale. The system integrates live data streaming, interactive visualizations including world maps, magnitude distribution charts, and seismic waveform signals. Additionally, the application features country-wise filtering, depth and time range filters, satellite imagery, and an admin panel for data management. Experimental results demonstrate 100% classification accuracy on the test dataset, with magnitude identified as the most important feature. The system is publicly deployed as a web application, making it accessible for disaster monitoring and research applications. Future work includes integration of deep learning models for improved prediction accuracy and real-time alert broadcasting.

title: Data Optimization for LLMs: A Survey
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs' training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs' data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs' training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs' data properties. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs' data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

title: Expressivity of IQP Feature-Map Quantum Kernels via Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
abstract: Quantum kernels are among the most promising methods in quantum machine learning, providing a natural way to embed data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces via quantum circuits and capturing non-linear relationships in data. Their learning behaviour is governed by the function class they represent, which is formally characterized by the structure of the associated Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). However, a theoretical characterization of this function class, and of how it depends on the choice of feature map and its hyperparameters, is still lacking. In this work, we focus on the Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) feature map and derive a Fourier representation of the associated RKHS generators as finite sums of trigonometric functions evaluated on polynomially transformed input variables, with a finite set of accessible frequencies determined by the circuit construction and scaled by the bandwidth hyperparameter. This representation identifies three bandwidth regimes with qualitatively distinct expressive properties from localised, through multimodal, to periodic. Numerical experiments on synthetic datasets with controlled periodic and multimodal structure, across data dimensions and feature-map configurations, reproduce the three regimes in both supervised classification and unsupervised anomaly detection, benchmarked against a classical Gaussian kernel. These results make the relationship between expressivity and data structure explicit for IQP kernels: expressive power translates into a practical benefit only when the accessible frequencies match with the structure of the data, which provides a criterion for selecting the bandwidth when the periodic or multimodal structure of data is known.

title: Diseño y validación preliminar de un chatbot basado en inteligencia artificial para la gestión de requerimientos e incidencias estudiantiles en la facultad de ciencias económicas de la Universidad Nacional Federico Villarreal, 2025
abstract: El estudio tuvo como objetivo diseñar y validar preliminarmente un Chatbot basado en inteligencia artificial para apoyar la gestión de requerimientos e incidencias de los estudiantes de la Facultad de Ciencias Económicas de la Universidad Nacional Federico Villarreal durante 2025. La investigación se desarrolló desde un enfoque cualitativo, con alcance exploratorio y propositivo, mediante la metodología de investigación-acción participativa. La información se recopiló a través de un grupo focal con estudiantes, una entrevista semiestructurada al personal administrativo, observación de procesos, revisión documental, elaboración del mapa de experiencia del usuario y análisis FODA institucional. Asimismo, se diseñó un prototipo funcional y se realizó una validación preliminar con usuarios. Los resultados evidenciaron demoras en la atención de solicitudes, fragmentación de los canales de comunicación, limitada trazabilidad de los trámites, información institucional poco estandarizada y sobrecarga del personal administrativo. El mapa de experiencia permitió identificar como momentos críticos la búsqueda de información, el inicio de los trámites, la espera de respuestas y el seguimiento de las solicitudes. A partir de estos hallazgos, se estructuró un Chatbot con módulos destinados a consultas académicas, trámites administrativos, incidencias relacionadas con los sistemas institucionales y consulta del estado de los procedimientos. La validación preliminar mostró una percepción favorable respecto de su utilidad, claridad y facilidad de navegación. Se concluye que el Chatbot constituye una alternativa tecnológica viable para fortalecer la orientación estudiantil y contribuir a la digitalización de los servicios universitarios, siempre que su implementación incluya actualización permanente de contenidos, capacitación de los usuarios, integración con los procesos institucionales y mecanismos de seguimiento.

evidence.title: Diseño y validación preliminar de un chatbot basado en inteligencia artificial para la gestión de requerimientos e incidencias estudiantiles en la facultad de ciencias económicas de la Universidad Nacional Federico Villarreal, 2025
evidence.abstract: El estudio tuvo como objetivo diseñar y validar preliminarmente un Chatbot basado en inteligencia artificial para apoyar la gestión de requerimientos e incidencias de los estudiantes de la Facultad de Ciencias Económicas de la Universidad Nacional Federico Villarreal durante 2025. La investigación se desarrolló desde un enfoque cualitativo, con alcance exploratorio y propositivo, mediante la metodología de investigación-acción participativa. La información se recopiló a través de un grupo focal con estudiantes, una entrevista semiestructurada al personal administrativo, observación de procesos, revisión documental, elaboración del mapa de experiencia del usuario y análisis FODA institucional. Asimismo, se diseñó un prototipo funcional y se realizó una validación preliminar con usuarios. Los resultados evidenciaron demoras en la atención de solicitudes, fragmentación de los canales de comunicación, limitada trazabilidad de los trámites, información institucional poco estandarizada y sobrecarga del personal administrativo. El mapa de experiencia permitió identificar como momentos críticos la búsqueda de información, el inicio de los trámites, la espera de respuestas y el seguimiento de las solicitudes. A partir de estos hallazgos, se estructuró un Chatbot con módulos destinados a consultas académicas, trámites administrativos, incidencias relacionadas con los sistemas institucionales y consulta del estado de los procedimientos. La validación preliminar mostró una percepción favorable respecto de su utilidad, claridad y facilidad de navegación. Se concluye que el Chatbot constituye una alternativa tecnológica viable para fortalecer la orientación estudiantil y contribuir a la digitalización de los servicios universitarios, siempre que su implementación incluya actualización permanente de contenidos, capacitación de los usuarios, integración con los procesos institucionales y mecanismos de seguimiento.

title: Learning Persistent Referential Identity for Two-Hop Retrieval in Event-Stream Models
abstract: We learn compatible destination and owner views in bounded, transcript-free records. Structural source/type/version addressing selects the first relation; authoritative, requested-attribute filtering reduces ordinary candidates to a mean of 3.28. Learned matching selects the second record and retrieves its value. Three seeds of a 24.35-million-parameter multitask model achieve 1.0000 one-hop, identity, and two-hop accuracy on shared sealed confirmation rows. Relation and value erasures collapse accuracy; counterfactual replacements redirect answers. A separately preregistered extension reserves disjoint compositional names across training, development, and sealed confirmation while matching tokenization. After 512 unrelated writes, challenge identity and two-hop accuracy are 0.9990–1.0000 with 16 or 32 candidates; ordinary held-out-name two-hop accuracy is 0.9328–0.9567. Ordinary-only training also solves the original naming distribution, so explicit challenge examples are not necessary there. Cutting direct writer credit reduces challenge identity. Complete replay succeeds, unlike last-32-event replay. Earlier protected bindings fail two-hop retrieval; generic recurrence fails in its tested multitask regime but a semantic-only GRU acquires shorter-delay memory. A separate zero-shot name/tokenization shift remains unsuccessful. These results establish causally functional two-access memory and controlled compositional-name transfer, not unrestricted language understanding or general reasoning. Several other families remain near chance.

title: Entropy Estimation in Cluster Graphs
abstract: Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) provide a powerful framework for modelling complex systems, but inference over loopy graphs requires approximate methods whose accuracy depends on how factors are clustered in the graphical representation. Existing factor clustering methods rely on the number of variables in a cluster to bound its memory footprint, or on the maximal possible entropy as a proxy for how informative a merged cluster would be—both loose approximations that can lead to suboptimal merging decisions. We address this limitation by proposing an efficient algorithm for estimating the joint entropy of a group of clusters directly, without explicitly multiplying out the constituent factors, thereby avoiding the exponential computational cost that makes exact computation prohibitive. The algorithm integrates naturally with both static and dynamic graph restructuring methods, and reduces to a specific case of the Kikuchi entropy approximation when applied to the complete graph. Building on the entropy estimation algorithm, we further propose an algorithm for estimating the number of non-zero probabilities in a factor product, again without explicit multiplication. Experiments on models with up to 24 variables demonstrate that the algorithm produces accurate entropy estimates (when compared with ideal junction tree performance) across diverse model types, with errors remaining within tight bounds. Scalability is further validated on a substantially larger model defined over 2640 random variables. Our results confirm that accurate entropy estimation is achievable wherever reliable probabilistic inference is possible, and that the proposed estimation algorithm yields approximations objectively close to the true entropy values, thereby supporting improved clustering decisions in PGM structuring algorithms.

title: Practical continuous-variable quantum key distribution with squeezed light
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) has gathered significant interest for its potential to achieve high secret key rates and seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. State-of-the-art CV-QKD systems primarily use coherent states for simplicity. However, squeezed states of light have been theoretically shown to offer significant advantages, including higher secret key rates, greater resilience to excess noise, and reduced requirements on information reconciliation efficiency. In this work, we experimentally verify these theoretical predictions and propose and demonstrate a practical squeezed-state CV-QKD system based on modern local-local oscillator and digital signal processing techniques. Operating over fiber channels and considering finite-size security against collective attacks, we show the advantages of our system over its coherent-state counterpart. Our work paves the way for squeezed states to become practical resources for quantum key distribution and other quantum information protocols.

title: Uncompressed 16-bit stereo PCM over a ~2 Mb/s audio radio block: the top bits of every sample under two symmetric, sample-interleaved BCH codewords with detection parity inside them, bare low bits, one keyed tag over everything, partial play with a straight-line fill of the samples a failed codeword carried, and a BCH decoder with a root-dividing byte-stepped Chien search
abstract: Every sample's 16 bits go on air in time order, MSB first. The top 10 bits of every sample are protected; the low 6 bits are bare: in no codeword, not checked, not gathered anywhere. The protected bits are split between two shortened BCH(255, 207) codewords (m = 8, t = 6): codeword 0 covers the even-numbered samples of the block, codeword 1 the odd ones, both channels. Each codeword also covers the block descriptor and the keyed tag, and carries detection parity bits inside its data (4 and 3 bits: interleaved parity checks), so that every one of the 103 spare bits is used. One keyed tag covers the descriptor and the top bits of all samples. The receiver decodes both codewords every time. If both decode and pass their detection parity, the tag is checked and the block plays or is concealed whole. If exactly one fails, the block plays (unless the receiver is re-arming after a failure) with the failed codeword's samples, every other sample of the block, each filled by the straight line between its two neighbours of the same block (a hold at the block's edge). If both fail, the block is concealed whole. In a simulation over three recordings this kept 70.8 dB segmental SNR at a bit error rate of 10^-3 and turned the 10 whole-block dropouts a second of one long BCH code at 10^-2 into 0.9 plus about 670 filled samples a second, with no wrong top bits played. A BCH decoder whose Chien search divides each root out of the error locator as it finds it, steps each term with one byte-table read and solves the last two roots in closed form makes the worst correctable block 2.6 times cheaper, about 44 000 cycles on an emulated Cortex-M7. Defensive publication, placed in the public domain as prior art. License: CC BY 4.0.
